countries.name: Italy
countries.tagline: The world's biggest wine producer and its most stubbornly local one: twenty regions, hundreds of native grapes and 3,000 years of vintages.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Vine and Wine Sector in 2025 (published 2026): 726 kha of vineyard (4th in the world), 44.4 mhl of wine (1st, 19.7% of world output), consumption 20.2 mhl (3rd), exports 21.0 mhl and EUR 7.8 bn. Denominations: 79 DOCG and 332 DOC (411 DOP) per Italian Wine Central, Nov 2025; about 118 IGT (Federdoc 2024).

countries.overview:
Italy makes more wine than any other country, 44.4 million hectolitres in 2025 according to the OIV, about one bottle in five drunk on earth, and it does so in every one of its twenty regions, from Alpine terraces in Valle d'Aosta to the volcanic island of Pantelleria, closer to Tunisia than to Sicily. No other wine country is so long, so mountainous and so fragmented. The peninsula stretches about 1,200 km from the Alps to the Mediterranean, with the Apennines running down its spine, so almost every region has hills, sea air and altitude to play with. That geography, plus 2,500 years of political division into city-states, duchies, papal lands and kingdoms, left Italy with an astonishing number of native grape varieties and local wine traditions that never merged into a single national style.

The grapes are the first thing a wine lover notices. Where France built its reputation on a dozen international varieties, Italy grows hundreds of its own: Nebbiolo and Barbera in Piedmont, Corvina and Garganega in the Veneto, Sangiovese across the centre, Montepulciano along the Adriatic, Aglianico, Fiano and Greco in Campania and Basilicata, Primitivo and Negroamaro in Puglia, Nerello Mascalese and Nero d'Avola in Sicily, Cannonau and Vermentino in Sardinia. Many survived only because the regions that grew them were too poor to replant, and the rediscovery of forgotten grapes (Timorasso, Pecorino, Tintilia, Nascetta, Susumaniello) is one of the great stories of the last 40 years.

The second thing is the law, which tries to tie every wine to a place. Since 1963 Italy has built a pyramid of denominations: at the top 79 DOCGs, the 'controlled and guaranteed' appellations such as Barolo, Brunello di Montalcino and Taurasi, then 332 DOCs and about 118 IGTs, regional categories that gave the Super Tuscans and many modern classics their freedom. The newest layer is geographic detail inside appellations: Barolo's MGAs, Chianti Classico's UGAs, Vino Nobile's Pievi and Etna's contrade, all moves toward a Burgundian idea of named places.

Italy is also a land of contrasts in scale. The country leads the world in volume and exports by volume (21 million hectolitres in 2025), much of it Prosecco, Pinot Grigio and everyday reds from Veneto, Puglia, Sicily, Emilia-Romagna and Abruzzo. At the same time thousands of family growers make tiny quantities of wines that rank among the most sought-after on earth. Veneto, Puglia and Sicily together hold almost half the vineyard area; Piedmont and Tuscany carry much of the prestige.

The last thirty years have redrawn that map. The south, long dismissed as a tank-wine reservoir for the north and for France, has become the most exciting part of the country: Etna's volcanic contrade, Irpinia's Fiano and Taurasi, Puglia's old-vine Primitivo and Sardinia's mountain Cannonau now sell on name and place rather than colour and strength. Climate change is part of the story, pushing growers uphill in Chianti Classico and toward cooler, higher sites everywhere, and so is a generation of small family estates that bottle their own wine instead of selling grapes to cooperatives. Italy's domestic thirst is falling (consumption dropped 9.4% to 20.2 million hectolitres in 2025), which makes exports and quality ever more important.

Finally, Italy is where wine history is visible in the landscape. Greek colonists called the south Oenotria, the land of trained vines. Etruscans traded wine to Gaul, Romans planted vineyards inside Pompeii, and monks, Medici dukes, English merchants and post-war cooperatives all left marks you can still visit. This atlas maps them alongside the appellations.

history.title: Copper Age wine on Monte Kronio
history.text: Residues of tartaric acid in storage jars from a cave on Monte Kronio near Sciacca in Sicily, published in 2017, point to wine about 6,000 years ago, among the earliest evidence in Italy. Bronze Age grape seeds from Nuragic Sardinia (Sa Osa, about 1300 to 1100 BC) show cultivated vines on the islands long before the Greeks.

history.title: The Greeks name Oenotria
history.text: Greek colonists founded Pithekoussai on Ischia around 770 BC, then Cumae, Naxos in Sicily (734 BC), Sybaris and Kroton, and called the southern peninsula Oenotria, a name linked to the Oenotrian people and, in later tradition, to *oinotron*, the stake used to train vines. They spread the low bush-trained *alberello*, still the hallmark of southern Italian vineyards. Nestor's cup, found at Pithekoussai, carries one of the oldest Greek verses, about wine and desire.

history.title: Etruscan wine trade
history.text: The Etruscans of Tuscany and northern Lazio grew vines up trees (*vite maritata*) and shipped wine in amphorae to southern France, where Etruscan jars appear at sites such as Lattes before the Greek and Roman trade took over. Their banquet scenes in the painted tombs of Tarquinia show wine at the centre of aristocratic life.

history.title: Roman authors write the manual
history.text: Cato's *De Agri Cultura* (about 160 BC) gives instructions for vineyards and slave-run farms; Varro, Virgil and Columella (*De Re Rustica*, about AD 60 to 65, with detailed advice on yields, pruning and grape varieties) follow; Pliny the Elder's *Natural History* (AD 77) ranks the best wines, with Caecuban and Falernian at the top. Falernian of the Opimian vintage (121 BC) was still being served decades later. By AD 92 Italy was so overplanted that Emperor Domitian banned new vineyards in Italy and ordered half those in the provinces uprooted, an edict never fully enforced.

history.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
history.text: The eruption of 24 August (or October) AD 79 sealed Pompeii, a wine town with vineyards inside its walls, taverns with price lists and amphorae from across the Mediterranean. Pliny the Elder died at Stabiae during the rescue. Since the 1990s Mastroberardino and the archaeological park have replanted vines in the excavated plots.

history.title: Cosimo III's bando
history.text: Grand Duke Cosimo III de' Medici issued a proclamation defining the boundaries of Chianti, Pomino, Carmignano and the Val d'Arno di Sopra and banning other wines from using their names, with a commission to enforce it. It is one of the first legal delimitations of wine zones in Europe. The name itself was older: in 1398 the Florentine notary Ser Lapo Mazzei recorded a purchase of 'Chianti' wine, then a white, and the Antinori family had joined Florence's wine merchants' guild in 1385.

history.title: John Woodhouse creates Marsala
history.text: The Liverpool merchant John Woodhouse shipped fortified wine from the Sicilian port of Marsala to England, launching an industry that Benjamin Ingham (from 1806) and Vincenzo Florio (from 1833) built into one of Italy's first international wine brands.

history.title: Ricasoli's Chianti recipe
history.text: In a letter of 26 September 1872 to Professor Cesare Studiati, Baron Bettino Ricasoli, at Brolio, described the blend he had settled on: Sangioveto for aroma and vigour, Canaiolo to soften it, and Malvasia only for wines meant for early drinking. A loose reading of this letter became the 20th-century Chianti formula, including the white grapes that later drove producers out of the DOC.

history.title: Phylloxera arrives
history.text: The root louse was identified in Lombardy in 1879 and in Sicily by 1880, and over the next decades destroyed most Italian vineyards. Replanting on American rootstocks changed the varietal map; volcanic and sandy soils (Etna, Pantelleria, the Campi Flegrei, the sands of the Sulcis) still hold ungrafted vines.

history.title: Brunello is born
history.text: Ferruccio Biondi-Santi bottled a pure Sangiovese Brunello di Montalcino from the 1888 vintage, intended for long ageing; the 1888 and 1891 Riservas became the founding bottles of Italy's most famous single-variety red.

history.title: The DOC law and the first DOCGs
history.text: Presidential Decree 930 of 12 July 1963 created the Denominazione di Origine Controllata system, building on a first 1924 law protecting 'typical' wines. Vernaccia di San Gimignano was the first wine recognised, in 1966. In 1980 the top tier arrived: Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, Barolo and Barbaresco became the first DOCGs, with tasting panels and numbered government seals on every bottle.

history.title: The Super Tuscan revolt
history.text: Sassicaia's 1968 vintage (released 1971) and Antinori's Tignanello (1971) broke the rules, Cabernet in one, barriques and no white grapes in the other, and were sold as humble *vino da tavola* while commanding the highest prices in Italy. They forced the law to change.

history.title: The methanol scandal
history.text: Wine cut with methanol by a few producers, notably the Ciravegna firm of Narzole in Piedmont, killed at least 19 people and blinded more than 20. Exports collapsed, and the government created a national anti-fraud inspectorate. The shock pushed Italy decisively from volume toward quality.

history.title: The Goria law, IGT and the Testo Unico
history.text: Law 164/1992, named after agriculture minister Giovanni Goria, created the IGT category and tightened DOC rules, giving Super Tuscans and many modern wines a legal home; Bolgheri gained a red DOC in 1994. The consolidated wine law of 2016 (Testo Unico, Law 238/2016) aligned the categories with EU PDO and PGI rules and formally recognised additional geographical units (UGA, MeGA, contrade, Pievi) inside appellations.

history.title: Place names and new DOCGs
history.text: Chianti Classico approved 11 UGAs in 2021 (in the rules from 2023), Vino Nobile di Montepulciano approved 12 Pievi in 2023 (first vintage 2021, released 2025), and in 2025 Cirò Classico in Calabria and Casauria in Abruzzo became DOCGs, bringing the national total to 79. Etna's DOCG application was still pending in October 2026.

countries.classification:
Italian wine law is a pyramid aligned since 2009 with the EU's PDO and PGI categories.

*DOCG* (Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, 79 as of November 2025) is the top tier: stricter yields and ageing, chemical and tasting approval of every lot by an official commission, and a numbered government strip (*fascetta*) on the bottle neck. Under the 2016 Testo Unico (Law 238/2016) a wine must normally have been a DOC for several years before promotion. The first four DOCGs (1980) were Barolo, Barbaresco, Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano; the newest (2025) are Cirò Classico and Casauria.

*DOC* (332) defines the zone, grapes, yields, minimum alcohol and ageing for each wine. Together DOCG and DOC make up the 411 Italian DOPs (the EU's PDO). *IGT* (Indicazione Geografica Tipica, about 118, the EU's PGI or IGP) covers larger areas (Toscana, Terre Siciliane, Puglia) with looser rules, and gave the Super Tuscans their freedom. *Vino* (formerly vino da tavola) is the basic level; it may now show grape and vintage as *Vino Varietale* for a few international varieties.

The *menzioni* are the words that add meaning on a label. *Classico* marks the historic heart of a zone (Chianti Classico, Soave Classico, Valpolicella Classico). *Superiore* means higher minimum alcohol, sometimes lower yields or longer ageing. *Riserva* means extra ageing, set by each appellation (two years for Chianti, five for Brunello). *Gran Selezione* is Chianti Classico's top tier (since 2014). *Vigna* followed by a name indicates a single registered vineyard. *Passito* (dried grapes), *Vendemmia Tardiva* (late harvest), *Recioto*, *Amarone*, *Vin Santo* and *Liquoroso* describe styles.

The most important recent trend is the official naming of places inside appellations: *menzioni geografiche aggiuntive* (MeGA) in Barolo and Barbaresco, *unità geografiche aggiuntive* (UGA) in Chianti Classico, Pievi in Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, contrade on Etna, and subzones in Abruzzo, Verdicchio and many others.
countries.climate_soils:
Italy's vineyards span about ten degrees of latitude, from roughly 47°N in Alto Adige to 36.7°N on Pantelleria, and almost every wine region is shaped by two things: mountains and sea. The Alps shield the north from cold northern air, while their foothills and lakes give cool, continental sites (Valtellina, Alto Adige, Franciacorta, Langhe). The Apennines run the length of the peninsula, so even in the hot south many vineyards sit at 400 to 1,000 m (Irpinia, Vulture, the Abruzzo hills), with big day-night temperature swings that keep acidity. On the peninsula the sea is always close, and its breezes moderate both the Tyrrhenian and Adriatic coasts.

The climate runs from continental in the Po valley (cold winters, hot humid summers, autumn fog) to Mediterranean in the centre and south (mild wet winters, long dry summers). Climate change is pushing harvests earlier and vineyards higher; altitude has become a selling point from Chianti Classico to Etna.

Soils are as varied as anywhere in Europe. Calcareous marls and clays dominate the Langhe and much of central Italy (galestro and alberese in Tuscany); morainic gravels sit around the Alpine lakes; alluvial gravel and sand in Bolgheri and the Friulian plains. Volcanoes are an Italian speciality: Etna, Vesuvius, the Campi Flegrei, Vulture, the Alban Hills, the Vulsini around Lake Bolsena, Soave's basalts, and the islands of Ischia, Pantelleria and the Aeolians, all giving mineral-rich, often ungrafted vineyards and wines with a saline, smoky edge.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.note: Italy's most planted red, the grape of Chianti, Brunello, Vino Nobile and Morellino, also widely grown in Romagna, Umbria and the Marche.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.note: The red of the Adriatic, from the Marche (Cònero) to Abruzzo and Molise; dark, soft and generous.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.note: The noble, pale, tannic red of Barolo, Barbaresco, Roero, Gattinara and Valtellina.

grapes.name: Barbera
grapes.note: Piedmont's high-acid everyday red, also important in Lombardy and Emilia.

grapes.name: Primitivo
grapes.note: Puglia's early-ripening red, identical to Zinfandel and Croatia's Tribidrag.

grapes.name: Nero d'Avola
grapes.note: Sicily's flagship red, also called Calabrese.

grapes.name: Aglianico
grapes.note: The structured, long-lived red of Taurasi and Aglianico del Vulture.

grapes.name: Negroamaro
grapes.note: The dark, bitter-edged red of the Salento.

grapes.name: Nerello Mascalese
grapes.note: Etna's pale, perfumed, Nebbiolo-like red.

grapes.name: Corvina
grapes.note: Main grape of Valpolicella and Amarone.

grapes.name: Cannonau
grapes.note: Sardinia's Grenache.

grapes.name: Glera
grapes.note: The grape of Prosecco, one of the most planted varieties in Italy by volume.

grapes.name: Pinot Grigio
grapes.note: The north-east's export white, Italy's best-known varietal wine abroad.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Toscano
grapes.note: Widely planted neutral white, the base of many central Italian whites and Vin Santo.

grapes.name: Catarratto
grapes.note: Sicily's most planted white, used in Marsala and island blends.

grapes.name: Garganega
grapes.note: The white of Soave and Gambellara.

grapes.name: Verdicchio
grapes.note: The Marche's age-worthy white, genetically the same as Trebbiano di Soave and Lugana.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.note: Campania's great white, also grown in Puglia, Sicily and Basilicata.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.note: Coastal white of Sardinia, Liguria (Pigato) and the Tuscan coast.

grapes.name: Moscato Bianco
grapes.note: Muscat à petits grains, base of Asti and Moscato d'Asti and many southern sweet wines.

grapes.name: Lambrusco
grapes.note: A family of red grapes for Emilia's frothy reds.

regions.name: Tuscany
regions.tagline: Sangiovese country: cypress ridges, Medici decrees and the Super Tuscan rebellion, all in one province of hills.
regions.summary:
Tuscany is where Italian wine learned to write its own rules and then to break them. Some 53,000 hectares of wine grapes (a 2025 Censis study based on ISTAT data) spread from the Apennine foothills above Florence to the Etruscan coast, but one grape, Sangiovese, ties nearly all of it together. It is the backbone of Chianti and Chianti Classico, the whole of Brunello di Montalcino, the core of Vino Nobile di Montepulciano and Morellino di Scansano, and a partner in Carmignano and Montecucco.

The region holds 11 DOCGs and 41 DOCs, more prestige per hectare than almost anywhere in Italy. The inland heart is a chain of Sangiovese hills (Chianti Classico between Florence and Siena, Montalcino and Montepulciano to the south). The coast tells a different story: at Bolgheri a marquis planted Cabernet in 1944, and the wine he made, Sassicaia, upended the idea that only native grapes and old laws could make great Italian wine. Between the two sits the Maremma, once malarial marshland and now Tuscany's frontier.

Tuscany also gave Europe one of its first legally defined wine zones: Cosimo III de' Medici's 1716 bando named Chianti, Pomino, Carmignano and the Val d'Arno di Sopra and threatened penalties for anyone who passed off other wine under those names.
regions.history:
Etruscans grew vines here long before Rome, training them up trees (the *vite maritata* that survived on Tuscan farms into the 20th century). Medieval Florence's merchant families, the Antinori from 1385 and the Frescobaldi from the 14th century, built fortunes partly on wine. In 1716 Cosimo III issued the edict delimiting Chianti and three other zones, and created a congregation to police the trade. In the 1870s Baron Bettino Ricasoli, at Brolio, set down the Sangiovese-led blend that became the template for Chianti, and in Montalcino the Biondi-Santi family began bottling pure Sangiovese as Brunello.

The 20th century was rougher. Phylloxera, two wars and the end of the *mezzadria* sharecropping system in the 1960s left Chianti producing oceans of thin wine in straw-covered fiaschi. The DOC laws of 1963 to 1967 froze a recipe that required white grapes in red Chianti. Ambitious producers walked away: Sassicaia (1968 vintage, released 1971) and Antinori's Tignanello (1971) were sold as humble *vino da tavola* and became the most famous Italian wines in the world. The rules eventually followed them: Chianti became DOCG in 1984, Chianti Classico separated in 1996, white grapes were banned from Chianti Classico from 2006, Bolgheri got its own red DOC in 1994, and Chianti Classico's Gran Selezione (2014) and 11 UGA village names (approved 2021, in the rules 2023) mark the latest turn toward place over brand.
regions.terroir:
Tuscany is mostly hills, and the hill is the unit that matters. Inland, the Chianti Classico zone sits on a jumble of Apennine sediments: *galestro*, a flaky, friable schistous clay that shatters in the hand and drains fast, gives perfumed, taut Sangiovese; *alberese*, a hard, pale limestone-marl, gives power and structure; sandstone (*macigno*) in the north and west gives lighter, aromatic wines; the Pliocene marine sands and clays south of Siena and around Montepulciano give rounder fruit. Altitude runs from about 200 m to the 700 m legal ceiling of Chianti Classico, and with warming summers the high, cool sites around Radda, Lamole and Gaiole have gained prestige.

Montalcino is a single isolated hill (to 661 m) with very different flanks: cooler, galestro-rich north slopes near the town, warmer clay and sand to the south near Sant'Angelo in Colle and Castelnuovo dell'Abate, all sheltered from storms by Monte Amiata. On the coast, Bolgheri's amphitheatre of alluvial gravel, clay and sand faces the sea, ripening Cabernet and Merlot under sea breezes, while the Maremma's warm, drier hills give riper, earlier Sangiovese (Morellino) and plenty of international blends.
regions.grapes: Sangiovese dominates (in Montalcino the local biotype is called Brunello, at Montepulciano Prugnolo Gentile, in Scansano Morellino). Traditional partners are Canaiolo Nero, Colorino, Mammolo, Ciliegiolo and Malvasia Nera; the 2027 Gran Selezione rules list a handful of these as the only permitted blenders. Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Syrah are central on the coast (Bolgheri, Suvereto, Val di Cornia) and appear in many IGT Toscana wines. Whites are a minority: Vernaccia di San Gimignano, Vermentino on the coast, Trebbiano Toscano and Malvasia Bianca Lunga (the classic Vin Santo grapes), Ansonica on the islands and Argentario, and Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco at Pomino. Aleatico makes the sweet red passito of Elba.
regions.styles: Mostly dry red, from bright, cherry-scented Chianti to long-lived Brunello and Gran Selezione. The coast makes Bordeaux-style blends and varietal Cabernet Franc and Merlot (Masseto, Paleo, Messorio). Whites range from saline Vernaccia to Vermentino. Vin Santo, made from grapes dried on mats or hung from rafters and aged for years in small sealed *caratelli*, is the region's sweet tradition; Occhio di Pernice is its rare red-grape version. Rosé is growing: the Chianti DOCG added a rosato in its 2026 rules.
regions.classification: Tuscany runs on DOCG, DOC and IGT (IGT Toscana, Costa Toscana and others give freedom to Super Tuscans). Chianti Classico has a three-tier pyramid: Annata, Riserva (24 months) and Gran Selezione (30 months, estate grapes only, minimum 90% Sangiovese from the 2027 vintage with international grapes banned). Gran Selezione can name one of 11 UGAs (*unità geografiche aggiuntive*), all approved together and in the rules since July 2023: Castellina, Castelnuovo Berardenga, Gaiole, Greve, Lamole, Montefioralle, Panzano, Radda, San Casciano, San Donato in Poggio and Vagliagli. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano has 12 Pievi (UGAs, approved 2023, published 2024) for an 85% Sangiovese estate-grown tier, first vintage 2021. Brunello di Montalcino has no official subzones; producers informally talk about north, south, east and west slopes and the hamlets of Castelnuovo dell'Abate, Sant'Angelo in Colle, Tavernelle, Camigliano, Torrenieri and Castelgiocondo. Chianti has eight subzones (Terre di Vinci added in 2026). Bolgheri Sassicaia is a DOC for a single estate.

regions.name: Umbria
regions.tagline: Italy's green, landlocked heart: the most tannic grape on earth, a white from tufa caves and a wine museum built by one family.
regions.summary:
Umbria is the only peninsular Italian region without a coast or a foreign border, a land of Franciscan hill towns, oak woods and the Tiber valley. It is small in wine terms (roughly 12,000 ha), but it holds two DOCGs and 13 DOCs and two wines with real personality: Sagrantino di Montefalco, a red so tannic that it was traditionally made sweet, and Orvieto, a white from the tufa cliff city that popes and painters drank for centuries.

The modern map was drawn by a few families. Giorgio Lungarotti turned Torgiano into a DOC in 1968 and a DOCG in 1990 and, with his wife Maria Grazia, opened one of Europe's finest wine museums. Arnaldo Caprai and his son Marco rescued Sagrantino from near-extinction in the 1970s and 1980s. Antinori's Castello della Sala showed in the 1980s that Orvieto's clay hills could also make world-class Chardonnay (Cervaro della Sala).
regions.history: Etruscans dug cellars into the volcanic tufa under Orvieto, and Roman writers praised the wines of the Tiber valley. Pliny the Elder mentions an *itriola* grape around Mevania (Bevagna), sometimes linked, without proof, to Sagrantino; the more likely story is that Franciscan friars brought the grape for sacramental passito. Orvieto's sweet *abboccato* white was favoured by popes, and the painter Luca Signorelli asked in his 1499 contract for the Orvieto cathedral frescoes to be paid partly in wine. Phylloxera and mezzadria collapse emptied the countryside in the 20th century; the DOCs (Torgiano 1968, Orvieto 1971, Montefalco 1979) and then the Sagrantino DOCG (1992) rebuilt the industry around quality.
regions.terroir: Umbria's vineyards lie mostly on hills of 200 to 500 m. Around Montefalco and Bevagna, clay and calcareous marl with sand give power to Sagrantino. Orvieto mixes volcanic tufa and ash from the Vulsini volcanoes (Lake Bolsena) with marine clays and sands; autumn fogs rising from the Paglia river and Lake Corbara encourage noble rot. Lake Trasimeno moderates the northwest, and the upper Tiber valley (Colli Altotiberini) is cool and continental.
regions.grapes: Sagrantino (red, extremely tannic, local to Montefalco), Sangiovese (the workhorse red), Grechetto (two biotypes: Grechetto di Orvieto and Grechetto di Todi, the latter genetically Pignoletto), Trebbiano Toscano (here called Procanico), Trebbiano Spoletino (a distinct, high-acid local white revived around Spoleto and Montefalco), Ciliegiolo, and the Trasimeno 'Gamay', which is actually Grenache.
regions.styles: Powerful dry Sagrantino and its rare sweet passito; Montefalco Rosso (Sangiovese with Sagrantino); Orvieto from dry (secco) to sweet (abboccato, amabile) and botrytised Muffa Nobile; fresh Grechetto; mineral, age-worthy Trebbiano Spoletino; Torgiano's Sangiovese-based Riserva.
regions.classification: Two DOCGs (Montefalco Sagrantino, Torgiano Rosso Riserva), 13 DOCs, six IGTs (Umbria IGT is widely used for Super-Umbrian blends such as Cervaro della Sala). Orvieto has a Classico core and a sweet Muffa Nobile category; Spoleto and Todi are recent DOCs (2011, 2010) built around single local whites.

regions.name: Marche
regions.tagline: Verdicchio country: comb-like river valleys running to the Adriatic, a white that ages like Riesling and a red sparkling wine made three times.
regions.summary:
Marche runs down the Adriatic between Romagna and Abruzzo, a region of parallel river valleys that cut from the Apennines to the sea like the teeth of a comb. It has about 17,000 ha of vines, five DOCGs and 15 DOCs. Its signature is Verdicchio, a white grape that for decades was sold in a fish-shaped amphora bottle and is now recognised as one of Italy's greatest and longest-lived whites, from two zones: the Castelli di Jesi hills near the coast and the inland valley of Matelica.

The reds are mostly Montepulciano, the same grape as Abruzzo's, at its best on the limestone promontory of Monte Conero, plus Sangiovese blends in Rosso Piceno. The south, around Offida and Ascoli Piceno, rescued two near-extinct whites, Pecorino and Passerina, in the 1980s. And there are two oddities a nerd should know: Lacrima di Morro d'Alba, an intensely rose-scented red, and Vernaccia di Serrapetrona, a red sparkling wine made with three fermentations.
regions.history: The Piceni people and then Greek traders from Syracuse (who founded Ancona around 387 BC) and Romans grew vines here. Pliny and other Roman writers praised the wines of Picenum. The name Verdicchio is documented from the 16th century (from *verde*, for the green tint of grape and wine). In 1953 the Fazi Battaglia winery launched a green amphora-shaped bottle designed by the architect Antonio Maiocchi, and it carried Verdicchio around the world as a cheerful fish-restaurant white. The quality turn came from the 1980s, when growers such as Bucci, Garofoli and Umani Ronchi showed that Verdicchio from old vines, aged longer, could rival great whites anywhere. The Riserva levels of both Verdicchio zones became DOCGs in 2010.
regions.terroir: Vineyards climb the hills between the sea and the Apennines on calcareous clays, marls and sandstones. The Castelli di Jesi zone follows the Esino river valley west of Ancona at 200 to 500 m, with sea breezes. Matelica is the only Marche valley that runs north to south, closed off from the sea, so it is more continental, with colder nights and higher acidity. Monte Conero is a block of white limestone rising 572 m straight out of the Adriatic. The south (Offida, Piceno) is warmer and rolls toward Abruzzo.
regions.grapes: Verdicchio (white, genetically the same as Trebbiano di Soave and Trebbiano di Lugana), Montepulciano, Sangiovese, Pecorino, Passerina, Lacrima, Vernaccia Nera, Biancame (Bianchello), Maceratino (Ribona), Aleatico (called Vernaccia di Pergola locally).
regions.styles: Dry Verdicchio from fresh to deep, mineral Riserva, plus sparkling and passito versions; Montepulciano-based reds (Rosso Cònero, Cònero Riserva, Rosso Piceno, Offida Rosso); aromatic Lacrima; Pecorino and Passerina whites; red sparkling Vernaccia di Serrapetrona.
regions.classification: Five DOCGs (Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva, Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva, Cònero, Offida, Vernaccia di Serrapetrona) and 15 DOCs. Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi has a Classico area and 99 recognised place names (*menzioni geografiche aggiuntive*) plus commune names that can appear on labels, one of the most detailed geographic systems in central Italy.

regions.name: Lazio
regions.tagline: Rome's own vineyards: volcanic hills, papal whites, a medieval bishop's 'Est!' and a native red finally getting respect.
regions.summary:
Lazio is the region of Rome, and for 2,000 years its wine was simply what Rome drank. The Castelli Romani, the volcanic Alban Hills southeast of the city, supplied the capital's taverns with Frascati and Marino; the tufa country around Lake Bolsena to the north made Est! Est!! Est!!! and Aleatico; and the Ciociaria hills to the southeast grew Cesanese, a red grape that stayed local for centuries. Roughly 18,000 to 20,000 ha of vines, 3 DOCGs and 27 DOCs.

Mass production in the 1970s and 1980s gave Frascati a reputation for thin, cheap wine. A new generation has worked hard to change that, with Frascati Superiore and Cannellino becoming DOCGs in 2011, Cesanese del Piglio a DOCG since 2008, and natural-leaning growers around Olevano Romano and Affile showing what Cesanese can do.
regions.history: Etruscans farmed vines north of the Tiber, and Rome's own hinterland was planted intensively in the Republic and Empire, with wine shipped up the Tiber to warehouses at Testaccio, where the Monte Testaccio hill is made of some 53 million broken amphorae (mostly olive oil, but evidence of the scale of Roman trade). Popes and Roman princes built summer villas in Frascati and kept vineyards; the Est! Est!! Est!!! legend dates to a German prelate travelling to Rome in 1111. The first DOCs came early (Frascati and Est! Est!! Est!!! in 1966), but the 20th century was dominated by cooperatives and volume, until a quality revival from the 1990s.
regions.terroir: Volcanic soils dominate: the Alban Hills (Colli Albani) volcano southeast of Rome, the Vulsini around Lake Bolsena, the Cimini and Sabatini volcanoes, all leaving potassium-rich tufa, ash and lapilli that give whites a mineral, savoury edge. The Ciociaria (Piglio, Olevano, Affile) has red clay and limestone on Apennine foothills at 300 to 700 m. The coast around Latina and the reclaimed Pontine Marshes (Aprilia, Circeo, Nettuno) is flat and warm.
regions.grapes: Malvasia Bianca di Candia and Malvasia del Lazio (Malvasia Puntinata, the finer local one), Trebbiano, Bellone, Bombino Bianco, Greco; Cesanese (di Affile and Comune), Montepulciano, Sangiovese, Nero Buono, Aleatico, plus Merlot and Cabernet on the coast and around Lake Bolsena.
regions.styles: Dry and sweet volcanic whites (Frascati, Marino, Est! Est!! Est!!!), Cesanese reds from light to structured, sweet Aleatico, and some international blends (Falesco's Montiano Merlot, Fiorano's historic Cabernet-Merlot).
regions.classification: Three DOCGs (Frascati Superiore, Cannellino di Frascati, Cesanese del Piglio), 27 DOCs (one shared with Umbria: Orvieto) and six IGTs. The Castelli Romani DOCs overlap heavily: Frascati, Marino, Colli Albani, Colli Lanuvini, Velletri, Zagarolo, Montecompatri Colonna and the umbrella Castelli Romani DOC. The Roma DOC (2011) covers the province of Rome.

regions.name: Abruzzo
regions.tagline: Montepulciano between the Gran Sasso and the sea: generous everyday red, a deep cherry rosé and two cult winemakers who made Trebbiano legendary.
regions.summary:
Abruzzo is half mountain: the Gran Sasso (2,912 m) and Maiella massifs rise less than 50 km from the Adriatic beaches. Vineyards cling to the hills between them, mostly trained on the high pergola called *tendone*, and the region (about 32,000 ha of vines) is one of Italy's largest producers. Most of it is the Montepulciano grape (no relation to the Tuscan town), which makes Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, one of the most exported red DOCs in Italy: dark, soft, juicy and cheap at the bottom, dense and long-lived at the top.

Abruzzo also makes Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo, a dark cherry-coloured rosé from the same grape, and Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, usually simple but in the hands of two legendary families, Valentini and Emidio Pepe, among Italy's most profound and long-lived whites. The province of Chieti makes the bulk of the wine, largely through cooperatives; the province of Teramo in the north has the Colline Teramane DOCG.
regions.history: Vines here date at least to the Italic tribes (Marrucini, Vestini, Frentani) and the Romans; Polybius wrote that Hannibal bathed his horses in Abruzzo wine to cure them after crossing the Apennines. Montepulciano was recorded in the region by the late 18th century. The DOCs came in 1968 (Montepulciano d'Abruzzo) and 1972 (Trebbiano d'Abruzzo). In the 1960s and 1970s Edoardo Valentini and Emidio Pepe, working with traditional methods, built the reputations that still define Abruzzo for collectors. The Colline Teramane DOCG followed in 2003, Tullum (Terre Tollesi) in 2019, and Casauria in 2025. A 2023 reform added provincial subzones to the four regional DOCs.
regions.terroir: The hills run from the sea up to about 600 m (700 m on south-facing slopes for Montepulciano). Soils are mostly calcareous clay and marl, with sand and gravel near rivers. Mountain air pours down at night, giving freshness even in hot summers. Inland, the Tirino valley around Ofena, called 'the oven of Abruzzo' for its heat by day, has cold nights from the Gran Sasso.
regions.grapes: Montepulciano (red; Cerasuolo is its rosé), Trebbiano Abruzzese (a distinct local variety, often confused with Bombino Bianco and Trebbiano Toscano, which are also planted), Pecorino, Passerina, Cococciola, Montonico.
regions.styles: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo from easy to powerful Riserva, deep rosé Cerasuolo, Trebbiano from neutral to great, Pecorino and other aromatic whites.
regions.classification: Three DOCGs (Colline Teramane Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, Terre Tollesi/Tullum, Casauria) and seven DOCs. Since the 2023 reform the four regional DOCs (Abruzzo, Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo) have provincial subzones (Colline Pescaresi, Colline Teramane, Terre di Chieti, Terre Aquilane), and only subzone wines may be called Superiore or Riserva. Montepulciano d'Abruzzo also keeps older subzones: Alto Tirino, Teate, Terre dei Peligni, Terre dei Vestini and San Martino sulla Marrucina.

regions.name: Molise
regions.tagline: Italy's forgotten region and its one native red, Tintilia, saved from extinction in the mountains.
regions.summary: Molise was part of Abruzzo until 1963, and in wine terms it still lives in its neighbour's shadow: around 5,000 ha of vines, mostly Montepulciano and Trebbiano for cooperatives, four DOCs and no DOCG. What makes it interesting is Tintilia, a red grape found only here, grown at altitude in the inland hills around Campobasso and Isernia. Abandoned in the 20th century for higher-yielding varieties, it was rescued in the 1990s and 2000s and got its own DOC in 2011.
regions.history: The Samnites, Rome's fierce rivals, lived in these mountains, and Roman sources mention wine from the Biferno valley. Molise's modern wine history begins with Di Majo Norante at Campomarino on the coast, which bottled quality wine from the 1960s and 1970s, and with the Tintilia revival led by a handful of growers and the University of Molise. The name Tintilia probably comes from Spanish *tinto*, from the Bourbon era, but DNA shows the grape is unique.
regions.terroir: Mountains cover most of the region; vineyards run from the Adriatic coast around Campomarino and Termoli up the Biferno and Trigno valleys to 600 to 800 m inland. Tintilia does best in cooler, higher clay and limestone sites with big day-night swings.
regions.grapes: Tintilia, Montepulciano, Aglianico, Trebbiano, Falanghina, Malvasia.
regions.styles: Montepulciano and Aglianico reds, fresh whites, and Tintilia red and rosé.
regions.classification: Four DOCs (Biferno, Molise, Pentro di Isernia, Tintilia del Molise) and two IGTs; no DOCG.

regions.name: Campania
regions.tagline: Volcanoes, Greek grapes and Roman legends: the land of Falernian, Taurasi and the vineyards inside Pompeii.
regions.summary:
The Romans called it *Campania felix*, the happy countryside, and for them it was the greatest wine country in the world: Falernian from the slopes of Monte Massico was the most famous wine of antiquity, and Pompeii was a wine town with vineyards inside its walls. Modern Campania has more than 20,000 ha of vines, four DOCGs and 15 DOCs, and a stock of ancient native grapes that survived because the region was too poor to replant with anything else.

The inland hills of Irpinia, around Avellino, are the heart of fine wine: Taurasi, one of Italy's great Aglianico reds, and two exceptional whites, Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo. The Sannio, around Benevento, is the land of Falanghina and Aglianico del Taburno. Along the coast, volcanic soils rule: Vesuvius and its Lacryma Christi, the Campi Flegrei craters west of Naples, the islands of Ischia and Capri, and the terraced cliffs of the Amalfi coast. Much of this is ungrafted: phylloxera cannot survive in loose volcanic sand.
regions.history: Greek colonists founded Pithekoussai on Ischia around 770 BC (where the 'Nestor's cup', inscribed with one of the oldest Greek verses, was found) and Cumae soon after, bringing vines whose descendants may include Greco and Aglianico (the latter name once wrongly traced to *Hellenico*). Roman Campania produced Falernian, Massic, Caecuban and Surrentine wines; Pliny ranked Falernian second only to Caecuban. When Vesuvius buried Pompeii in AD 79, it preserved wine shops, amphorae, vineyard plots and even root cavities. After centuries of decline, Antonio and later Walter Mastroberardino kept Irpinia's grapes alive and bottled Taurasi, Fiano and Greco at a time (1950s to 1980s) when almost nobody else did. The 1980 Irpinia earthquake devastated the area; the revival of the 1990s (Feudi di San Gregorio, Montevetrano, Galardi) and a generation of small growers since have made Campania one of Italy's most exciting regions.
regions.terroir: Two geologies dominate. The volcanic arc along the coast (Roccamonfina, Campi Flegrei, Vesuvius, Ischia) gives loose ash, pumice and lapilli soils, often ungrafted vines and saline, smoky wines. Inland, the Apennine hills of Irpinia and Sannio (300 to 700 m) mix clay, limestone and marl with layers of volcanic ash blown from Vesuvius, and the climate is surprisingly cold: Taurasi is often harvested in November, among the latest in Italy.
regions.grapes: Aglianico (red, high acid and tannin), Piedirosso (Per' e Palummo, 'dove's foot', soft and aromatic), Sciascinoso, Casavecchia, Pallagrello Nero, Tintore di Tramonti; whites Fiano, Greco, Falanghina, Coda di Volpe, Biancolella, Forastera, Asprinio, Caprettone, Pallagrello Bianco, Ripoli, Fenile, Ginestra.
regions.styles: Dry structured reds (Taurasi, Aglianico del Taburno), lighter volcanic reds (Piedirosso), mineral whites that age (Fiano, Greco), coastal whites, red frizzante (Gragnano, Lettere) and traditional-method sparkling.
regions.classification: Four DOCGs (Taurasi, Fiano di Avellino, Greco di Tufo, Aglianico del Taburno), 15 DOCs and nine IGTs (Campania IGT, Pompeiano IGT and others). Irpinia DOC covers the province of Avellino; Sannio and Falanghina del Sannio cover Benevento with four subzones each.

regions.name: Puglia
regions.tagline: The heel of the boot: old bush vines, Primitivo and Negroamaro, and a flat, sunbaked land that once made Europe's blending wine.
regions.summary:
Puglia is the long heel of Italy, about 400 km of mostly flat limestone between two seas. It has about 93,000 ha of wine grapes (third in Italy after Sicily and Veneto, per a 2025 Censis study) and was for a century the tank-wine supplier of Europe, shipping deep-coloured, high-alcohol reds north to bolster thin wines in France and northern Italy. Since the 1990s it has turned toward bottled wine built on its own grapes: Primitivo (the same variety as California's Zinfandel and Croatia's Tribidrag), Negroamaro in the Salento, and Nero di Troia in the north.

The region has four DOCGs and 28 DOCs. The key zones are the Salento peninsula (Salice Salentino, Brindisi, Copertino, Squinzano and other Negroamaro DOCs), Manduria and Gioia del Colle for Primitivo, and the Murge plateau around Castel del Monte for Nero di Troia and Bombino Nero. Rosé has a long history here: the first bottled Italian rosé, Leone de Castris's Five Roses, came from Salice Salentino in 1943.
regions.history: Greek colonists founded Taras (Taranto) around 706 BC and the Messapians grew vines in the Salento before them. In the Middle Ages Frederick II of Hohenstaufen built Castel del Monte. Primitivo was named by a priest of Gioia del Colle, Francesco Filippo Indellicati, who around 1799 selected an early-ripening ('primativo') vine; it reached Manduria in the late 19th century as a dowry of the Countess Sabini of Altamura. Its link to Zinfandel was confirmed by DNA in the 1990s and to Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski/Tribidrag in 2001. After phylloxera hit France, Puglia's cutting wine was in heavy demand; the 20th century brought cooperatives, EU vine-pull schemes (many old bush vines were grubbed up) and, from the 1990s, a quality revival led by family estates.
regions.terroir: Mostly flat or gently rolling limestone, often under a thin layer of red earth (*terra rossa*), with sand and clay near the coasts. The Murge plateau in the north and centre rises to about 680 m and is cooler; the Salento is low, hot and windy, cooled by both seas. Summers are long and dry; old vines are often trained as low bush vines (*alberello pugliese*).
regions.grapes: Primitivo, Negroamaro, Nero di Troia (Uva di Troia), Malvasia Nera, Susumaniello, Bombino Nero, Montepulciano, Aleatico, Ottavianello (Cinsault); whites Verdeca, Bianco d'Alessano, Bombino Bianco, Fiano Minutolo, Pampanuto, Falanghina, Moscato.
regions.styles: Ripe, soft reds from Primitivo and Negroamaro; structured Nero di Troia; rosato (Puglia is one of Italy's biggest rosé producers); sweet Primitivo Dolce Naturale; light whites from the Valle d'Itria.
regions.classification: Four DOCGs (Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale and three Castel del Monte DOCGs), 28 DOCs and six IGTs, of which IGT Puglia and IGT Salento carry much of the volume.
appellations: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva

regions.name: Basilicata
regions.tagline: One volcano, one grape: Aglianico on the slopes of Monte Vulture, aged in caves cut into tuff.
regions.summary: Basilicata, the ancient Lucania, is the instep of the boot: mountainous, thinly populated and poor for most of its history. Only about 740 ha are declared under its DOC and DOCG wines, but it has one great wine: Aglianico del Vulture, from the slopes of an extinct volcano in the north of the region. Monte Vulture (1,326 m) left behind deep layers of volcanic tuff and ash, and the villages of Rionero, Barile and Rapolla are riddled with caves (*cantine* and *grotte*) carved into the tuff, where Aglianico has been aged for centuries. The region has one DOCG and four DOCs.
regions.history: Greek colonists settled the Ionian coast (Metapontum, Heraclea), and the poet Horace was born in Venusia (Venosa), on the edge of the Vulture, in 65 BC. The villages around the volcano were resettled by Albanian refugees (Arbëreshë) in the 15th century, who dug the cave cellars of Barile's 'Sheshë' district. The Aglianico del Vulture DOC came in 1971; producers such as Paternoster (1925) and D'Angelo kept quality alive, and since 2000 Elena Fucci, Cantine del Notaio and others have brought international attention.
regions.terroir: On Monte Vulture vineyards run from about 200 to 700 m on volcanic tuff, ash and lapilli over clay. The climate is continental with cold winters; Aglianico ripens slowly and is harvested in late October or November. Elsewhere, the Matera hills and the Agri valley have clay and limestone.
regions.grapes: Aglianico above all, plus Primitivo, Malvasia, Moscato, Greco and international varieties in the south.
regions.styles: Structured, long-lived Aglianico; some Aglianico sparkling and rosé; Matera reds and whites.
regions.classification: One DOCG (Aglianico del Vulture Superiore, 2010), four DOCs (Aglianico del Vulture, Matera, Grottino di Roccanova, Terre dell'Alta Val d'Agri) and one IGT.

regions.name: Calabria
regions.tagline: The toe of the boot, Oenotria of the Greeks: Gaglioppo at Cirò, sweet Greco at Bianco and a new DOCG in 2025.
regions.summary: Calabria is the toe of Italy, a long mountainous peninsula between the Tyrrhenian and Ionian seas. The Greeks called this coast Oenotria, 'land of vines', and founded Sybaris, Kroton and Locri here. Wine in Calabria today is small (under 10,000 ha, a fraction of what it once was), but it has distinct native grapes: Gaglioppo for reds, Magliocco and Greco Nero, and the white Greco Bianco, Mantonico and Pecorello. The heart is Cirò on the Ionian coast, where a group of young growers, the 'Cirò Revolution', has rebuilt the reputation of Gaglioppo, and in 2025 the Classico core became Calabria's first DOCG.
regions.history: Greek colonies founded from the 8th century BC (Sybaris 720 BC, Kroton 710 BC) made Calabria part of Magna Graecia. A wine called Krimisa, from a temple of Apollo Aleo at Punta Alice near Cirò, was said to be offered to athletes returning from the Olympic Games; the story is popular locally but hard to document. The region was later poor and emigrant, and the DOCs (Savuto 1975, Cirò 1969) did not stop decline. Librandi, at Cirò Marina since 1953, led a research-based revival from the 1990s with the University of Milan, cataloguing hundreds of local vine accessions.
regions.terroir: Calabria is mostly mountains (Pollino, Sila, Aspromonte), with vineyards on coastal hills and terraces. Cirò's hills of clay, marl and sand run from the Ionian shore up to about 460 m, with sea breezes and dry, hot summers; the Sila plateau behind brings cool air. The Tyrrhenian side (Lamezia, Savuto) is greener and wetter.
regions.grapes: Gaglioppo, Magliocco Canino and Magliocco Dolce, Greco Nero, Nerello, Calabrese (Nero d'Avola); whites Greco Bianco, Mantonico, Pecorello, Guardavalle, Montonico.
regions.styles: Pale but tannic Gaglioppo reds and rosés; Magliocco reds; sweet passito whites (Greco di Bianco).
regions.classification: One DOCG (Cirò Classico, registered in the EU on 18 July 2025) and nine DOCs, plus about ten IGTs (Calabria IGT is widely used). Terre di Cosenza DOC (2011) absorbed four older DOCs.
appellations: S. Anna di Isola Capo Rizzuto

regions.name: Sicily
regions.tagline: The Mediterranean's crossroads: Greek alberello, Arab raisins, English fortified wine and a volcano that became Italy's hottest appellation.
regions.summary:
Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean and the largest vineyard of any Italian region, over 118,000 ha of wine grapes (17.8% of the national total in a 2025 Censis study), ahead of Veneto and Puglia. For most of the 20th century it made bulk wine and Marsala; since the 1990s it has reinvented itself twice. First came the Nero d'Avola and Grillo boom, led by estates such as Planeta, Tasca d'Almerita and Donnafugata, and the creation of the island-wide Sicilia DOC in 2011 (about 24,600 ha). Then came Etna, where old bush vines on black lava at up to 1,000 m and more turned a forgotten DOC into one of the most talked-about wine regions in the world.

The island has one DOCG (Cerasuolo di Vittoria) and 23 DOCs, with Etna's application for DOCG status still pending in October 2026. Beyond Etna and Vittoria, its treasures are its sweet and fortified wines: Marsala, created by English merchants; Passito di Pantelleria, from Zibibbo grapes dried under the African sun on an island closer to Tunisia than to Sicily; and Malvasia delle Lipari from the Aeolian volcanoes.
regions.history: Residues in Copper Age jars from a cave on Monte Kronio near Sciacca, published in 2017, suggest wine was being made here around 4000 BC, among the earliest evidence in Italy. Phoenicians at Motya and Greeks at Naxos (734 BC), Syracuse and Selinunte spread vines and the low *alberello* bush training. Pliny praised the Mamertine wine of Messina, served by Julius Caesar at a banquet in 46 BC. Arab rule (9th to 11th centuries) brought the Zibibbo grape name (from Arabic *zabib*, raisin) and dried-grape techniques to Pantelleria. In 1773 the Liverpool merchant John Woodhouse shipped fortified wine from Marsala to England; Benjamin Ingham (from 1806) and Vincenzo Florio (from 1833) built an industry around it. Phylloxera arrived around 1880 and devastated the island, except on Etna's sandy volcanic soils. After decades of cooperatives and subsidised bulk wine, the modern revival began in the 1980s and 1990s.
regions.terroir: Sicily runs from hot, flat coastal plains to the 3,300 m cone of Etna. The west (Trapani, Marsala, Mazara) is low and windy, with limestone and sandy soils and most of the vineyard. The centre (Sclafani, Contessa Entellina) is a high inland plateau at 400 to 800 m with clay and big temperature swings. The southeast (Vittoria, Noto, Pachino) has red sand over limestone (*terra rossa*). Etna's volcanic sands and the volcanic islands (Pantelleria, Lipari, Salina) form their own world. The African sirocco and the sea temper everything.
regions.grapes: Nero d'Avola (Calabrese), Nerello Mascalese, Nerello Cappuccio, Frappato, Perricone, Nocera; whites Catarratto (the most planted), Grillo, Inzolia (Ansonica), Carricante, Grecanico (Garganega), Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria), Malvasia di Lipari, Moscato Bianco, Damaschino, Minnella. International grapes (Syrah, Chardonnay, Cabernet) are widely planted in the west and centre.
regions.styles: Ripe Nero d'Avola reds and fresh Frappato; perfumed, high-altitude Etna Rosso and mineral Etna Bianco; Cerasuolo di Vittoria; fortified Marsala; sweet passito (Pantelleria, Malvasia delle Lipari, Moscato di Noto and Siracusa); Grillo and Catarratto whites.
regions.classification: One DOCG (Cerasuolo di Vittoria, 2005), 23 DOCs and seven IGTs (Terre Siciliane IGT is the main one). The Sicilia DOC (2011) covers the whole island and has one UGA, Salemi. Etna DOC (1968, Sicily's first DOC) recognises 133 contrade in its rules (142 on the consorzio's 2022 map) and has applied for DOCG status.

regions.name: Sardinia
regions.tagline: An island apart: Cannonau from the land of centenarians, Vermentino on granite and a flor-aged white older than sherry's fame.
regions.summary:
Sardinia sits alone in the middle of the western Mediterranean, closer to Corsica and Tunisia than to Rome, and its wine reflects centuries of separate history: Nuragic, Phoenician, Roman, Byzantine, Pisan, Catalan-Aragonese and Piedmontese. It has about 26,000 ha of vines, one DOCG (Vermentino di Gallura) and 17 DOCs. Three region-wide DOCs carry most of the volume: Cannonau di Sardegna, Vermentino di Sardegna and Monica di Sardegna.

Cannonau (Grenache) is the soul of the mountainous east, around Nuoro, Oliena, Mamoiada and Jerzu, in the Ogliastra, one of the world's 'Blue Zones' of exceptional longevity, which locals happily link to their red wine. Vermentino reaches its peak on the granite of Gallura in the northeast. The southwest (Sulcis) has ungrafted Carignano on sand dunes, and the west keeps two extraordinary oxidative whites: Vernaccia di Oristano, aged under flor, and Malvasia di Bosa.
regions.history: Grape pips found at the Nuragic site of Sa Osa near Cabras and at other sites, dated to around 1300 to 1100 BC, show that grapes were cultivated on the island in the Bronze Age; some Sardinians argue that Cannonau is native and travelled to Spain, while most DNA evidence points to a Spanish origin for Garnacha, perhaps arriving with the Aragonese rulers from the 14th century. Phoenicians and Carthaginians traded wine here, and Romans grew vines on the Campidano plain. From the 14th to the early 18th century, Aragonese and Spanish rule brought many grapes (Bovale, Monica, Girò and probably Carignano and Cannonau). Phylloxera arrived in the 1880s. Piedmontese entrepreneurs founded Sella & Mosca in 1899; cooperatives dominated the 20th century; and in the 1980s and 1990s Giacomo Tachis's work with Argiolas (Turriga) and Santadi (Terre Brune) showed the island's potential.
regions.terroir: Old, varied geology: granite in Gallura and parts of the centre, schist and volcanic rock (trachyte, basalt) in the middle, limestone around Alghero and Oliena, alluvial plains in the Campidano and sand dunes in the Sulcis. The climate is hot and dry, with the mistral (*maestrale*) blowing hard from the northwest; mountains rise to 1,834 m in the Gennargentu, so inland vineyards at 400 to 700 m are much cooler.
regions.grapes: Cannonau (Grenache), Carignano, Monica, Bovale (Bovale Sardo, genetically Graciano), Cagnulari, Girò, Pascale; whites Vermentino, Nuragus, Nasco, Torbato, Semidano, Vernaccia di Oristano, Malvasia di Sardegna, Moscato.
regions.styles: Warm, spicy Cannonau reds, from fresh to powerful; saline Vermentino; dense Carignano; flor-aged Vernaccia; sweet and oxidative Malvasia, Nasco, Moscato and Girò.
regions.classification: One DOCG (Vermentino di Gallura, 1996), 17 DOCs and 15 IGTs (Isola dei Nuraghi IGT is widely used). The three island-wide DOCs are Cannonau di Sardegna (with subzones Capo Ferrato, Jerzu, Oliena or Nepente di Oliena, and a Classico for Nuoro and Ogliastra), Vermentino di Sardegna and Monica di Sardegna.

appellations.name: Chianti Classico
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (minimum 80%; 90% for Gran Selezione from 2027), with Canaiolo, Colorino, Malvasia Nera, Ciliegiolo and, outside Gran Selezione, some international reds.
appellations.summary:
Chianti Classico is the original Chianti: the hills between Florence and Siena that Cosimo III named in 1716, long before the name spread across half of Tuscany. It covers about 70,000 hectares, of which only around 10,000 are vineyard (7,200 ha registered to the DOCG); the rest is oak and chestnut forest, olive groves and stone villages, which is why the landscape still looks like a Renaissance painting. About 480 members, 342 of them bottlers, make 35 to 38 million bottles a year, every one carrying the black rooster (*gallo nero*) on the neck, a symbol taken from the medieval Lega del Chianti formed by Castellina, Gaiole and Radda.

The modern wine was rebuilt from a low point. The 1967 DOC rules froze a recipe that demanded white Trebbiano and Malvasia in a red wine, and the best producers responded by leaving the system. The consorzio fought back: 100% Sangiovese became legal in 1995, Chianti Classico became its own DOCG in 1996, and white grapes were banned from the 2006 vintage. Today the wine is Sangiovese at its most transparent: sour cherry, violets, dried herbs and a savoury, saline acidity, with tannins that can be chalky in Gaiole or silky in Panzano.

The pyramid has three levels. *Annata* is released after about a year; Riserva needs 24 months; Gran Selezione (created 2014) needs 30 months and estate-grown fruit, and is moving to a minimum 90% Sangiovese with only native partners from the 2027 vintage. Gran Selezione can also carry one of 11 UGA village names, the first legal recognition that Radda tastes different from Castelnuovo Berardenga.
appellations.terroir: The zone runs about 50 km north to south across all or part of eight communes. Soils change ridge by ridge: galestro (crumbly schistous clay) around Gaiole, Radda and Panzano gives perfume and tension; alberese limestone gives structure; macigno sandstone in Lamole and San Casciano gives finesse; the Pliocene sands and clays near Castelnuovo Berardenga give riper, rounder wines. Vineyards climb from about 200 m to the legal limit of 700 m, and the high, cool sites have gained ground as summers warm. The Pesa, Greve and Arbia valleys and the Monti del Chianti ridge on the east frame most of the best slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: The 2027 Gran Selezione rules allow only eight native blending partners (Canaiolo, Ciliegiolo, Colorino, Foglia Tonda, Malvasia Nera, Mammolo, Pugnitello and Sanforte) up to 10%: Cabernet and Merlot, once the secret of many 'modern' Chianti Classico, are out at the top of the pyramid.

appellations.name: Castellina
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: One of the three founding members of the medieval Lega del Chianti, Castellina sits on the ridge that splits the Pesa and Elsa valleys. Its whole commune forms the UGA. The western side looks toward the Elsa and is warmer; soils mix alberese, sandstone and clay, and the wines tend to be broad-shouldered and dark-fruited, with Fonterutoli (Mazzei, in Chianti since 1435) as the historic name. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: Castelnuovo Berardenga
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: The southernmost and warmest UGA, where Chianti Classico runs down toward the clay hills of the Crete Senesi. Soils shift to Pliocene sands and marine clays with alberese, giving the zone's ripest, most generous Sangiovese with firm tannin. Its western part around Vagliagli forms a separate UGA. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: Gaiole
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: Gaiole spreads across the eastern Monti del Chianti, a high, wooded commune that includes Brolio, Coltibuono, Ama and Rietine. It was a founding Lega member and is home to some of the zone's highest vineyards (above 600 m at Lamole's neighbour ridges and around Montegrossi). Galestro and alberese give tense, mineral wines with long life. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: Greve
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: The Greve UGA is the northern and eastern part of the commune once Panzano, Lamole and Montefioralle are carved out. It is a large, varied area along the Greve valley with sandstone and galestro, and includes Ruffoli's high slopes (Querciabella) and Verrazzano, the family castle of the explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: Lamole
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: A tiny hamlet of terraces high above Greve (roughly 500 to 650 m), with dry-stone walls rebuilt by hand and sandstone soils (macigno) that give pale, high-toned, floral Sangiovese. Lamole is its own UGA and a poster child for altitude in a warming climate. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: Montefioralle
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: A walled medieval village on the hill just west of Greve, believed to be the family home of Amerigo Vespucci. It is one of the smallest UGAs. Its slopes of galestro and alberese give fine, elegant wines. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: Panzano
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: Panzano is the frazione in the southwest of Greve commune famous for the Conca d'Oro, a south-facing amphitheatre of galestro and alberese that collects heat and gives some of the most complete Sangiovese in Tuscany. Its growers pioneered collective organic farming (the Unione Viticoltori di Panzano), and most of the slopes are organic. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: Radda
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: Radda was the capital of the Lega del Chianti and is now the reference for high-altitude, galestro-driven Sangiovese: pale, perfumed and nervy, sometimes austere in youth. Vineyards sit at roughly 400 to 650 m. A group of growers, the Radda nel Bicchiere association, promoted the commune's identity long before UGAs existed. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: San Casciano
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: The northern gateway to the zone, on lower, gentler hills toward Florence, with sandstone and Pliocene sands. Antinori's Tignanello vineyard and its Bargino winery sit in this area; the wines are often supple and aromatic. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: San Donato in Poggio
match: Chianti Classico San Donato in Poggio
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: This UGA joins the western half of Barberino Tavarnelle with the northern tip of Poggibonsi, centred on the walled village of San Donato. It includes Isole e Olena and Monsanto, two estates that helped prove the area's class with sandstone and alberese slopes and cool evenings. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: Vagliagli
appellations.created: UGA of Chianti Classico (approved June 2021; effective 2023 rules)
appellations.summary: A hamlet in western Castelnuovo Berardenga, higher and cooler than the southern part of the commune, with alberese and sandstone. It forms its own UGA, separate from the rest of Castelnuovo Berardenga. For now the UGA name may appear only on Chianti Classico Gran Selezione.

appellations.name: Vin Santo del Chianti Classico
appellations.grapes: Trebbiano Toscano and Malvasia Bianca (Occhio di Pernice version mostly Sangiovese)
appellations.summary: The sweet wine of the Chianti Classico hills, made from Trebbiano and Malvasia grapes dried for months on straw mats or hung from rafters, then pressed and sealed into small barrels (*caratelli*) with a little of the old *madre* (mother) sediment. It must age at least three years. Good examples are amber, nutty and tangy rather than simply sweet, with flavours of dried apricot, walnut and orange peel. Isole e Olena, Fèlsina, San Giusto a Rentennano (whose Vin San Giusto is legendary) and Badia a Coltibuono make some of the best.
appellations.nerd_note: Vin Santo caratelli are traditionally kept under the roof, not in a cool cellar, so the wine goes through hot summers and cold winters; that cycle drives the slow, oxidative development.

appellations.name: Chianti
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (minimum 60%; 75% in the Colli Senesi), with Canaiolo, Colorino and other reds (Cabernet up to 15%) and up to 10% white grapes; a rosato was added in 2026.
appellations.summary:
Chianti is the big tent around Chianti Classico: a DOCG of roughly 13,700 hectares and more than 700,000 hectolitres a year across six provinces, from the Arno hills west of Florence to Arezzo and the Sienese countryside. The name spread outward in the 20th century as merchants and growers outside the historic zone fought to use it; a 1932 decree drew the seven subzones that still exist (Classico was one of them until it split off in 1996).

Most Chianti (minimum 60% Sangiovese) is fresh, cherry-fruited wine for the table, released from March after the harvest; Superiore and Riserva (24 months) add depth, and the subzones carry the character. Rùfina, in the cool, high Sieve valley northeast of Florence, makes the longest-lived wines (its producers created the TerraElectae single-vineyard mark). Colli Senesi wraps around Siena, Montalcino and Montepulciano and must contain at least 75% Sangiovese. Colli Fiorentini, Montespertoli, Montalbano (next to Carmignano), Colline Pisane, Colli Aretini and the new Terre di Vinci (2026, around Leonardo's birthplace) complete the map.

The 2026 rule change also created Chianti Rosato, made from at least 60% Sangiovese. The old *governo all'uso toscano*, refermenting young wine with a share of dried grapes for a softer, slightly prickly wine, is still allowed for the red.
appellations.terroir: The zone is too large for one terroir: galestro and alberese in Rùfina and the Colli Senesi, sandier Pliocene soils around Montespertoli and the Colline Pisane, and Arno-valley clays nearer Florence. Rùfina's altitude (to about 500 m) and Apennine air give acidity and long ageing.
appellations.nerd_note: Selvapiana's Bucerchiale Rùfina Riserva, first bottled as a single vineyard in 1979, shows how Chianti can age 30 years when the site is cool enough.

appellations.name: Chianti Rùfina
appellations.summary: One of the smallest and the highest-regarded Chianti subzone, in the Sieve valley about 20 km northeast of Florence, with about 750 ha. Vineyards climb to 500 m and catch cold air from the Apennines through the Consuma pass, so harvests are late and the wines are tense, perfumed and long-lived. Selvapiana, Frescobaldi's Nipozzano, Colognole, Grati and I Veroni lead; since 2016 the consorzio's TerraElectae mark identifies single-vineyard Riservas. Pomino is an enclave within it.

appellations.name: Chianti Colli Senesi
appellations.summary: The largest subzone, wrapping around Siena and reaching south to Montalcino, Montepulciano and San Gimignano, so many Brunello and Vino Nobile producers also make Colli Senesi from younger vines or declassified fruit. It requires at least 75% Sangiovese, more than the rest of Chianti, and the style is warm and ripe.

appellations.name: Chianti Colli Fiorentini
appellations.summary: The hills around Florence on both sides of the Arno and down the Pesa and Greve valleys toward Chianti Classico, with about 900 ha. Wines are medium-bodied and aromatic, released a little later than basic Chianti.

appellations.name: Chianti Montespertoli
appellations.summary: A small subzone carved out of Colli Fiorentini in 1996 around the town of Montespertoli, southwest of Florence, on sandy Pliocene soils. It has only a few dozen hectares declared.

appellations.name: Chianti Montalbano
appellations.summary: The slopes of Monte Albano west of Florence around Vinci, Lamporecchio and Quarrata, surrounding the Carmignano enclave. The wines are soft and fruity.

appellations.name: Chianti Colline Pisane
appellations.summary: The westernmost subzone, on the hills southeast of Pisa around Terricciola and Casciana Terme, with marine sands and clays, giving softer, rounder Chianti close to the coast.

appellations.name: Chianti Colli Aretini
appellations.summary: The eastern subzone, on the hills of the upper Arno around Arezzo, facing the Val d'Arno di Sopra, with cooler Apennine influence and lively, fruity wines.

appellations.name: Chianti Terre di Vinci
appellations.summary: The newest Chianti subzone, added in the 2026 rules, around Vinci, the birthplace of Leonardo, and neighbouring communes in the lower Arno hills between Empoli and Monte Albano. Its reds may be released from 1 September after the vintage.

appellations.name: Vin Santo del Chianti
appellations.grapes: Trebbiano Toscano, Malvasia (Occhio di Pernice from Sangiovese)
appellations.summary: The Vin Santo of the wider Chianti zone, with the same subzones (Rùfina, Colli Senesi, Colli Fiorentini and others). Grapes are dried until the new year, pressed and aged at least three years in small casks. Quality ranges from simple dessert wine to complex amber wines; Selvapiana's Rùfina Vin Santo is a reference.

appellations.name: Brunello di Montalcino
appellations.created: DOC 1966; DOCG 1980 (one of the first four)
appellations.summary:
Brunello di Montalcino is Sangiovese on its own, and for many people the summit of Italian red wine. The hill town of Montalcino, 40 km south of Siena, gave its name to a wine that the Biondi-Santi family made famous: Clemente Santi showed a 'Brunello' (from the dark, brownish skins of the local Sangiovese) in the 1860s, and his grandson Ferruccio bottled pure Sangiovese for long ageing from the 1888 vintage. The story is part history, part founding myth, since other families also made Brunello, but the 1888 and 1891 Riservas still exist and they set the template: a wine built to last decades.

For most of the 20th century Montalcino was poor and nearly forgotten; in 1960 there were barely a dozen bottlers. Brunello was one of the four original DOCGs in 1980, and the arrival of the American-owned Banfi estate and a wave of new growers in the 1970s and 1980s turned it into a boom town. Today about 2,100 hectares are registered to Brunello and the zone produces roughly 9 million bottles a year (about 30% of exports go to the United States).

The rules are strict and the ageing long: at least two years in wood and release only on 1 January of the fifth year after harvest (sixth for Riserva). That long wait in wood gives the classic style: brick-tinged colour even when young, cherry and blood orange, leather, tobacco and dried herbs, high acidity and firm tannin that soften over 10 to 30 years. A debate between large Slavonian oak casks (Biondi-Santi, Soldera, Poggio di Sotto) and French barriques has largely settled toward large wood.

The 2008 'Brunellopoli' scandal, when prosecutors investigated several large houses for blending other grapes into Brunello and 6.7 million litres were impounded, ended with plea bargains, declassifications and a firm recommitment to 100% Sangiovese.
appellations.terroir: Montalcino is a roughly square block of hills (about 24,000 ha, of which only 15% is vineyard) bounded by the Orcia, Asso and Ombrone rivers, with Monte Amiata (1,738 m) to the southeast shielding it from storms. The northern slopes near the town (Montosoli, Canalicchio, Torrenieri) are cooler, with galestro and give perfumed, fine wines. The southern flank (Sant'Angelo in Colle, Castelnuovo dell'Abate, Tavernelle) is warmer and closer to the sea's influence, with clay, sand and volcanic-derived soils toward Amiata, giving riper, rounder wines. Western sites around Castelgiocondo and Camigliano catch the sea breeze; the east near Castelnuovo dell'Abate is more sheltered. No subzones are official, but most nerds read a label by hamlet.
producers: Case Basse di Gianfranco Soldera (sold as IGT)
appellations.nerd_note: Lisini owns a half-hectare plot of ungrafted Sangiovese that survived phylloxera; since 1985 it has been bottled in tiny quantities as 'Prefillossero'.

appellations.name: Rosso di Montalcino
appellations.summary:
The younger sibling of Brunello, from the same zone and the same grape but released from 1 September after the harvest with no minimum time in wood. It was created to give growers cash flow and a way to declassify lesser lots, and the best producers now treat it as a serious wine from younger vines or specific parcels: bright cherry, fresh acidity and much of Brunello's character at a fraction of the price and wait.

In September 2024 the consorzio reassigned 352 hectares of existing vineyard to Rosso, taking its registered area to about 872 ha (no new planting), so potential output from the 2024 vintage more than doubles to about 7.3 million bottles. Producers are now debating whether Rosso is a second wine or a terroir wine in its own right.

appellations.name: Sant'Antimo
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Nero, Sangiovese, Chardonnay and others
appellations.summary: A catch-all DOC covering the whole commune of Montalcino, named after the Romanesque abbey of Sant'Antimo near Castelnuovo dell'Abate. It exists for wines that cannot be Brunello or Rosso: international varieties, blends and Vin Santo. Banfi and Castello Romitorio have used it, but most producers now prefer IGT Toscana.

appellations.name: Moscadello di Montalcino
appellations.summary: Before Brunello, Montalcino was known for a sweet, aromatic Moscato, praised by the poet Francesco Redi in his 1685 *Bacco in Toscana*. Moscadello survives as a tiny DOC for still, frizzante and late-harvest Moscato. Col d'Orcia and Il Poggione are among the few still making it.
appellations.nerd_note: Redi's verse calls Moscadello di Montalcino 'il leggiadretto, il sì divino', the graceful, divine one, long before anyone wrote about Brunello.

appellations.name: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano
appellations.created: DOC 1966; DOCG 1980; Pieve UGAs approved 2023, in force from the 2021 vintage
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese (locally Prugnolo Gentile) minimum 70%; Pieve tier minimum 85% with only native partners.
appellations.summary:
Vino Nobile comes from the Renaissance hill town of Montepulciano (not to be confused with the Montepulciano grape of Abruzzo), 25 km east of Montalcino. It was praised in 1685 by Francesco Redi, who called Montepulciano 'd'ogni vino è re', king of all wines, and the 'noble' label probably came from the aristocratic families who made it. In 1980 it became one of Italy's first four DOCGs, with Brunello di Montalcino, Barolo and Barbaresco, though its reputation sagged in the 1980s and 1990s.

The zone has about 1,200 hectares of Vino Nobile (2024) and some 81 member wineries; in 2024 it sold 6.7 million bottles, 65.5% abroad. The wine sits between Chianti and Brunello in weight: Sangiovese (here called Prugnolo Gentile) with up to 30% other grapes, two years of ageing (three for Riserva), and flavours of plum, cherry, earth and spice with sturdy tannin.

The big change is the *Pieve*. In 2023 the consortium won approval for 12 UGAs named after the ancient parish churches (pievi) of the territory: Ascianello, Badia, Caggiole, Cerliana, Cervognano, Gracciano, Le Grazie, San Biagio, Sant'Albino, Sant'Ilario, Valardegna and Valiano. A Vino Nobile Pieve must be at least 85% Sangiovese with only native partners, from the bottler's own vines at least 15 years old in a single pieve, at no more than 7 t/ha, aged three years. The first vintage, 2021, reached the market in 2025, making Montepulciano the first Tuscan denomination to tie a whole quality tier to named places.
appellations.terroir: Montepulciano's ridge (about 600 m at the town) separates the Val di Chiana to the east from the Val d'Orcia to the west. Vineyards lie between 250 and 600 m, mostly on the eastern and southern slopes toward the Chiana plain and Lake Trasimeno, on Pliocene marine sands and clays with fossil shells, some with tufa and silty alluvium. The sandy soils give a softer, more aromatic Sangiovese than Montalcino's galestro, and the Chiana valley brings cool night air.
appellations.nerd_note: The town is honeycombed with cellars cut into the tufa under its palazzi; Contucci and De' Ricci still age wine in Renaissance-era vaults beneath the main street.

appellations.name: Rosso di Montepulciano
appellations.summary: The early-release red of Montepulciano, sold from March after the vintage: juicy, cherry-scented Sangiovese for drinking young. About 390 ha and over 2 million bottles a year. It lets producers keep their best fruit for Vino Nobile and the new Pieve wines.

appellations.name: Vin Santo di Montepulciano
appellations.grapes: Malvasia Bianca, Grechetto (Pulcinculo), Trebbiano; Occhio di Pernice from Prugnolo Gentile
appellations.summary: Montepulciano's rare Vin Santo includes the most extreme style in Tuscany: the Occhio di Pernice ('partridge eye') from Sangiovese, aged up to 8 years in tiny caratelli. Avignonesi's version, aged about a decade in 50-litre casks, is one of Italy's most concentrated sweet wines, dark, viscous and tangy.
appellations.nerd_note: Avignonesi's Occhio di Pernice yields only about 15 to 20 litres of wine from each 100 kg of dried grapes.

appellations.name: Bolgheri
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot (any proportion), up to 50% Syrah and 50% Sangiovese; whites from Vermentino, Sauvignon Blanc, Viognier.
appellations.summary:
Bolgheri is the Italian appellation that Bordeaux varieties built. Until the 1970s this strip of coast in the commune of Castagneto Carducci, south of Livorno, was known for cattle, cypress avenues and Carducci's poetry, not wine. Then came Sassicaia, planted by Marchese Mario Incisa della Rocchetta at Tenuta San Guido in the 1940s and released from the 1968 vintage; in 1985 his nephew Lodovico Antinori founded Ornellaia, and Piero Antinori's Guado al Tasso, Grattamacco, Le Macchiole, Michele Satta and later Gaja's Ca' Marcanda followed.

Until 1994 the reds had no DOC at all and were sold as vino da tavola, even at record prices. The 1994 rules created Bolgheri Rosso and Superiore, a red DOC built around Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot, with Syrah and Sangiovese allowed up to half. Today the consorzio counts 78 members and about 1,379 ha, 99% of the vineyard. Bolgheri Superiore needs two years of ageing, one in wood; the most expensive wines (Ornellaia, Guado al Tasso, Paleo, Grattamacco) are Superiore, while some icons such as Masseto (pure Merlot) and Messorio sit outside as IGT Toscana.

The style is plush and polished: blackcurrant, cedar and Mediterranean scrub (the *macchia*), riper and fleshier than Bordeaux but with a coastal freshness. Cabernet Franc has become a local speciality (Le Macchiole's Paleo is pure Franc).
appellations.terroir: Vineyards sit between the Tyrrhenian Sea and the Colline Metallifere, from near sea level to about 400 m, in a crescent between Bolgheri and Castagneto. Soils are a mosaic of alluvial gravel and pebbles washed down from the hills (*sassi*, as in Sassicaia, 'stony place'), sand, silt and clay; the gravelly fans drain like the Médoc and suit Cabernet, while clay pockets (Masseto's blue clay) suit Merlot. Sea breezes and the hills behind moderate heat and keep disease low.
producers: Tenuta San Guido (also Guidalberto, Le Difese)
appellations.nerd_note: Bolgheri allows the vineyard name on Rosso and Superiore labels (minimum 12.5%), so a 'cru' system is quietly forming inside a DOC that is barely 30 years old.

appellations.name: Bolgheri Sassicaia
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon (minimum 80%), with Cabernet Franc; in practice about 85% Cabernet Sauvignon and 15% Cabernet Franc.
appellations.summary:
The only Italian DOC owned, in practice, by a single estate.
