Marchese Mario Incisa della Rocchetta, a Piedmontese aristocrat who married into the Gherardesca family, planted Cabernet cuttings (said to come from Château Lafite) at Tenuta San Guido in the 1940s to make a claret for family use; the wine was drunk at home for two decades. His nephew Piero Antinori and the oenologist Giacomo Tachis helped refine it, and the 1968 vintage was released commercially in 1971. In 1978 a Decanter blind tasting in London put the 1972 Sassicaia first among 33 Cabernet-based wines from 11 countries, and Italian wine was never the same.

Sassicaia became a subzone of Bolgheri in 1994 and its own DOC in 2013. About 80 ha, roughly 85% Cabernet Sauvignon and 15% Cabernet Franc, aged about two years in French barriques. Compared with its neighbours it is lean, cedar-scented and tense, a wine of finesse that needs 15 years.
appellations.terroir: The vineyards spread over several parcels at roughly 80 to 400 m between the coast and the hills of Castiglioncello di Bolgheri, on stony alluvial soils (the original Sassicaia plot was named for its stones) with limestone and clay higher up.
appellations.nerd_note: The original 1940s vineyard, Castiglioncello, sits high (about 350 m) in the hills; the estate later moved its core plantings lower toward the sea when it found the stony fans there gave riper fruit.

appellations.name: Carmignano
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese minimum 50%, Cabernet Franc and/or Cabernet Sauvignon 10 to 20%, Canaiolo up to 20%.
appellations.summary:
Carmignano, on the Montalbano ridge west of Florence and Prato, was one of the four zones in Cosimo III's 1716 edict, and its wine was a Medici favourite: the family's hunting reserve, the Barco Reale, was walled here, and the villa La Ferdinanda at Artimino looks over the vines. Cabernet has grown here since at least the 18th century (locally called *uva francesca*), so when the DOC was created in 1975 Carmignano was the first Italian appellation to require Cabernet in the blend, decades before the Super Tuscans made it fashionable.

The wine is Sangiovese-led with 10 to 20% Cabernet: medium-full, with red cherry, cassis and a herbal, slightly austere finish. Only about 117 ha are planted. The Contini Bonacossi family of Tenuta di Capezzana, whose records show wine made on the estate in 804, did most to save the name.
appellations.terroir: Hills of 50 to 400 m on the southern flank of Monte Albano, with galestro, alberese and sandy clay, warmer and drier than Chianti Classico to the south.
appellations.nerd_note: A rental contract dated 804, kept at Capezzana, records vines and olives on the property, one of the oldest written mentions of a specific Tuscan wine estate.

appellations.name: Barco Reale di Carmignano
appellations.summary: The younger, earlier-release red of the Carmignano zone, named after the Medici's walled hunting park. The rosato is called Vin Ruspo, from the farm workers' tradition of 'stealing' (ruspare) juice from the press before it took colour.

appellations.name: Vin Santo di Carmignano
appellations.grapes: Trebbiano, Malvasia; Occhio di Pernice from Sangiovese
appellations.summary: A tiny DOC for Carmignano's Vin Santo. Capezzana's version, aged for years in small chestnut and oak caratelli, is one of Tuscany's great sweet wines. About 4 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 7,100 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Vernaccia di San Gimignano
appellations.grapes: Vernaccia di San Gimignano minimum 85%; up to 10% Riesling and/or Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary:
Vernaccia di San Gimignano was the first wine in Italy to receive DOC status, by a decree of 1966, and it is Tuscany's only white DOCG. The grape has been documented around the town of towers since the 13th century; Dante put Pope Martin IV in Purgatory for gorging on eels drowned in Vernaccia, and Michelangelo the Younger wrote that it 'kisses, licks, bites, thrusts and stings'.

About 580 ha surround the town, and the wine ranges from simple, almond-scented whites to serious, saline wines that age. Good Vernaccia has a firm, slightly bitter finish of almond and citrus pith, a waxy texture and a mineral edge from the sandy, fossil-rich soils. Riserva needs 11 months of ageing; several growers now use skin contact, large wood or concrete for more depth.
appellations.terroir: Hills of 200 to 500 m around San Gimignano with Pliocene marine sands, often yellow and full of fossil shells, over clay. The sands give finesse and the saline character; clay-rich parcels give weight.
appellations.nerd_note: Elisabetta Fagiuoli of Montenidoli was making long-macerated and long-aged Vernaccia (Carato, Fiore) when the rest of the zone was chasing light, early-bottled whites.

appellations.name: San Gimignano
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Pinot Nero; Vin Santo from Trebbiano and Malvasia
appellations.summary: The red, rosé and Vin Santo companion DOC to Vernaccia, covering the same commune. It is small and mostly used for Sangiovese-based reds and international blends; most producers sell their reds as Chianti Colli Senesi or IGT instead.

appellations.name: Pomino
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio, Trebbiano; Pinot Nero, Sangiovese, Merlot
appellations.summary: Pomino is a mountain enclave inside the Chianti Rùfina zone, named in Cosimo III's 1716 edict and since the 19th century almost a Frescobaldi monopoly. The family planted French varieties here in 1855 (Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Nero), so the DOC, created in 1983, is one of the few in Tuscany built on Burgundian grapes. Vines reach about 700 m, and the cool air gives crisp whites and light reds. The Castello Pomino Bianco is the flagship, Benefizio a barrel-fermented Chardonnay.
appellations.nerd_note: Frescobaldi's Benefizio, first made in 1973, was one of the first barrique-fermented Chardonnays in Italy.

appellations.name: Morellino di Scansano
appellations.summary: Morellino is the Maremma's Sangiovese, grown in the hills around the village of Scansano between the Ombrone and Albegna rivers, a few kilometres from the sea. The local name may come from the dark colour of the grape (like a *morello* cherry) or from the dark Maremma horses. Warmer and drier than Chianti, the area gives a riper, softer, more immediate Sangiovese with plum and red cherry and gentle tannins, most of it for drinking within five years; Riserva (two years, one in wood) is more serious. About 1,100 ha and close to 9 million bottles a year.
appellations.terroir: Hills from about 100 to 500 m, with sandstone, clay and limestone; the sea 20 km away moderates temperatures and the long, dry summers ripen Sangiovese early.
producers: Cantina dei Vignaioli del Morellino di Scansano
appellations.nerd_note: Elisabetta Geppetti's Le Pupille made Saffredi (a Cabernet-Merlot IGT) in 1987 that helped put the Maremma on the fine-wine map before most Tuscans took it seriously.

appellations.name: Montecucco Sangiovese
appellations.summary: Montecucco Sangiovese is the DOCG for Sangiovese from the hills of Cinigiano, Castel del Piano and neighbouring communes on the western slopes of Monte Amiata, just across the Orcia river from Montalcino. The wines need 17 months of ageing (34 for Riserva) and show a Brunello-like profile with more Mediterranean warmth. Seven communes and 18 frazioni may appear on labels. More than 60% of the area is farmed organically, one of the highest shares in Italy.

appellations.name: Montecucco
appellations.summary: The DOC umbrella around Montecucco Sangiovese for blends with at least 60% Sangiovese, varietal Ciliegiolo, Vermentino and Vin Santo, from the slopes of Monte Amiata between Montalcino and the Maremma.

appellations.name: Suvereto
appellations.created: subzone of Val di Cornia 1989; separate DOCG 2011
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot (blends or varietal), Sangiovese
appellations.summary: Suvereto, a medieval village south of Bolgheri named for its cork oaks (*sughere*), became one of Tuscany's newest DOCGs in 2011. Its reds, built on Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot (with varietal versions of each and of Sangiovese), are warmer and denser than Bolgheri's, from iron-rich, stony soils on the hills above the Cornia valley. Tua Rita's Redigaffi, a pure Merlot first made in 1994, gave the area cult status.

appellations.name: Val di Cornia Rosso
match: Val di Cornia Rosso / Rosso della Val di Cornia
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
appellations.summary: A small DOCG for Sangiovese-led reds (with Cabernet and Merlot) from the Val di Cornia hills around Campiglia Marittima, San Vincenzo and Piombino, on the coast south of Bolgheri. It covers the same area as the Val di Cornia DOC but with stricter ageing, and is rarely seen outside Tuscany.

appellations.name: Val di Cornia
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Ciliegiolo, Aleatico; Vermentino, Ansonica
appellations.summary: The broad coastal DOC of the Cornia valley around Piombino and Campiglia Marittima, now mostly used for Vermentino, Ansonica, rosé and simple reds since Suvereto and Val di Cornia Rosso split off as DOCGs in 2011.

appellations.name: Elba Aleatico Passito
match: Elba Aleatico Passito / Aleatico Passito dell'Elba
appellations.summary: A sweet red passito from Aleatico grapes dried in the sun on the island of Elba, one of the smallest DOCGs in Italy (about 15 ha). Napoleon, exiled on Elba in 1814 and 1815, is said to have enjoyed it. The wine is deep ruby, with rose petals, cherry jam and spice, sweet but kept lively by acidity.

appellations.name: Elba
appellations.summary: The island DOC of Elba, off the Tuscan coast, for whites from Ansonica, Vermentino and Procanico, Sangiovese reds and sweet Moscato. The island once had several thousand hectares of vines; now only about 80 remain, on granite and schist terraces facing the sea. Arrighi has experimented with Ansonica aged in amphorae sunk in the sea.

appellations.name: Maremma Toscana
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Ciliegiolo, Alicante; Vermentino, Ansonica, Trebbiano, Viognier
appellations.summary: The Maremma is Tuscany's deep south, the coastal province of Grosseto that was malarial marsh until reclamation in the 19th and 20th centuries. The Maremma Toscana DOC, promoted from IGT in 2011, covers the whole province and works as a flexible umbrella for blends and varietals of almost anything: Vermentino, Sangiovese, Cabernet, Syrah, Ciliegiolo and Alicante (local Grenache). About 2,400 ha and a fast-growing reputation; many estates from Bolgheri, Chianti and Montalcino have bought land here. 23 communes and 168 frazioni can appear on labels.

appellations.name: Ansonica Costa dell'Argentario
appellations.summary: A tiny white DOC for Ansonica from the Monte Argentario promontory, Isola del Giglio and the coast around Orbetello. On Giglio the vines grow on granite terraces above the sea and give salty, sun-baked whites, sometimes made with long skin contact by small growers.

appellations.name: Bianco di Pitigliano
appellations.grapes: Trebbiano Toscano plus Greco, Malvasia, Verdello, Grechetto and others
appellations.summary: One of Italy's first DOCs (1966), from the tufa plateau around Pitigliano, the 'little Jerusalem' of the Maremma whose Jewish community made kosher wine in cellars cut into the volcanic rock. The white is light and soft; a sweet Vin Santo and Superiore exist. The tufa cellars beneath the town are still used.

appellations.name: Sovana
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Ciliegiolo, Aleatico, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
appellations.summary: The red counterpart to Bianco di Pitigliano, from the same volcanic tufa country around Sovana, Pitigliano and Sorano. Ciliegiolo and Aleatico are local specialities; the Etruscan necropolis of Sovana lies among the vineyards.

appellations.name: Capalbio
appellations.summary: A small DOC in the far south of the Maremma near the Lazio border, around the hill town of Capalbio. Most wines from here are now labelled Maremma Toscana. About 2 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 11,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Parrina
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon; Ansonica, Vermentino, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A near-monopoly DOC around the Tenuta La Parrina estate near Orbetello, on the coast facing Monte Argentario. Reds are Sangiovese-based with Merlot and Cabernet; whites use Ansonica and Vermentino. About 45 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 45,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Monteregio di Massa Marittima
appellations.summary: A DOC in the northern Maremma around the mining town of Massa Marittima in the Colline Metallifere, for Sangiovese reds, Vermentino and Vin Santo, including Occhio di Pernice. About 21 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 65,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Montescudaio
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet, Merlot; Trebbiano, Vermentino, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A coastal DOC in the Cecina valley just north of Bolgheri, for reds based on Sangiovese and international varieties, whites from Trebbiano and Vermentino, and Vin Santo. It sits in Bolgheri's shadow but has similar soils.

appellations.name: Terratico di Bibbona
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah; Trebbiano, Vermentino
appellations.summary: A small coastal DOC around Bibbona, immediately north of Bolgheri. Its gravel and sand soils are much like Bolgheri's, but it has little commercial presence. About 6 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 25,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Terre di Pisa
appellations.summary: A red-only DOC covering the hills of the province of Pisa, for Sangiovese and international varieties alone or blended. It overlaps the Chianti Colline Pisane subzone and the old San Torpè area.

appellations.name: San Torpè
appellations.summary: Named after the Roman officer Torpè, martyred under Nero, this DOC in the Pisan hills is for Trebbiano-based whites and Vin Santo. It is nearly extinct in practice, with well under a hectare declared.

appellations.name: Colline Lucchesi
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Canaiolo, Ciliegiolo, Merlot, Syrah; Trebbiano, Vermentino, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: The hills north of Lucca, with a long history of villa estates and mixed blends. Biodynamic pioneers such as Tenuta di Valgiano have shown that these sandstone and clay slopes can give fine Sangiovese-based reds.

appellations.name: Montecarlo
appellations.grapes: Trebbiano with Sémillon, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio, Roussanne, Sauvignon, Vermentino; Sangiovese, Syrah, Merlot
appellations.summary: A small hill town east of Lucca where French varieties (Sémillon, Roussanne, Pinot) were planted in the 19th century, giving an unusual white blend with Trebbiano. Reds use Sangiovese with Syrah and Merlot.

appellations.name: Valdinievole
appellations.summary: A near-dormant DOC in the Nievole valley near Montecatini Terme for Trebbiano whites, Sangiovese reds and Vin Santo; only about a hectare is declared. About 1 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 17,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Candia dei Colli Apuani
appellations.summary: Steep terraces under the Apuan Alps near Massa and Carrara, within sight of the marble quarries, for Vermentino whites and rare reds from Barsaglina and Vermentino Nero. It is close in spirit to Liguria's Colli di Luni next door.

appellations.name: Bianco dell'Empolese
appellations.summary: A Trebbiano-based white and Vin Santo DOC around Empoli and Vinci in the lower Arno valley, an area now better known for the new Chianti Terre di Vinci subzone.

appellations.name: Colli dell'Etruria Centrale
appellations.summary: Created in 1990 as a home for wines from the Chianti zone that did not fit the Chianti rules (whites, rosé, Vin Santo, novello and international blends). The IGT Toscana has made it almost redundant.

appellations.name: Val d'Arbia
appellations.summary: A white and Vin Santo DOC in the Arbia valley southeast of Siena. Production is now negligible. Barely 0.1 ha were declared in 2019, so the name is close to dormant.

appellations.name: Grance Senesi
appellations.summary: Named after the medieval *grance*, fortified farms run by Siena's Santa Maria della Scala hospital, this DOC covers the Crete Senesi and hills south of Siena. It is very small.

appellations.name: Orcia
appellations.summary: The Val d'Orcia, the UNESCO-listed landscape of rolling wheat fields and cypresses between Montalcino and Montepulciano, has its own DOC, mostly for Sangiovese reds. The wines are often good value next to their famous neighbours, and a few estates (Podere Forte, Sante Marie) aim high.

appellations.name: Terre di Casole
appellations.summary: A small DOC around Casole d'Elsa, west of Siena, for Sangiovese-based reds and Chardonnay-based whites. About 9 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 20,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Cortona
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet; Chardonnay, Grechetto
appellations.summary: The Etruscan hill town of Cortona, above the Val di Chiana near Lake Trasimeno, has made Syrah its signature, an unusual choice in Tuscany that works well in the warm, open valley. Stefano Amerighi (biodynamic) and Tenimenti Luigi d'Alessandro made the case for peppery, fresh Cortona Syrah.

appellations.name: Valdichiana Toscana
appellations.grapes: Trebbiano, Grechetto, Chardonnay; Sangiovese and international reds
appellations.summary: The old Bianco Vergine Valdichiana DOC, renamed in 2011, covers the broad Chiana plain between Arezzo and Montepulciano. It began as a light white from Trebbiano and Grechetto and now also includes reds and sparkling.

appellations.name: Val d'Arno di Sopra
match: Val d'Arno di Sopra / Valdarno di Sopra
Val d’Arno di Sopra / Valdarno di Sopra
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Pugnitello, Foglia Tonda; Chardonnay, Malvasia Bianca Lunga, Orpicchio
appellations.summary: The upper Arno valley between Florence and Arezzo was one of the four zones in Cosimo III's 1716 edict, but it only became a DOC in 2011. In 2024 producers rewrote the rules completely: all vineyards must be organic, varietal wines from rare natives such as Orpicchio and Foglia Tonda are allowed, and communes and estates can be named. Petrolo's Galatrona Merlot and Il Borro come from here.
appellations.nerd_note: It is the first Italian DOC whose rules require organic certification for every vineyard.

appellations.name: Montefalco Sagrantino
appellations.summary:
Sagrantino is the most tannic grape variety commonly grown anywhere, with polyphenol levels well above Cabernet Sauvignon or Nebbiolo, and it grows almost nowhere except the hills around Montefalco, the 'balcony of Umbria'. For centuries it was made sweet, as a passito for Easter and family feasts, because the sugar tamed its tannin. By the 1960s only a few hectares remained. Arnaldo Caprai, a textile industrialist, bought land here in 1971, and his son Marco pushed for a dry style: the Caprai 25 Anni (first vintage 1993) made Sagrantino famous.

Today about 374 ha are planted. The dry wine needs 37 months of ageing, including 12 in wood, and cannot be released until four years after the harvest. It is inky purple, with blackberry, black cherry, cinnamon, clove and earth, and a wall of tannin that takes a decade to relax. The Passito, also 100% Sagrantino from dried grapes, is a dark, sweet, tannic rarity. The consorzio counts 118 members and 66 member wineries (2026).
appellations.terroir: Five communes (Montefalco, Bevagna, Gualdo Cattaneo, Castel Ritaldi and Giano dell'Umbria) on hills of roughly 220 to 470 m between the Topino and Clitunno valleys. The consorzio describes four soil zones: alluvial sands near Bevagna, clay and limestone in the centre, and stonier, more calcareous ground near Giano dell'Umbria. Hot summers and cool nights help phenolic ripeness, which Sagrantino needs badly.
appellations.nerd_note: Paolo Bea's Sagrantinos are fermented with long skin contact and aged in large casks for years; Giampiero Bea also helped found the Vini Veri natural-wine movement.

appellations.name: Montefalco
appellations.grapes: Rosso: Sangiovese 60 to 80% with 10 to 25% Sagrantino; Bianco: Trebbiano Spoletino and Grechetto
appellations.summary: The broader DOC of the Montefalco hills. Montefalco Rosso blends Sangiovese with a share of Sagrantino, giving a more approachable wine than the DOCG; Riserva ages 30 months. Montefalco Bianco and Grechetto use local whites, and Trebbiano Spoletino is increasingly bottled here and in the Spoleto DOC.

appellations.name: Torgiano Rosso Riserva
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese 70% or more, with Canaiolo and other reds
appellations.summary: A DOCG that is essentially the work of one family. Giorgio Lungarotti modernised the estate near the medieval village of Torgiano, where the Chiascio and Tiber meet south of Perugia, and his Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio (first made in 1964) became the model for the DOCG, granted in 1990. The wine is Sangiovese-based, aged three years, and evolves for decades into a savoury, leathery, tobacco-scented red. Only a handful of hectares are declared each year.
appellations.nerd_note: Lungarotti releases Vigna Monticchio Riserva only after years in bottle; the estate's library holds vintages back to the 1960s.

appellations.name: Torgiano
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Canaiolo, Cabernet, Merlot, Pinot Nero; Trebbiano, Grechetto, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: One of Umbria's first DOCs, around the village of Torgiano. Lungarotti's Rubesco (Rosso) and Torre di Giano (Bianco, Trebbiano and Grechetto) are the reference wines; the estate's MUVIT wine museum (1974) and olive oil museum make Torgiano the region's wine-culture centre.

appellations.name: Orvieto
appellations.grapes: Grechetto and Procanico (Trebbiano Toscano) minimum 60%, with Malvasia, Verdello, Drupeggio and others
appellations.summary:
Orvieto is one of Italy's historic whites, from the hills around the cliff-top city that sits on a block of volcanic tufa. Underneath, Etruscans and medieval monks dug hundreds of caves, many used to ferment and store wine at a steady cool temperature. For centuries the style was *abboccato*, gently sweet, the wine of popes and the 'liquid sunlight' Signorelli asked to be paid in.

The DOC (1971, about 2,100 ha, 95% in Umbria and 5% in Lazio) makes mostly dry whites today, light, almond-scented and fresh. The Classico core around the city gives more depth, and the best producers (Palazzone, Barberani, Decugnano dei Barbi) make wines that age. Orvieto also has a rare noble-rot category, Muffa Nobile: autumn fogs off the Paglia river and Lake Corbara let *Botrytis cinerea* concentrate the grapes, as in Sauternes.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic soils (tufa, ash, lapilli) from the Vulsini volcanoes near the city, with marine clay and sandy marls elsewhere; vineyards between 100 and 500 m. Humid autumns favour botrytis in the low valleys.
appellations.nerd_note: Barberani's Calcaia is a Muffa Nobile Orvieto from botrytised Grechetto and Procanico near Lake Corbara, made only in years when the fog cooperates.

appellations.name: Rosso Orvietano
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Canaiolo, Aleatico and others
appellations.summary: The red-wine companion to Orvieto, covering the same zone. It allows blends and varietals from Sangiovese and international grapes; production is small. About 14 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 53,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Lago di Corbara
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Pinot Nero; Grechetto, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A small DOC on the hills around the artificial lake of Corbara on the Tiber, between Orvieto and Todi. The lake's mists and the warm slopes suit Bordeaux varieties and Pinot Nero; Decugnano dei Barbi and Barberani make wines here.

appellations.name: Todi
appellations.grapes: Grechetto (the Todi biotype, G5), Sangiovese, Merlot
appellations.summary: A DOC around the hill town of Todi built on Grechetto di Todi, a biotype genetically identical to Emilia's Pignoletto and distinct from Orvieto's Grechetto. The whites are textured and nutty; Superiore and passito versions exist. Roccafiore and Todini are leading producers.

appellations.name: Spoleto
appellations.summary: A white-wine DOC created in 2011 to rescue Trebbiano Spoletino, a distinct local grape once trained on maple trees along the Spoleto valley (some vines are a century old). It is high in acidity and ages into a waxy, citrus and herb-scented white that has become a cult wine. Superiore, spumante and passito versions exist.

appellations.name: Colli Martani
appellations.grapes: Grechetto, Trebbiano, Sangiovese; Vernaccia di Cannara
appellations.summary: A hilly DOC between Todi, Montefalco and Assisi, best known for Grechetto. Its Cannara subzone keeps alive Vernaccia di Cannara (the Cornetta grape), a sweet red passito made in tiny quantities around Easter.

appellations.name: Assisi
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Pinot Nero; Grechetto, Trebbiano
appellations.summary: A DOC on the slopes of Monte Subasio below the city of Saint Francis, for Sangiovese-based reds, Grechetto and rosé. Small and mostly sold locally. About 57 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 211,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Colli Perugini
appellations.summary: A DOC on the hills south and west of Perugia between the Tiber and Nestore valleys, for Sangiovese-based reds and Trebbiano-Grechetto whites. It has little commercial profile.

appellations.name: Colli Altotiberini
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet, Pinot Nero; Trebbiano, Grechetto
appellations.summary: The upper Tiber valley around Città di Castello and Umbertide, the coolest corner of Umbria, close to the Tuscan border. Reds are Sangiovese-based and whites light. About 31 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 48,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Colli del Trasimeno
appellations.grapes: Gamay del Trasimeno (Grenache), Sangiovese, Merlot, Cabernet; Trebbiano, Grechetto
appellations.summary: The hills around Lake Trasimeno, where Hannibal ambushed a Roman army in 217 BC. The local speciality is 'Gamay del Trasimeno' (also called Gamay Perugino), which DNA testing has shown to be Grenache, brought by Spanish rulers or monks centuries ago. The lake moderates temperatures and the wines are juicy and spicy.
appellations.nerd_note: Trasimeno Gamay is a cousin of Sardinia's Cannonau and Spain's Garnacha, not of Beaujolais' Gamay.

appellations.name: Amelia
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Ciliegiolo, Merlot; Trebbiano, Grechetto, Malvasia
appellations.summary: The southernmost Umbrian DOC, around the Roman walled town of Amelia near the Lazio border. Ciliegiolo, a cherry-scented red related to Sangiovese, is a local strength (Zanchi makes a well-known one).

appellations.name: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi
match: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico
appellations.summary:
Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi is the larger of the two Verdicchio zones, about 1,500 ha on the hills of the Esino valley around the walled hill towns (*castelli*) that once defended Jesi. For years it was the white in the amphora bottle; today it is one of the most serious whites in Italy. Verdicchio has naturally high acidity, a slightly bitter almond finish and a texture that grows richer with age; good Classico Superiore from old vines can develop like Riesling, gaining honey, fennel and petrol notes over 10 to 20 years.

The Classico area covers the heart of the zone (Cupramontana, Staffolo, Montecarotto, San Paolo di Jesi, Serra de' Conti and others). The rules allow 99 named places and 18 communes on labels. Riserva (18 months) has been a separate DOCG since 2010. Sparkling Verdicchio, by both tank and classic method, has a long tradition here, and Sartarelli's late-harvested Balciana showed the grape's sweet potential.
appellations.terroir: Hills of roughly 150 to 550 m on both banks of the Esino. The right (south) bank around Cupramontana and Staffolo is higher, with calcareous clay and limestone marl, and gives tense, long-lived wines; the left (north) bank around Montecarotto and Serra de' Conti has more clay and sand and gives broader wines. Sea breezes from the Adriatic 30 km away keep the grapes healthy.
appellations.nerd_note: Verdicchio is genetically identical to Trebbiano di Soave and Trebbiano di Lugana, probably carried north by farmers moving from the Marche to the Veneto in the 15th century after a plague.

appellations.name: Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva
appellations.summary: The Riserva tier of Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi, a DOCG since 2010. It needs 18 months of ageing including six in bottle and at least 12.5% alcohol, and it is where the grape's ability to age shows best: Villa Bucci Riserva, from old vines around Montecarotto and Serra de' Conti, is aged in large old casks and often drinks well after two decades. Classico Riserva comes from the historic core.

appellations.name: Verdicchio di Matelica
appellations.summary: The smaller, higher, inland Verdicchio zone, about 220 ha in the upper Esino valley around Matelica, roughly 50 km from the sea. The valley runs north to south and is shut off from Adriatic breezes, giving a continental climate with warm days and cold nights. Matelica Verdicchio is generally tighter, more acidic and saltier than Jesi's, with citrus, green almond and a stony finish, and it ages remarkably. The Riserva became a separate DOCG in 2010.
appellations.terroir: Vineyards at roughly 350 to 650 m on clay, limestone and sandstone over ancient marine sediments, with big day-night temperature swings.

appellations.name: Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva
appellations.summary: The DOCG for Riserva Verdicchio from Matelica, aged at least 18 months. Belisario's Cambrugiano and La Monacesca's Mirum show how the high-altitude valley gives Verdicchio a lean, mineral backbone that carries it for 15 years or more.

appellations.name: Cònero
appellations.summary: Cònero is the DOCG for Riserva reds from Monte Conero, a limestone headland that rises 572 m straight out of the Adriatic just south of Ancona, covered in holm oak and *corbezzolo* (strawberry tree, *komaros* in Greek, which gave the mountain its name). The wine is Montepulciano, at least 85%, aged two years: dark, plush and spicy, with black cherry and Mediterranean herbs, firmer and fresher than most Abruzzo Montepulciano because of the limestone and sea air.
appellations.terroir: A small zone of about 170 ha on the slopes of Monte Conero and the hills toward Osimo and Camerano, on limestone and calcareous clay, from sea level to about 400 m.

appellations.name: Rosso Cònero
appellations.summary: The non-Riserva red of Monte Conero, a Montepulciano-based wine with lively acidity and dark fruit, released after a few months. When the Riserva became the Cònero DOCG in 2004, this DOC kept the younger wines.

appellations.name: Lacrima di Morro d'Alba
match: Lacrima di Morro / Lacrima di Morro d'Alba
appellations.summary: Lacrima ('tear') is a rare aromatic red grape found almost only around Morro d'Alba, a walled village west of Senigallia. The name may come from the teardrop shape of the berries or from the way their thin skins split and weep juice when ripe. The wine smells like a bouquet of roses and violets with strawberry and spice, an unusual perfume for a red, and is usually drunk young. Passito and Superiore versions exist. Stefano Mancinelli is credited with saving the grape in the 1980s.
appellations.nerd_note: Frederick Barbarossa is said to have demanded Lacrima as tribute when he besieged Morro d'Alba in 1167, a story locals still tell.

appellations.name: Vernaccia di Serrapetrona
appellations.summary: One of the strangest wines in Italy: a red sparkling wine made with three fermentations, from Vernaccia Nera grown around the hill village of Serrapetrona in the Macerata Apennines. At least 40% of the grapes are dried on racks until December or January; the rest are fermented normally, then the dried grapes are crushed and added to start a second fermentation, and finally the wine is made sparkling by a third fermentation, usually in tank. It comes dry or sweet, purple and frothy, with black cherry, pepper and violets. Only about 9 ha are declared, making it one of Italy's smallest DOCGs.

appellations.name: Serrapetrona
appellations.summary: The still, dry red version of Vernaccia Nera from Serrapetrona, created when the sparkling wine became a DOCG in 2004. Peppery and juicy, sometimes with a share of dried grapes for depth (Terre di Serrapetrona's Collequanto).

appellations.name: Offida
appellations.grapes: Pecorino or Passerina (minimum 85% each); Rosso from Montepulciano minimum 85%
appellations.summary: Offida, a hill town famous for its bobbin lace, gives its name to a DOCG that rescued a grape. Pecorino (the name may come from sheep, *pecore*, nibbling the grapes along transhumance routes) had almost vanished when Guido Cocci Grifoni found old vines in the mountains around Arquata del Tronto in the early 1980s and replanted them. The result is a white with surprising acidity and weight, with flavours of green apple, sage and liquorice and a saline finish. Passerina, crisper and lighter, is the other white. Offida Rosso is a Montepulciano aged two years.
appellations.terroir: Rolling hills of clay, sand and limestone between the Tronto and Tesino rivers in the province of Ascoli Piceno, at 100 to 500 m, with the Sibillini mountains to the west and the sea 20 km east.

appellations.name: Terre di Offida
appellations.summary: The old Offida DOC, renamed when Offida became a DOCG, now covering Passerina sparkling, passito and Vin Santo from the Offida hills. About 5 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 33,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Rosso Piceno
appellations.summary: Rosso Piceno, named for the ancient Piceni people, is the broad Montepulciano-Sangiovese red of southern and central Marche, about 765 ha. Superiore comes only from a delimited southern area around Ascoli Piceno and Offida and is the more serious wine. Velenosi and Saladini Pilastri make widely exported versions.

appellations.name: Falerio
appellations.summary: A white blend from the province of Ascoli Piceno and Fermo, named for the Roman town of Falerio Picenus. Trebbiano is blended with Passerina and Pecorino; a varietal Pecorino version exists. Light and fresh, it is the everyday white of the southern Marche.

appellations.name: Bianchello del Metauro
appellations.summary: A light, zesty white from Biancame grown along the Metauro river in the north of the region. Local legend claims that in 207 BC the Carthaginian army of Hasdrubal lost the battle of the Metaurus after drinking too much of the local white.

appellations.name: Colli Pesaresi
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Pinot Nero, Cabernet; Trebbiano, Biancame, Pinot Bianco
appellations.summary: The hills behind Pesaro, near the Romagna border, mostly for Sangiovese reds. Subzones include Focara (Pinot Nero), Roncaglia (whites) and Parco Naturale Monte San Bartolo, a cliff-top park on the sea.

appellations.name: Colli Maceratesi
appellations.grapes: Maceratino (Ribona) minimum 70%; Sangiovese and others for reds
appellations.summary: The DOC of the province of Macerata, notable for Ribona (Maceratino), a local white grape related to Greco. Whites are soft and floral; reds are Sangiovese-based. About 87 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 568,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Esino
appellations.summary: A catch-all DOC covering the Esino basin (the Verdicchio country) for wines outside the Verdicchio rules: lighter whites and Montepulciano-Sangiovese reds. About 8 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 40,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: San Ginesio
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese with Vernaccia Nera, Cabernet, Merlot, Ciliegiolo
appellations.summary: A tiny DOC in the Sibillini foothills around San Ginesio, for Sangiovese-based reds and a sparkling Vernaccia Nera, close to Serrapetrona in style. About 7 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 40,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: I Terreni di Sanseverino
appellations.summary: A small DOC around San Severino Marche for reds from Vernaccia Nera, Montepulciano and Sangiovese, including a Moro red and a passito. About 2 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 4,700 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Pergola
appellations.summary: A small DOC around Pergola in the Cesano valley where Aleatico, locally called Vernaccia di Pergola, makes dry, perfumed reds and passito. About 5 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 32,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Frascati
appellations.grapes: Malvasia Bianca di Candia and/or Malvasia del Lazio minimum 70%, with Bellone, Bombino, Greco, Trebbiano
appellations.summary: Frascati is Rome's house white, from the volcanic slopes of the Alban Hills 20 km southeast of the city, where popes and princes built the Tuscolo villas (Villa Aldobrandini, Villa Falconieri) among the vines. One of the first Italian DOCs (1966), it was ruined by its own success in the 1970s, when vast volumes of thin wine made the name a byword for cheap trattoria wine. The best producers have rebuilt it around Malvasia del Lazio (Malvasia Puntinata), which gives more aroma and structure than the neutral Trebbiano that dominated the volume era. Good Frascati is pale gold, with almond, white flowers and a volcanic, slightly salty finish. Superiore and the sweet Cannellino became separate DOCGs in 2011.
appellations.terroir: Slopes of the extinct Alban (Laziale) volcano at 100 to 400 m, with soils of volcanic ash, tufa and lapilli rich in potassium, overlooking Rome and the sea.

appellations.name: Frascati Superiore
appellations.summary: The top dry Frascati, a DOCG since 2011, with lower yields and at least 12% alcohol; Riserva ages 12 months. Fontana Candida's Luna Mater and Castel de Paolis's wines show how much more texture old-vine Malvasia Puntinata gives.

appellations.name: Cannellino di Frascati
appellations.summary: The traditional sweet Frascati, made from late-harvested grapes with at least 35 g/l of residual sugar. 'Cannellino' was the name Romans gave to the lightly sweet wine served with *ciambelline* biscuits. It is gently honeyed rather than heavy.
appellations.nerd_note: Cannellino is one of the few Italian DOCGs dedicated solely to a late-harvest sweet white.

appellations.name: Cesanese del Piglio
appellations.summary: Lazio's only red DOCG, from the hill towns of Piglio, Serrone, Acuto, Anagni and Paliano in the Ciociaria, southeast of Rome. Cesanese has two forms: Cesanese di Affile, small-berried and finer, and Cesanese Comune, larger-berried. The wine is medium-bodied with red cherry, pepper, rose and a touch of earth, sometimes compared to a lighter Syrah or Pinot Noir. Superiore and Superiore Riserva are aged longer. It was Lazio's first DOCG (2008).
appellations.terroir: Apennine foothills at about 300 to 700 m, with red clay, limestone and volcanic deposits; cool nights help aroma.

appellations.name: Cesanese di Olevano Romano
match: Cesanese di Olevano Romano / Olevano Romano
appellations.summary: A small DOC around Olevano Romano on the hills east of Rome, which has become the most exciting place for Cesanese thanks to growers such as Damiano Ciolli, whose Cirsium from 1950s vines showed how fine and aromatic the grape can be.

appellations.name: Cesanese di Affile
appellations.summary: The tiny DOC of Affile, the mountain village (about 700 m) that gave its name to the finer Cesanese biotype. Only a few hectares remain; the wines are fresh, spicy and light-bodied.

appellations.name: Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone
appellations.summary: The wine with the best name in Italy comes with a legend. In 1111 a German prelate, often called Bishop Johannes Defuk (or Fugger), travelled to Rome for the coronation of Emperor Henry V and sent his servant Martino ahead to mark inns with good wine by writing 'Est' (it is) on the door. At Montefiascone, on the rim of the Bolsena crater, Martino was so impressed he wrote 'Est! Est!! Est!!!'. The bishop stayed, drank and, the story goes, died there; his tomb is in the church of San Flaviano. The DOC (1966) makes light, soft whites from Trebbiano and Malvasia on the volcanic slopes above Lake Bolsena; a Classico area covers Montefiascone and Bolsena.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic soils of the Vulsini complex around Lake Bolsena, the largest volcanic lake in Europe, at 300 to 600 m.
appellations.nerd_note: The bishop's tombstone in San Flaviano reads 'Est Est Est pr(opter) nim(ium) est hic Jo(annes) de Fuc d(ominus) meus mortuus est', roughly 'Because of too much Est Est Est my master Johannes de Fuk died here'.

appellations.name: Roma
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano, Cesanese, Sangiovese, Syrah; Malvasia del Lazio, Bellone, Bombino
appellations.summary: A DOC created in 2011 to put the name of the capital on a bottle, covering much of the province of Rome. Reds must be at least 50% Montepulciano; whites at least 50% Malvasia Puntinata. Romanella is its sparkling white. A Classico area covers the historic vineyard belt around the city.

appellations.name: Castelli Romani
appellations.grapes: Malvasia, Trebbiano; Cesanese, Merlot, Montepulciano, Nero Buono, Sangiovese
appellations.summary: An umbrella DOC over the whole Alban Hills district (the 'Roman castles', the hill towns around the old volcano), for simpler whites, reds and rosés that do not fit the local village DOCs. It accounts for a large share of the area's volume.

appellations.name: Marino
appellations.grapes: Malvasia del Lazio, Malvasia di Candia, Trebbiano, Bellone, Bombino
appellations.summary: Frascati's neighbour on the western slope of the Alban Hills, with similar volcanic whites. Marino's grape festival, the Sagra dell'Uva held since 1925, is famous for the moment the town's fountains run with wine. The Gotto d'Oro cooperative dominates volume; Paola Di Mauro's Colle Picchioni showed the area's quality.

appellations.name: Colli Albani
appellations.summary: A white-wine DOC on the southwestern slopes of the Alban volcano around Albano Laziale, Ariccia and Castel Gandolfo, the popes' summer residence. About 45 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 223,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Colli Lanuvini
appellations.summary: A small Castelli Romani DOC around Lanuvio and Genzano di Roma on the southern rim of the Alban Hills, overlooking the plain toward the sea. Its whites are Malvasia-Trebbiano blends from volcanic ash soils; Genzano is known for its Infiorata, when the main street is carpeted with flowers each June.

appellations.name: Velletri
appellations.summary: The southernmost Castelli Romani DOC, around Velletri, where reds from Montepulciano, Sangiovese and Cesanese are more important than elsewhere in the hills. About 9 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 67,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Zagarolo
appellations.summary: A tiny white-wine DOC around Zagarolo and Gallicano on the eastern edge of the Castelli Romani. About 7 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 60,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Montecompatri Colonna
appellations.summary: A small Castelli Romani white DOC around Montecompatri, Colonna and Rocca Priora, with soils of volcanic ash similar to Frascati. About 5 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 31,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Genazzano
appellations.summary: A small DOC around Genazzano, a medieval town of the Colonna family in the hills east of Rome near Olevano Romano. Whites are Malvasia-based and reds use Sangiovese and Cesanese with a little Ciliegiolo. Little wine is declared under the name today; most local growers prefer the Cesanese DOCs or IGT.

appellations.name: Cori
appellations.grapes: Bellone, Malvasia, Trebbiano; Nero Buono, Montepulciano, Cesanese
appellations.summary: A DOC on the Lepini mountains around Cori, home of two local grapes: Bellone, an ancient white (possibly Pliny's *uva pantastica*), and Nero Buono di Cori, a dark, soft red. Marco Carpineti, a biodynamic grower, has made both known.

appellations.name: Aprilia
appellations.summary: A DOC on land reclaimed from the Pontine Marshes in the 1930s and settled by farmers from northern Italy, who planted Merlot, Sangiovese and Trebbiano. The flat, sandy-clay coastal plain gives soft, easy wines.

appellations.name: Nettuno
appellations.summary: A coastal DOC around Nettuno and Anzio, the Allied landing beaches of 1944, where Bellone is called Cacchione and gives a light, saline white. About 12 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 73,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Circeo
appellations.summary: A coastal DOC around the promontory of Monte Circeo (home, in legend, of the sorceress Circe) and Sabaudia, on the reclaimed Pontine plain. About 66 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 587,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Terracina
appellations.summary: A DOC for Moscato di Terracina, a distinctive local Muscat grown near the sea around Terracina and Monte San Biagio, made dry, amabile, sparkling and passito. About 42 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 256,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Atina
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Syrah; Sémillon
appellations.summary: An unusual DOC in the Comino valley in southern Lazio where Bordeaux varieties were brought in the 19th century by Pasquale Visocchi, an agronomist who studied in France. Cabernet is the backbone.

appellations.name: Cerveteri
appellations.summary: A DOC around Cerveteri, the Etruscan city of Caere with its UNESCO necropolis, on the coast northwest of Rome. About 10 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 12,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Tarquinia
appellations.summary: A coastal DOC around Tarquinia, another Etruscan city famous for the painted tombs of its necropolis, which show banquets with wine. About 12 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 47,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Colli Etruschi Viterbesi
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Montepulciano, Canaiolo, Grechetto Rosso (Violone); Trebbiano, Malvasia, Grechetto, Moscato
appellations.summary: A broad DOC covering the province of Viterbo (the ancient Tuscia), with many varietal types including the rare Grechetto Rosso and sweet Moscatello. About 89 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 123,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Vignanello
appellations.summary: A small DOC around Vignanello on the slopes of the Cimini mountains, with volcanic soils; its Greco is a local speciality. About 12 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 71,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Aleatico di Gradoli
appellations.summary: A tiny DOC for sweet and fortified red Aleatico from the volcanic slopes above Lake Bolsena around Gradoli. Perfumed with roses and cherries. About 1 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 5,600 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Bianco Capena
appellations.summary: A white DOC north of Rome around Capena, Fiano Romano and Morlupo, on the volcanic tuff of the Sabatini hills above the Tiber valley. It is a Malvasia-Trebbiano blend in the Castelli Romani mould, created in 1975, but production under the name is now negligible.

appellations.name: Colli della Sabina
appellations.summary: The Sabine hills northeast of Rome, better known for olive oil (Sabina was Italy's first oil DOP), with a small wine DOC. About 8 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 19,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
appellations.summary:
Montepulciano d'Abruzzo covers hills across all four provinces of the region and is one of Italy's biggest red DOCs: in 2014 about 8,700 ha and 857,000 hl, more than two-thirds of it from the province of Chieti. The grape gives deep colour, soft tannins and generous black-cherry and plum fruit, which made it the classic bulk and supermarket red, but its best wines are anything but simple. Emidio Pepe's Montepulciano, foot-trodden and aged in bottle for years before release, and Valentini's, made in tiny quantities, are cult wines that age for decades.

The 2023 reform introduced provincial subzones and reserved Superiore and Riserva for them; older subzones (Alto Tirino, Teate, Terre dei Peligni, Terre dei Vestini, San Martino sulla Marrucina) also remain. Teramo's hills have their own DOCG, Colline Teramane, and since 2025 the Casauria area near Pescara does too.
appellations.terroir: Calcareous clay hills from near the coast to 600 m (700 m facing south), under the Gran Sasso and Maiella. The province of Chieti, with the most vines, is warmer and lower; Teramo and the inland valleys (Tirino, Peligna) are cooler.

appellations.name: Colline Teramane Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
appellations.summary: Abruzzo's first DOCG (2003), for Montepulciano from the hills of the province of Teramo in the north of the region, between the Gran Sasso and the sea. The area is cooler and more exposed to mountain air than Chieti, and the wines are firmer and more structured, with two years of ageing (three for Riserva). Emidio Pepe at Torano Nuovo and Illuminati at Controguerra are the reference names.

appellations.name: Casauria
appellations.summary: Italy's newest Abruzzo DOCG, approved in 2025 after nearly a decade of lobbying. Casauria was a subzone (Terre di Casauria) of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo from 2006; it covers the hills of the Val Pescara foothills in the province of Pescara, around Tocco da Casauria and Castiglione a Casauria, centred on the Benedictine abbey of San Clemente a Casauria (founded 871). The rules require at least 90% Montepulciano, 18 months of ageing (24 for Riserva), and vineyards no higher than 500 m (600 m facing south), and they stress place rather than grape. A local clone, also called 'Casauria', is recognised.

appellations.name: Terre Tollesi
appellations.summary: A DOCG limited to the single commune of Tollo in the province of Chieti, named after its Latin name, Tullum. It covers Montepulciano reds (Rosso and Riserva), Pecorino and Passerina whites and sparkling and passito wines, one of the smallest DOCGs in Italy by area.

appellations.name: Trebbiano d'Abruzzo
appellations.grapes: Trebbiano Abruzzese and/or Trebbiano Toscano (Bombino Bianco also historically allowed) minimum 85%
appellations.summary:
Most Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a neutral, cheap white from high-yielding tendone vines. A few wines are among the greatest whites in Italy. Edoardo Valentini (died 2006), at Loreto Aprutino, selected the true Trebbiano Abruzzese, kept yields low and made a wine of extraordinary depth and longevity; his son Francesco Paolo continues, releasing only what meets the family standard. Emidio Pepe's Trebbiano, foot-trodden and aged in glass-lined cement, is equally legendary, and growers such as Tiberio (Fonte Canale, from vines planted around 1960) and Cataldi Madonna have proved the local variety's potential.

The 2023 reform added provincial subzones for Superiore and Riserva. The challenge is that the name covers several different grapes: true Trebbiano Abruzzese, Trebbiano Toscano and Bombino Bianco (locally also called Trebbiano).
appellations.nerd_note: Valentini never used consultants or new oak; he made wine in large old casks and simply refused to bottle vintages he did not like. Bottles from the 1970s and 1980s are still alive.

appellations.name: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo
appellations.summary: Cerasuolo means 'cherry-coloured', and this is a rosé dark enough to be mistaken for a light red: Montepulciano pressed after a short maceration, giving a deep pink wine with cherry, wild strawberry and a grip of tannin. It was a style of Montepulciano d'Abruzzo until 2010, when it got its own DOC. It is the classic partner for Abruzzo's fish soups (*brodetto*). Valentini's and Emidio Pepe's Cerasuolos age for years.

appellations.name: Abruzzo
appellations.grapes: Pecorino, Passerina, Cococciola, Montonico, Malvasia; Montepulciano
appellations.summary: A regional DOC created in 2010 mainly to give the native whites a home: Pecorino (the region's rising white), Passerina, Cococciola and Montonico, plus sparkling and passito wines. Since 2023 it has the same four provincial subzones as the other regional DOCs.

appellations.name: Controguerra
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano, Merlot, Cabernet; Trebbiano, Passerina, Pecorino, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A DOC in the far north of the province of Teramo near the Marche border, allowing international varieties alongside Montepulciano. Illuminati is the main producer. About 39 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 297,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Villamagna
appellations.summary: A small red DOC for Montepulciano from the communes of Villamagna, Bucchianico and Vacri in the hills of Chieti. About 43 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 60,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Ortona
appellations.summary: A small DOC around the port town of Ortona in the province of Chieti, the scene of fierce fighting in December 1943, for Montepulciano reds and Trebbiano whites. About 4 ha were declared in 2021.

appellations.name: Tintilia del Molise
appellations.summary: Tintilia is Molise's own grape and the region's calling card. Small-berried and low-yielding, it was almost abandoned by the 1970s; growers began replanting it in the 1990s and the DOC followed in 2011, with about 80 ha today and vineyards required to sit above 200 m. The wine is medium-bodied with dark berries, black pepper, Mediterranean herbs and a touch of liquorice, with fresh acidity; Riserva ages two years. A rosato is also made.
appellations.nerd_note: Molise once called Tintilia 'the wine of the transhumance', drunk by shepherds moving flocks along the *tratturi*, the ancient grass highways to Puglia.

appellations.name: Biferno
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano 70 to 80% with Aglianico; Trebbiano for whites
appellations.summary: A DOC in the Biferno river valley and the coastal hills around Campomarino and Termoli, for Montepulciano-Aglianico reds and Trebbiano-based whites. Di Majo Norante's Ramitello is the best-known wine. About 48 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 393,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Molise
appellations.grapes: Montepulciano, Aglianico, Tintilia, Cabernet, Merlot, Sangiovese; Falanghina, Fiano, Greco, Trebbiano, Moscato
appellations.summary: A region-wide DOC for varietal wines from many grapes, from Aglianico and Montepulciano to Falanghina and Moscato. It is the label for most of Molise's quality bottlings outside Tintilia. About 177 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 632,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Pentro di Isernia
appellations.summary: An inland DOC in the province of Isernia, named for the Pentri, a Samnite tribe. Very little wine is declared under this name. About 74 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 900 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Taurasi
appellations.summary:
Taurasi is the 'Barolo of the South', a nickname that captures its tannin, acidity and longevity, if not its flavour. It was the first DOCG of southern Italy (1993), and for decades it was almost synonymous with one producer: Mastroberardino, whose 1968 Taurasi Riserva is one of the legendary Italian wines of the 20th century.

The wine comes from 17 communes in the hills of Irpinia, east of Avellino, around the village of Taurasi and the Calore river valley. Aglianico ripens very late here, often into November, and must be aged three years (one in wood) before release, four for Riserva. Young Taurasi is dark and severe, with black cherry, plum, tar, tobacco and volcanic smoke; with 15 years it turns savoury, earthy and fine. Styles range from traditional large-cask wines to modern barrique-aged versions.
appellations.terroir: Hills of about 300 to 700 m on both sides of the Calore. The northern and central communes (Taurasi, Castelfranci, Montemarano, Paternopoli, Lapio) have clay, limestone and layers of volcanic ash from Vesuvius; Montemarano and Castelfranci, higher and colder, give the most acidic, slow-ageing wines. The continental climate, with snow in winter and big day-night swings, is unusual for the south.
appellations.nerd_note: Phylloxera reached Irpinia late, in the 1920s and 1930s, and some old Aglianico vines in Taurasi are still ungrafted; Guastaferro's Primum comes from pre-phylloxera vines said to be over 200 years old.

appellations.name: Fiano di Avellino
appellations.summary: Fiano is one of the great white grapes of Italy, and its home is the hills around Avellino. The Latin name *Vitis apiana*, the vine loved by bees (*apis*), may refer to it, and the label may still carry the ancient name Apianum. Mastroberardino kept it alive in the mid-20th century when it nearly disappeared. Today about 430 ha in 26 communes make wines that start out reserved, with pear, hazelnut, smoke and herbs, and gain honey, beeswax and flint over 10 years or more. Unlike most southern whites, Fiano ages beautifully.
appellations.terroir: Hills of 300 to 650 m. Lapio, high above the Calore valley, gives taut, mineral wines; Summonte and the slopes of Monte Partenio give cool, fragrant ones; Montefredane, with clay, gives power and longevity. Volcanic ash layers and cold nights keep acidity.

appellations.name: Greco di Tufo
appellations.grapes: Greco minimum 85%, Coda di Volpe up to 15%
appellations.summary: Greco, probably brought by Greek settlers, is grown in eight communes north of Avellino around the village of Tufo. The village sits on sulphur-bearing rock: sulphur mines operated here from the 19th century (the Di Marzo family) until the 1980s, and many growers find a flinty, smoky edge in the wines. Greco di Tufo is fuller, more phenolic and more structured than Fiano, with peach, almond, citrus peel and a bitter, saline finish; it can be made as a traditional-method sparkling wine too. About 670 ha.
appellations.terroir: Hills of 400 to 600 m along the Sabato river, with clay, limestone, volcanic ash and veins of sulphur-rich rock in Tufo and Santa Paolina.
appellations.nerd_note: Cantine Di Marzo, founded in 1648, is one of the oldest wineries in southern Italy; the Di Marzo family also ran the sulphur mines under Tufo.

appellations.name: Irpinia
appellations.grapes: Aglianico, Piedirosso, Sciascinoso; Fiano, Greco, Falanghina, Coda di Volpe
appellations.summary: A DOC covering the whole province of Avellino, for Aglianico and varietal whites that fall outside the three DOCGs, including the Campi Taurasini subzone for Aglianico from the Taurasi area with shorter ageing.

appellations.name: Aglianico del Taburno
appellations.summary: Aglianico from the slopes of Monte Taburno, the 'sleeping woman' mountain in the province of Benevento, a DOCG since 2011. Compared with Taurasi it is often more supple and fruity, with black cherry, spice and violets, from clay and limestone soils with volcanic deposits. It needs two years of ageing (three for Riserva); a rosato is also allowed.

appellations.name: Falanghina del Sannio
appellations.summary: The province of Benevento is the heartland of Falanghina, Campania's most planted white: about 1,360 ha in this DOC, created in 2011 to gather the Falanghina of four older DOCs, which survive as subzones (Guardia Sanframondi or Guardiolo, Sant'Agata dei Goti, Solopaca and Taburno). The wines are bright and floral, with citrus, peach and a saline finish; the name may come from *falanga*, the stakes that supported the vines.

appellations.name: Sannio
appellations.grapes: Aglianico, Piedirosso, Sciascinoso, Barbera; Coda di Volpe, Fiano, Greco, Malvasia, Moscato
appellations.summary: The umbrella DOC for the province of Benevento, with varietal wines from nearly every Campanian grape and subzones such as Solopaca and Guardia Sanframondi. Mustilli at Sant'Agata de' Goti was the first to bottle a varietal Falanghina, in 1979.

appellations.name: Falerno del Massico
appellations.grapes: Rosso: Aglianico 60% or more with Piedirosso; Primitivo varietal; Bianco: Falanghina
appellations.summary:
Falerno del Massico is the modern heir to Falernian, the most celebrated wine of ancient Rome. Falernian grew on the slopes of Monte Massico near the border of Latium and Campania; Pliny described three crus (Caucinian on the upper slopes, Faustian in the middle, plain Falernian below) and noted that Faustian Falernian was the only wine that would catch fire from a flame. Wine from the Opimian vintage of 121 BC was still served at banquets 60 years later.

Nobody knows which grapes made Falernian. The modern DOC (1989), on the same mountain around Sessa Aurunca, Falciano del Massico and Mondragone, makes a red from Aglianico and Piedirosso, a varietal Primitivo and a white from Falanghina. Villa Matilde, founded by the lawyer Francesco Paolo Avallone in the 1960s with the aim of recreating Falernian, did most to revive the name.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic soils from the extinct Roccamonfina volcano mixed with limestone on Monte Massico (813 m), a ridge running toward the sea; vineyards at 50 to 400 m enjoy sea breezes.
appellations.nerd_note: Pliny wrote that Falernian could be ignited with a flame, which suggests it was naturally very high in alcohol, perhaps from late-harvested, partly dried grapes.

appellations.name: Galluccio
appellations.summary: A DOC on the slopes of the Roccamonfina volcano in northern Campania, for Aglianico reds and Falanghina whites from volcanic soils. Galardi's Terra di Lavoro (IGT) comes from the same volcano.

appellations.name: Casavecchia di Pontelatone
appellations.summary: Casavecchia ('old house') is a red grape rediscovered in the 19th century, the story goes, as a single ancient vine growing against the ruins of an old house near Pontelatone. Its DOC (2011) covers a few communes in the hills north of Caserta. The wines are dark, tannic and spicy.

appellations.name: Aversa
appellations.summary: Home of Asprinio, a sharp, low-alcohol white grape traditionally trained up poplar trees in the *alberata aversana* system, with vines reaching 15 m and harvested by pickers on tall, narrow ladders. This Etruscan-style training survives in a few hectares north of Naples, and the wine is made still or sparkling.
appellations.nerd_note: The alberata aversana is one of the last places in Europe where the ancient practice of marrying vines to living trees (*vite maritata*) is still used commercially.

appellations.name: Vesuvio
appellations.grapes: Bianco: Caprettone and/or Coda di Volpe 45% or more, Falanghina, Greco; Rosso: Piedirosso and/or Aglianico
appellations.summary: The vineyards on the slopes of Vesuvius produce one of the most famous wine names in the world, Lacryma Christi, the 'tears of Christ'. A legend says that Christ wept on seeing the Bay of Naples, stolen from heaven by Lucifer, and where his tears fell, vines grew. The Vesuvio DOC (1983, about 200 ha) uses the name Lacryma Christi for wines with slightly higher alcohol. Whites come from Caprettone and Coda di Volpe, reds from Piedirosso and Aglianico. The loose volcanic sand means many vines are ungrafted.
appellations.terroir: The southern and eastern slopes of Vesuvius (1,281 m) between about 150 and 500 m, on loose volcanic sand, ash and lapilli from many eruptions, including AD 79 and 1944. Low rainfall and hot sun are balanced by sea breezes.

appellations.name: Campi Flegrei
appellations.summary: The Campi Flegrei, the 'burning fields' west of Naples, are a giant active caldera with more than 20 craters, hot springs and the bradyseism that raises and lowers the ground at Pozzuoli. The vineyards grow on loose volcanic sand, many ungrafted, some inside craters (the Astroni, Agnano). The DOC (1994) is built on Falanghina, here a different biotype from Sannio's, and Piedirosso, which gives light, aromatic, smoky reds that are the region's hidden treasure.
appellations.nerd_note: Raffaele Moccia's Agnanum vineyards sit on the edge of the Astroni crater nature reserve inside the city of Naples, on terraces of pure volcanic sand.

appellations.name: Ischia
appellations.summary: Ischia was the first Greek colony in the West: Pithekoussai, founded around 770 BC, where archaeologists found 'Nestor's cup', a clay drinking cup inscribed with verses about wine and love, one of the oldest examples of Greek writing. The island's DOC dates from 1966, among Italy's first. Vines grow on steep volcanic terraces held up by green tuff walls (*parracine*), worked by hand or with monorails; Biancolella and Forastera make saline, herb-scented whites. About 100 ha remain of thousands once planted.
appellations.nerd_note: Casa d'Ambra's Frassitelli vineyard sits on terraces at 500 to 600 m on Monte Epomeo, reached by monorail.

appellations.name: Capri
appellations.summary: The island of Capri has its own DOC but barely a hectare of declared vines. Emperor Tiberius lived here from AD 27, and Roman villas once had vineyards; today Capri wine is a curiosity sold to visitors.

appellations.name: Penisola Sorrentina
appellations.grapes: Piedirosso, Aglianico, Sciascinoso (Olivella); Falanghina, Biancolella, Greco
appellations.summary: The Sorrento peninsula DOC is famous for two subzones that make red frizzante: Gragnano and Lettere, dark, fruity, lightly sparkling and slightly sweet or dry, the classic wine of Neapolitan pizza. A Sorrento subzone covers still wines. The Romans praised Surrentine wine as good for convalescents.

appellations.name: Costa d'Amalfi
appellations.grapes: Falanghina, Biancolella, Fenile, Ginestra, Ripoli, Pepella; Piedirosso, Aglianico, Tintore
appellations.summary: Vineyards on the Amalfi Coast hang on terraces cut into limestone cliffs above the sea, some so steep that grapes are carried down on shoulders or by monorail. The DOC (1995) has three subzones. Furore, a village with almost no centre, is the domain of Marisa Cuomo, whose Fiorduva (from Fenile, Ginestra and Ripoli) is one of Italy's most famous coastal whites. Ravello makes whites and reds on the hills above the town. Tramonti, inland in the Lattari mountains, has ungrafted Tintore and Piedirosso vines, some 150 years old or more, trained on chestnut pergolas.
appellations.nerd_note: Tintore di Tramonti is a teinturier (red-fleshed) grape; Tenuta San Francesco's E' Iss comes from ungrafted vines more than a century old.

appellations.name: Cilento
appellations.summary: The hills of the Cilento national park south of Salerno, near the Greek temples of Paestum and the ancient city of Velia. Fiano here is broader and sunnier than in Irpinia, and Aglianico is softer. Luigi Maffini and De Conciliis brought it attention in the 1990s.

appellations.name: Castel San Lorenzo
appellations.summary: A small DOC in the hills of the Calore Salernitano valley, oddly based on Barbera for reds, plus a sweet Moscato. About 11 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 10,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Primitivo di Manduria
appellations.summary:
Primitivo di Manduria is Puglia's best-known wine and one of Italy's fastest-growing DOCs, with about 3,900 ha around the town of Manduria and 17 neighbouring communes in the provinces of Taranto and Brindisi. The grape, genetically the same as Zinfandel, ripens early (hence the name), accumulates sugar fast and gives wines of 14 to 16% alcohol, with blackberry jam, dried fig, liquorice and sweet spice. Riserva needs two years including nine months in wood.

Much of the volume is soft and slightly sweet in style for export, but old bush vines on red earth near the coast, such as Gianfranco Fino's Es, show how dense and complex it can be. The sweet version has its own DOCG.
appellations.terroir: Flat to gently rolling land between the Murge and the Ionian Sea, with red earth over limestone near the coast and deeper clay inland. Hot, dry summers; sea breezes keep nights a little cooler.

appellations.name: Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale
appellations.summary: A naturally sweet red from late-harvested Primitivo, often left to raisin on the vine or briefly dried, with at least 50 g/l of residual sugar and no fortification. A DOCG since 2011, it revives the old local habit of making sweet wine from the ripest grapes. Dark, port-like but unfortified, with fig, prune and chocolate.

appellations.name: Gioia del Colle
appellations.grapes: Primitivo (varietal minimum 90%); Rosso blends with Montepulciano, Negroamaro, Malvasia Nera
appellations.summary: Gioia del Colle, on the Murge plateau at 300 to 450 m between Bari and Taranto, is the cradle of Primitivo: the priest Francesco Filippo Indellicati selected the variety here around 1799. Altitude and cooler nights give a fresher, more structured Primitivo than Manduria's, with red fruit, Mediterranean herbs and firmer acidity, from limestone and red clay. Polvanera, Pietraventosa and Fatalone lead the area.
appellations.nerd_note: Gioia del Colle's growers argue their Primitivo is the original, and that Manduria's came later, when the grape travelled south as a dowry in the 1880s.

appellations.name: Salice Salentino
appellations.grapes: Negroamaro minimum 75% (often with Malvasia Nera); whites from Chardonnay, Fiano, Verdeca
appellations.summary: The best-known Negroamaro DOC, about 1,700 ha in the flat heart of the Salento between Lecce and Brindisi. Negroamaro ('black-bitter') gives dark, soft reds with plum, tobacco, earth and a bitter, almond finish, often blended with a little Malvasia Nera. Rosato has a special place: Leone de Castris, based in Salice, bottled Five Roses in 1943, said to be the first rosé bottled in Italy, after American officers asked for a pink wine.
appellations.terroir: Flat red earth and sandy clay over limestone, swept by winds from both seas (the hot sirocco and the cooler tramontana); bush-trained vines resist heat and drought.
appellations.nerd_note: Cosimo Taurino's Patriglione, from late-harvested Negroamaro in Guagnano, was one of the first Puglian wines to be taken seriously abroad in the 1980s.

appellations.name: Brindisi
appellations.grapes: Negroamaro, Malvasia Nera, Susumaniello; whites Chardonnay, Fiano, Malvasia Bianca
appellations.summary: A Salento DOC around Brindisi and Mesagne, for Negroamaro reds and rosés and, increasingly, Susumaniello, a dark, juicy local grape rescued from near extinction. Tenute Rubino and Agricole Vallone are key producers; Vallone's Graticciaia (from partially dried Negroamaro) is a classic.

appellations.name: Negroamaro di Terra d'Otranto
appellations.summary: A DOC covering the provinces of Lecce, Brindisi and Taranto for varietal Negroamaro, red, rosé and sparkling, created in 2011 to give the grape a single regional name.

appellations.name: Terra d'Otranto
appellations.grapes: Primitivo, Aleatico, Malvasia Nera; Fiano, Verdeca, Chardonnay, Malvasia Bianca
appellations.summary: A broad Salento DOC (2011) covering the old Terra d'Otranto, the historic name of the southern heel, for many varietal wines. About 28 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 43,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Copertino
appellations.summary: A Negroamaro DOC around Copertino, south of Lecce, known for its large cooperative and earthy, plummy reds. About 76 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 829,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Squinzano
appellations.summary: A Negroamaro DOC north of Lecce around Squinzano, close to Salice Salentino in style. About 52 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 147,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Leverano
appellations.grapes: Negroamaro; whites Malvasia Bianca, Chardonnay, Fiano
appellations.summary: A Negroamaro DOC west of Lecce, notable for Conti Zecca's wines and for a passito white. About 105 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 710,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Nardò
appellations.summary: A small Negroamaro DOC around Nardò, near the Ionian coast of the Salento. About 24 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 119,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Alezio
appellations.summary: A tiny DOC near Gallipoli, historically known for its Negroamaro rosato; Michele Calò's Mjère is the reference. About 4 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 15,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Galatina
appellations.summary: A small DOC around Galatina in the southern Salento, famous for its frescoed basilica and the tarantismo rituals. About 2 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 18,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Matino
appellations.summary: One of the southernmost DOCs in Italy, created in 1971 in the Salento near Gallipoli, for Negroamaro reds and rosés with Malvasia Nera. The red-earth hills of the Serre Salentine give dark, warm wines, but production under the name is now almost nil, as growers use IGT Salento instead.

appellations.name: Lizzano
appellations.summary: A DOC east of Taranto known for Malvasia Nera di Lizzano and Negroamaro reds and rosés. About 24 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 51,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Colline Joniche Tarantine
appellations.summary: A DOC created in 2008 on the hills that ring the Gulf of Taranto, the ancient Greek city of Taras, for Primitivo, Cabernet Sauvignon and whites from Verdeca and Chardonnay. It overlaps Primitivo di Manduria and Lizzano, and very little wine carries the name.

appellations.name: Castel del Monte
appellations.grapes: Nero di Troia, Aglianico, Montepulciano, Bombino Nero, Cabernet; whites Bombino Bianco, Pampanuto, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Named after Frederick II's 13th-century octagonal castle, which sits alone on a hill of the Murge plateau, this DOC covers the hills around Andria, Corato, Minervino and Ruvo. It is the home of Nero di Troia, a late-ripening grape with firm tannin and violet, black cherry and spice aromas, and of Bombino Nero, which gives delicate rosé. Three styles have been separate DOCGs since 2011: Rosso Riserva, Nero di Troia Riserva and Bombino Nero (rosato).
appellations.terroir: Limestone plateau and slopes at 200 to 500 m, with thin red soils and big day-night swings; cooler and windier than the Salento.
contains: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva

appellations.name: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva
match: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva
appellations.summary: The top expression of Nero di Troia (Uva di Troia), a DOCG since 2011: at least 90% of the grape and two years of ageing, one in wood. Firm, dark and perfumed with violets and spice. Rivera's Puer Apuliae and Torrevento's Vigna Pedale are references.

appellations.name: Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva
appellations.grapes: Nero di Troia minimum 65%, with Aglianico, Montepulciano and others
appellations.summary: A Riserva red DOCG with Nero di Troia as the main grape blended with Aglianico or Montepulciano, aged two years. Rivera's Il Falcone, made since 1971, is the classic. About 46 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 316,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Castel del Monte Bombino Nero
appellations.summary: A rosé-only DOCG, one of the very few in Italy. Bombino Nero ripens unevenly, which keeps acidity high and makes it ideal for fresh, cherry-scented pink wine. Torrevento and Rivera make good examples.

appellations.name: Barletta
appellations.summary: A DOC around the port of Barletta on the Adriatic coast, created as Rosso Barletta in 1977 and widened in 2011, for Nero di Troia reds and Malvasia whites. In the 19th century Barletta was a busy wine port shipping deep, strong reds to France after phylloxera.

appellations.name: Moscato di Trani
appellations.summary: A sweet Muscat from the coastal plain around Trani, made as a naturally sweet or fortified (liquoroso) wine. It was famous in the 19th century; today only a hectare or so is declared. Villa Schinosa and Rivera have kept it alive.

appellations.name: Gravina
appellations.grapes: Malvasia, Greco, Bianco d'Alessano; Montepulciano, Primitivo
appellations.summary: A small DOC on the edge of the Murge around Gravina in Puglia, near the Basilicata border, mostly for whites. About 11 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 14,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Locorotondo
appellations.summary: Locorotondo is a round white hill town in the Valle d'Itria, the land of *trulli*, the conical dry-stone houses. Its DOC makes light, crisp whites from Verdeca and Bianco d'Alessano on the cooler Murge plateau, a rare fresh white in hot Puglia; the cooperative Cantina di Locorotondo makes most of it.

appellations.name: Martina Franca
appellations.summary: A twin of Locorotondo across the Valle d'Itria, around the baroque town of Martina Franca, for light Verdeca whites. In the 19th century these wines were shipped north as base for vermouth.

appellations.name: Ostuni
appellations.summary: A small DOC below the white town of Ostuni, notable for rare local grapes: the whites Impigno and Francavidda, and Ottavianello, the local name for Cinsault, which makes a light red.

appellations.name: San Severo
appellations.grapes: Bombino Bianco, Trebbiano; Montepulciano, Sangiovese, Nero di Troia
appellations.summary: One of Puglia's oldest DOCs, on the Tavoliere plain north of Foggia, for Bombino Bianco whites (including sparkling) and Montepulciano reds. About 121 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 720,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Tavoliere delle Puglie
appellations.summary: A DOC created in 2011 for Nero di Troia on the Tavoliere, the great plain of the province of Foggia, Italy's second-largest after the Po valley. About 21 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 30,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Cacc'e mmitte di Lucera
appellations.grapes: Nero di Troia, Montepulciano, Sangiovese, with white Bombino and Trebbiano
appellations.summary: The name, in local dialect, means roughly 'drink it up and pour again': in the old days farmers drank the wine fast so the vats could be refilled. It is a light red blend around the hill town of Lucera, whose castle was built by Frederick II.

appellations.name: Rosso di Cerignola
appellations.summary: A nearly dormant DOC for Nero di Troia-based reds around Cerignola on the Tavoliere. About 1 ha were declared in 2021.

appellations.name: Orta Nova
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese minimum 60%, with Nero di Troia, Montepulciano
appellations.summary: A small DOC south of Foggia, unusual for Puglia in using Sangiovese as its main grape. About 2 ha were declared in 2019, giving roughly 7,500 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Aleatico di Puglia
appellations.summary: A region-wide DOC for sweet and fortified Aleatico, the rose-scented red Muscat relative. Barely any is declared today, though a few producers in the Salento and Gioia del Colle still make it.

appellations.name: Aglianico del Vulture
appellations.summary: Aglianico del Vulture comes from 15 communes on the slopes of Monte Vulture, an extinct volcano last active about 40,000 years ago. The soils of tuff and ash give the wine a smoky, mineral side to go with Aglianico's black cherry, plum, tar and violets, and its high acid and tannin make it age as well as Taurasi. The basic wine is released after about a year; the Superiore and Riserva are a separate DOCG since 2010. About 580 ha.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic soils at 200 to 700 m, highest around Barile, Rionero and Ripacandida; the east-facing slopes toward the Ofanto valley get cool winds, and harvests run late into autumn.
