appellations.nerd_note: Elena Fucci's Titolo comes from a single 6 ha vineyard in Contrada Solagna del Titolo at Barile, at about 600 m, with vines 55 to 70 years old.

appellations.name: Aglianico del Vulture Superiore
appellations.summary: The DOCG tier of Aglianico del Vulture, created in 2010 and Basilicata's only DOCG: at least three years of ageing with a year in wood and a year in bottle (five years for Riserva), and 13.5% minimum alcohol. These are dark, smoky, firmly tannic wines that need a decade.

appellations.name: Matera
appellations.grapes: Primitivo, Sangiovese, Aglianico, Cabernet; Greco, Malvasia
appellations.summary: A DOC covering the province of Matera, the city of the Sassi cave dwellings (UNESCO site), for Primitivo, Moro (a Cabernet-Primitivo-Merlot blend) and Greco whites. About 57 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 140,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Grottino di Roccanova
appellations.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet, Malvasia Nera; Malvasia Bianca
appellations.summary: A small DOC around Roccanova in southern Basilicata, named for the *grottini*, small caves dug into the hillside where farmers aged their wine. About 11 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 31,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Terre dell'Alta Val d'Agri
appellations.summary: A small DOC in the high Agri valley around Viggiano and Grumento Nova, for Merlot and Cabernet-based reds, a legacy of plantings by local aristocrats. About 16 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 13,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Cirò Classico
appellations.grapes: Gaglioppo minimum 90%, Magliocco and/or Greco Nero up to 10%
appellations.summary:
Calabria's first DOCG, recognised in 2025 and registered by the European Commission on 18 July 2025 (Regulation 2025/1518), it is one of two DOCGs created in 2025 (with Abruzzo's Casauria), which took Italy's total to 79. It covers only the communes of Cirò and Cirò Marina, the historic heart of the Cirò DOC, on hills from sea level to 462 m above the Ionian coast. The wine is a red of at least 90% Gaglioppo with up to 10% Magliocco or Greco Nero, no international varieties, aged at least three years with six months in wood, with yields capped at 8 t/ha and production and bottling inside the zone.

Gaglioppo is a paradox: pale in colour, like Nebbiolo, but with firm tannin, flavours of red cherry, orange peel, dried herbs and earth, and real ageing ability. Its modern revival owes much to Librandi and to the Cirò Revolution, a group of small growers founded around 2010 (Sergio Arcuri, A Vita of Francesco De Franco, Cataldo Calabretta, Tenuta del Conte) who went back to old bush vines, large casks and minimal intervention.
appellations.terroir: Clay, marl and sand hills between the Ionian Sea and the Sila foothills, with mineral-rich sedimentary soils; the mountains to the west and the sea to the east shape a warm, dry climate with ventilated nights.
appellations.nerd_note: Gaglioppo is a cross of Sangiovese and Mantonico Bianco, which may explain its Tuscan-looking colour and its southern warmth.

appellations.name: Cirò
appellations.grapes: Rosso and Rosato: Gaglioppo minimum 80%; Bianco: Greco Bianco minimum 80%
appellations.summary: Calabria's most important DOC, on the Ionian coast in the province of Crotone, covering Cirò, Cirò Marina, Crucoli and Melissa. Reds and rosés come from Gaglioppo, whites from Greco Bianco. The Classico Superiore Riserva reds of Cirò and Cirò Marina moved into the new Cirò Classico DOCG in 2025, so this DOC now covers the rest: fresh Cirò Rosso and Rosato, Bianco and wines from outside the Classico core.

appellations.name: Greco di Bianco
appellations.grapes: Greco Bianco (a local variety, also called Greco di Bianco) minimum 95%
appellations.summary: A sweet white passito from the town of Bianco and Casignana on the Ionian coast near the tip of the boot, made from late-harvested Greco grapes dried in the sun on cane mats until shrivelled. The wine is amber, with orange blossom, candied citrus, apricot and honey, at least 17% alcohol, and is one of the most distinctive sweet wines of southern Italy. The local grape is a distinct variety (genetically the same as Malvasia di Lipari). Umberto Ceratti made it famous.
appellations.nerd_note: The grape is genetically identical to Malvasia di Lipari and Malvasia di Sardegna, a Greek family of aromatic whites scattered across the southern islands.

appellations.name: Melissa
appellations.summary: A Ionian DOC south of Cirò around Melissa and neighbouring communes, for Gaglioppo reds and Greco whites similar to Cirò's. About 14 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 135,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: S. Anna di Isola Capo Rizzuto
match: S. Anna di Isola Capo Rizzuto
appellations.grapes: Gaglioppo with Nocera, Nerello, Malvasia Nera
appellations.summary: A small coastal DOC south of Crotone near the Capo Rizzuto marine reserve, for Gaglioppo-based reds and rosés. About 3 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 8,700 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Lamezia
appellations.grapes: Gaglioppo, Magliocco, Greco Nero; Greco, Montonico
appellations.summary: A Tyrrhenian-side DOC around Lamezia Terme on the narrow isthmus of Calabria, for reds from Gaglioppo, Magliocco and Greco Nero. Statti is the leading estate. About 10 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 93,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Savuto
appellations.grapes: Gaglioppo, Magliocco, Greco Nero, Nerello, Sangiovese
appellations.summary: A small DOC on the steep terraces of the Savuto river valley between Cosenza and Lamezia, one of Calabria's oldest, for blended reds; it has a Classico area. About 6 ha were declared in 2021.

appellations.name: Scavigna
appellations.grapes: Aglianico, Gaglioppo, Nerello; Trebbiano, Chardonnay, Greco
appellations.summary: A small DOC on the Tyrrhenian coast near Nocera Terinese and Falerna, with blends of local and international grapes. Little is produced.

appellations.name: Bivongi
appellations.grapes: Gaglioppo, Greco Nero, Nocera, Castiglione, Calabrese; Greco, Guardavalle, Mantonico
appellations.summary: A DOC in the Stilaro valley on the Ionian coast of southern Calabria, near the Byzantine Cattolica of Stilo, for blended reds and whites from local grapes. About 12 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 60,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Terre di Cosenza
appellations.grapes: Magliocco, Gaglioppo, Greco Nero, Aglianico; Greco, Pecorello, Mantonico, Guarnaccia
appellations.summary: A big DOC created in 2011 covering the province of Cosenza, absorbing the former DOCs Donnici, Pollino, San Vito di Luzzi and Verbicaro as subzones (with Colline del Crati, Condoleo and Esaro). It is the home of Magliocco, a dark, tannic red, and Pecorello, a rare white revived by Cantine Spadafora and others.

appellations.name: Etna
appellations.created: 1968 (Sicily's first DOC); contrade on labels since 2011; DOCG application pending
appellations.grapes: Rosso and Rosato: Nerello Mascalese minimum 80%, Nerello Cappuccio (Mantellato) up to 20%; Bianco: Carricante minimum 60% with Catarratto; Bianco Superiore: Carricante minimum 80% from Milo; Spumante: Nerello Mascalese minimum 80% (classic method, 18 months on lees).
appellations.summary:
Etna is Europe's highest active volcano (over 3,300 m) and, since the early 2000s, Italy's most dynamic wine region. Its DOC, created in 1968, was Sicily's first, but by the 1990s the old terraces were being abandoned and only a handful of families (Benanti, Barone di Villagrande, Murgo) bottled wine. Then outsiders arrived: the importer Marco de Grazia (Tenuta delle Terre Nere, 2002), the Tuscan winemaker Andrea Franchetti (Passopisciaro, 2000), the Belgian Frank Cornelissen (2001), and locals such as Alberto Graci and Giuseppe Russo. They found century-old, often ungrafted bush vines of Nerello Mascalese on north-slope terraces at 600 to 1,000 m, and wines that recalled Burgundy and Barolo more than Sicily.

The zone forms a crescent on the north, east and south slopes, in 20 communes. Growth has been explosive: about 670 ha were claimed in 2013, 1,347 in 2024 and 1,449 in 2025, with roughly 474 growers and 5.8 million bottles a year, and bottling up 13.6% in the first eight months of 2026. Since 2011 producers have been able to name one of 133 *contrade*, the traditional named districts, often defined by a single lava flow of a known age; the consorzio's 2022 map counts 142.

Etna Rosso, from Nerello Mascalese with a little Nerello Cappuccio, is pale, with red cherry, wild herbs, smoke and fine, firm tannins. Etna Bianco, from Carricante, is lean and saline, and Bianco Superiore must come from the commune of Milo on the east slope. Members voted unanimously on 10 November 2023 to seek DOCG status; signatures were still being gathered at the end of 2025 and, as of October 2026, the DOCG had not been granted. The proposed rules cut yields (8 t/ha for Etna Rosso, about 6.5 to 7 t/ha for contrada wines), set minimum vine ages for contrada bottlings, cap new planting, allow commune names, and open sparkling wine to Carricante and pas dosé.
appellations.terroir: Each contrada sits on lava of a different age and texture, from ancient, weathered flows with deeper soils to young, coarse lava sand with almost no organic matter, all very low in clay (under about 3%) and too loose for phylloxera to thrive, which is why ungrafted vines survive. The north slope (Randazzo, Passopisciaro, Solicchiata) is the heart of red wine, between about 500 and 1,000 m, with warm days and cold nights; it lies in the rain shadow and harvests run into October. The east slope (Milo, Zafferana, Santa Venerina) faces the sea and catches most of the rain (more than 1,000 mm a year in places), perfect for Carricante. The south and southwest slopes (Viagrande, Trecastagni, Biancavilla, Santa Maria di Licodia) are warmer and drier. The DOC boundary follows contour lines, with vineyards up to about 1,100 m; some plantings now exceed it.
appellations.nerd_note: Many Etna vineyards are planted *ad alberello* at about 10,000 vines per hectare and staked with chestnut poles, worked by hand on terraces of dry-stone lava walls (*muretti a secco*); Salvo Foti's I Vigneri is named after a 15th-century guild of Etna vineyard workers.

appellations.name: Cerasuolo di Vittoria
appellations.summary: Sicily's only DOCG, from the southeastern corner of the island around Vittoria, Comiso and Acate in the province of Ragusa. Despite the name (*cerasuolo*, cherry-coloured), it is a red, a blend of the dark, structured Nero d'Avola with the pale, perfumed Frappato, which gives flavours of red cherry, pomegranate and violets with gentle tannin and lively acidity. The Classico area, the historic core, needs about 18 months of ageing. Two growers changed its fortunes: COS, founded in 1980 by Giambattista Cilia, Giusto Occhipinti and Cirino Strano, who later revived amphora ageing, and Arianna Occhipinti, whose Frappato became a natural-wine icon.
appellations.terroir: Red sand (*terra rossa*) over limestone tuff on a plateau at 150 to 300 m, close to the sea, with hot days and breezy nights. Sandy soils protected some vines from phylloxera.

appellations.name: Vittoria
appellations.summary: The companion DOC to Cerasuolo di Vittoria, created in 2005, mostly used for varietal Frappato, a light, fragrant red that is best slightly chilled, plus Nero d'Avola and Inzolia. About 127 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 356,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Marsala
appellations.grapes: Oro and Ambra: Grillo, Catarratto, Ansonica (Inzolia), Damaschino; Rubino: Perricone, Nero d'Avola, Nerello Mascalese (up to 30% white grapes)
appellations.summary:
Marsala is Sicily's fortified wine and an English invention. In 1773 the Liverpool merchant John Woodhouse, sheltering from a storm in the port of Marsala, tasted the local *perpetuum*, an oxidised wine topped up year after year in casks, and shipped some to England with added spirit to survive the voyage. It sold. In 1796 he began production in earnest, and Nelson is said to have ordered it for his fleet. Benjamin Ingham of Leeds arrived in 1806 and built a rival baglio, and in 1833 Vincenzo Florio, a Calabrian-born Palermo entrepreneur, set up between the two and eventually outgrew them. Garibaldi landed his Thousand at Marsala in 1860, and a sweet 'Garibaldi Dolce' style was named after him.

The 20th century turned Marsala into a cooking wine and flavoured mixes (egg, almond); a 1984 reform removed those from the DOC and tightened the categories. Today Marsala is classified by colour (Oro and Ambra from white grapes, Ambra coloured with cooked must, Rubino from red grapes), sweetness (secco up to 40 g/l, semisecco, dolce over 100 g/l) and age: Fine (1 year), Superiore (2 years), Superiore Riserva (4), Vergine or Soleras (5) and Vergine Stravecchio or Riserva (10). Vergine is the purist's Marsala: dry, never sweetened, fortified only with spirit and aged in a solera-like system. Marco De Bartoli revived the old unfortified *perpetuum* style in the 1980s with Vecchio Samperi.
appellations.terroir: The flat to gently rolling coast of the province of Trapani (excluding the islands and Alcamo), with sandy, limestone-rich soils and hot, windy summers; the salt pans and lagoon of the Stagnone lie just north of the town.
appellations.nerd_note: Label codes survive from the English trade: I.P. (Italia Particolare) on Fine; L.P. (London Particular), S.O.M. (Superior Old Marsala) and G.D. (Garibaldi Dolce) on Superiore.

appellations.name: Pantelleria
match: Pantelleria / Moscato di Pantelleria / Passito di Pantelleria
appellations.summary:
Pantelleria is a windswept volcanic island 100 km southwest of Sicily and only 70 km from Tunisia. Its name in Arabic, *Bint al-Riyah*, means 'daughter of the winds', and the winds shaped its viticulture: Zibibbo vines are grown as tiny bushes in hollows dug into the black soil, protected by dry-stone walls, so the leaves shade the grapes and the plants catch every drop of dew. On 26 November 2014 UNESCO inscribed the 'traditional agricultural practice of cultivating the vite ad alberello' of Pantelleria on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list, the first agricultural practice ever recognised.

Passito di Pantelleria is made by drying part of the harvest in the sun for weeks on mats, then adding the raisins to fresh must from late-picked grapes, so the wine ferments slowly into an amber, intensely sweet wine of apricot, candied orange, fig and Mediterranean herbs, balanced by acidity and minerality. About 430 ha remain, many tended by elderly growers. Moscato, dry Zibibbo and liqueur versions exist too.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic soils of ash, pumice and lava, rich in minerals and potassium but poor in organic matter; constant wind, almost no rain in summer, and vineyards from sea level to about 400 m, on terraces held up by dry-stone walls.
appellations.nerd_note: Zibibbo takes its name from the Arabic *zabib*, raisin; on Pantelleria the bushes are pruned so low that pickers work on their knees.

appellations.name: Malvasia delle Lipari
appellations.grapes: Malvasia di Lipari minimum 95% (Corinto Nero up to 8%)
appellations.summary: The Aeolian islands north of Sicily, especially Salina, make Malvasia delle Lipari, a sweet golden wine that was famous in the 18th and 19th centuries until phylloxera and emigration emptied the islands. The Milanese designer Carlo Hauner, who settled on Salina in the 1960s, revived it in the 1970s and 1980s. The grapes are dried on cane mats for 10 to 15 days; the Passito is amber, with apricot, honey, capers and sea salt. A light, unfortified version (Naturale) and a fortified Liquoroso also exist. Only about 9 ha are declared.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic slopes of Salina (twin extinct volcanoes), Lipari and Vulcano, on pumice and ash, with sea winds and strong sun.
appellations.nerd_note: Malvasia di Lipari is genetically the same grape as Greco di Bianco in Calabria and Malvasia di Sardegna.

appellations.name: Faro
appellations.grapes: Nerello Mascalese 45 to 60%, Nerello Cappuccio, Nocera, with Nero d'Avola, Gaglioppo, Sangiovese
appellations.summary: Faro, named for the lighthouse at the tip of Sicily on the Strait of Messina, is one of Italy's smallest DOCs. By the 1980s it was nearly extinct, until the critic Luigi Veronelli encouraged the architect Salvatore Geraci to revive his family's vineyards; Geraci's Palari Faro, a blend of Nerello Mascalese, Nerello Cappuccio and Nocera from steep terraces above the strait, became one of Sicily's great reds in the 1990s.
appellations.nerd_note: Faro's blend includes Nocera, an almost forgotten Sicilian red, and the vines grow on steep terraces that look across to Calabria.

appellations.name: Mamertino
appellations.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Nocera; Grillo, Inzolia, Catarratto
appellations.summary: A DOC on the Tyrrhenian coast west of Messina around Milazzo, named after Mamertine wine, which Pliny praised and Julius Caesar served at a banquet for his third consulship in 46 BC. Today it covers Nero d'Avola and Nocera reds and Grillo-Inzolia whites.

appellations.name: Noto
appellations.summary: The baroque town of Noto gives its name to a DOC for two very different wines. Moscato di Noto was the original, a sweet, sparkling or fortified Muscat with an ancient reputation. Since the 1990s the area has become the heartland of Nero d'Avola: the grape takes its name from the nearby town of Avola, and the red sand and limestone around Noto and Pachino give its most elegant, age-worthy versions, such as Planeta's Santa Cecilia.
appellations.nerd_note: Nero d'Avola is also called Calabrese, possibly a corruption of 'Calea-aulisi', grape of Avola in dialect, rather than a sign of Calabrian origin.

appellations.name: Eloro
appellations.summary: A DOC in the far southeastern tip of Sicily around Pachino, Noto and Rosolini, overlapping Noto, for varietal Nero d'Avola, Frappato and Pignatello. Its Pachino subzone is for a Nero d'Avola-based red; the area is better known for its tomatoes.

appellations.name: Siracusa
appellations.summary: Moscato di Siracusa, sometimes linked by enthusiasts to the ancient Pollio wine of Greek Syracuse, had almost disappeared when the Pupillo family revived it in the 1990s. The DOC was expanded in 2011 to include reds and whites.

appellations.name: Sicilia
appellations.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Grillo, Catarratto, Inzolia, Frappato, Nerello, Perricone, Carricante, Zibibbo and international varieties
appellations.summary: An island-wide DOC created in 2011 from the old Sicilia IGT, about 24,600 ha and 800,000 hl a year, which makes it one of Italy's biggest denominations. It was designed to protect the names Nero d'Avola and Grillo, which until then could be used on wines bottled anywhere: since 2017 those varietal names on labels are reserved for DOC Sicilia. The quality ranges from supermarket wine to estate bottlings, and Salemi was added as the first UGA.

appellations.name: Contea di Sclafani
match: Contea di Sclafani / Valledolmo-Contea di Sclafani
appellations.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Perricone, Cabernet, Syrah; Inzolia, Catarratto, Grecanico, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A DOC on the high central plateau between Palermo and Caltanissetta, essentially defined by one estate: Tasca d'Almerita's Regaleali, owned by the family since 1830, at 400 to 900 m. Count Giuseppe Tasca made Rosso del Conte (from 1970), one of the first great modern Sicilian reds, and Regaleali showed that the cool interior could make fresh wines. The altitude and clay soils give big day-night swings.

appellations.name: Menfi
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Grecanico, Fiano, Inzolia; Nero d'Avola, Syrah, Cabernet
appellations.summary: A DOC on the southwest coast around Menfi, the home base of the Planeta family, whose first vintage in 1995 (with a barrel-fermented Chardonnay from the Ulmo estate) symbolised the new Sicily. Settesoli, one of Italy's largest cooperatives, is also here. Sandy limestone near the sea suits whites.

appellations.name: Sambuca di Sicilia
appellations.grapes: Ansonica, Chardonnay, Grillo; Nero d'Avola, Cabernet, Syrah
appellations.summary: A small DOC around Sambuca di Sicilia and Lake Arancio, where Planeta's Ulmo estate is located.

appellations.name: Santa Margherita di Belice
appellations.grapes: Ansonica, Catarratto, Grecanico; Nero d'Avola, Sangiovese, Cabernet
appellations.summary: A tiny DOC in the Belice valley, where the 1968 earthquake destroyed the town that Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa's family palace (Donnafugata in *The Leopard*) once dominated. Barely 0.5 ha were declared in 2019, so the name is close to dormant.

appellations.name: Sciacca
appellations.grapes: Inzolia, Catarratto, Grecanico, Chardonnay; Nero d'Avola, Merlot, Cabernet, Sangiovese
appellations.summary: A small DOC around the spa town of Sciacca, below Monte Kronio, where Copper Age jars with wine residues (about 4000 BC) were found. Its Rayana subzone is for a Catarratto-Inzolia white Riserva.

appellations.name: Contessa Entellina
appellations.grapes: Ansonica, Catarratto, Grecanico, Chardonnay; Nero d'Avola, Syrah, Cabernet
appellations.summary: An inland DOC around Contessa Entellina, an Arbëreshë (Albanian-Sicilian) village. It is essentially the home of Donnafugata's Tenuta di Contessa Entellina, at 200 to 600 m, source of its Mille e una Notte and Chiarandà.

appellations.name: Salaparuta
appellations.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah; Catarratto, Inzolia, Grillo, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A small DOC around Salaparuta in the Belice valley. The town gave its name to the Duca di Salaparuta family, whose Corvo brand (founded 1824 at Casteldaccia near Palermo) was Sicily's most famous wine label for a century.

appellations.name: Alcamo
appellations.grapes: Catarratto, Inzolia, Grillo, Grecanico; Nero d'Avola, Calabrese, Frappato, Perricone
appellations.summary: One of Sicily's older DOCs, on the hills between Palermo and Trapani around Alcamo and Monte Bonifato, built on Catarratto. Bianco Classico from Catarratto Bianco Lucido is the traditional style; Rapitalà is the best-known estate.

appellations.name: Monreale
appellations.grapes: Catarratto, Inzolia, Grillo; Perricone, Nero d'Avola, Syrah
appellations.summary: A DOC on the hills behind Palermo around Monreale, famous for its Norman cathedral mosaics. Perricone, a tannic native red, is a local speciality. About 46 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 100,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Erice
appellations.grapes: Catarratto, Grillo, Inzolia, Zibibbo; Nero d'Avola, Frappato, Perricone, Syrah
appellations.summary: A DOC in the hinterland below the hill town of Erice near Trapani, for whites, reds and sweet Zibibbo. About 52 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 156,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Delia Nivolelli
appellations.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Perricone; Grecanico, Inzolia, Grillo, Damaschino
appellations.summary: A small DOC between Mazara del Vallo, Marsala and Salemi, named after the Delia river and the Nivolelli plain, with varietal wines from Sicilian and international grapes. About 2 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 13,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Riesi
appellations.grapes: Nero d'Avola, Cabernet, Syrah; Ansonica, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: A DOC in the province of Caltanissetta around Riesi and Butera, sulphur-mining country in the hot centre-south, mostly for Nero d'Avola-based reds; Feudo Principi di Butera (Zonin) is here. About 12 ha were declared in 2021.

appellations.name: Cannonau di Sardegna
appellations.summary:
Cannonau is Sardinia's Grenache, and the island's most important red: about 2,100 ha in the DOC, which covers the whole island. It thrives in the mountainous east, where small growers keep old bush vines on granite and schist at 300 to 700 m. Good Cannonau is warm and spicy, with red berries, Mediterranean scrub, dried herbs and a firm, slightly bitter finish; the alcohol is often high, but altitude and the mistral give freshness. The DOC also allows rosé, Riserva, passito and fortified (liquoroso) wines.

Three subzones carry extra prestige. Jerzu, in the Ogliastra, is a village of terraced vineyards below limestone *tacchi* (cliffs) and a large cooperative, Antichi Poderi di Jerzu. Oliena, below the limestone of Monte Corrasi near Nuoro, makes 'Nepente di Oliena', the name the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio gave to its wine in 1909, comparing it to the drug of oblivion in Homer. Capo Ferrato, on the southeast coast, is warmer. Classico, from the provinces of Nuoro and Ogliastra, requires 90% Cannonau. Mamoiada, though not an official subzone, has become a byword for high-altitude, artisanal Cannonau, with dozens of tiny family producers.
appellations.terroir: Granite sands in the Barbagia and around Mamoiada (600 to 700 m), limestone near Oliena and Jerzu, schist in the Mandrolisai; hot, dry summers with strong winds, cold winters inland.
appellations.nerd_note: In the 1990s a Sardinian study claimed that Cannonau's high polyphenol content helped explain the longevity of Ogliastra's centenarians; the link is unproven, but the region's long-lived shepherds still drink it daily.

appellations.name: Vermentino di Gallura
appellations.summary: Sardinia's only DOCG, from the granite highlands of Gallura in the northeast, including the communes of Tempio Pausania, Calangianus, Luras, Berchidda, Monti and Arzachena, the hinterland of the Costa Smeralda. The decomposed granite and the wind give Vermentino a mineral, saline intensity found nowhere else: lemon, white peach, Mediterranean herbs, a hint of bitter almond and a long, salty finish. Superiore must reach 13% alcohol; frizzante, spumante, late-harvest and passito versions exist. Capichera's barrel-aged, late-picked Vermentino helped show the grape's potential for depth and age.
appellations.terroir: Weathered granite sands (*sabbione*) and rocky outcrops at 50 to 500 m, battered by the mistral, with cork-oak woods around Calangianus and Tempio.
appellations.nerd_note: Vermentino is genetically the same as Liguria's Pigato and Piedmont's Favorita, and as Corsica's Vermentinu (Rolle in Provence).

appellations.name: Vermentino di Sardegna
appellations.summary: The island-wide Vermentino DOC, about 1,500 ha and 10 million bottles a year, produced everywhere from Alghero to the Campidano. It is generally lighter and fruitier than Vermentino di Gallura; the best come from Argiolas, Sella & Mosca and smaller hill growers.

appellations.name: Carignano del Sulcis
appellations.summary: In the Sulcis, the southwestern corner of Sardinia, and on the islands of Sant'Antioco and San Pietro, Carignano (Carignan) grows as old bush vines on sand, many ungrafted because phylloxera cannot live in sand. The wines are dark and spicy, with blackberry, myrtle and a saline edge, far richer than most Carignan. Cantina di Santadi and the oenologist Giacomo Tachis put it on the map with Terre Brune (first vintage 1984) and Rocca Rubia.
appellations.terroir: Sandy coastal soils and dunes around Sant'Antioco and Calasetta, with clay and limestone inland around Santadi; hot, windy and dry.
appellations.nerd_note: Some of Sardus Pater's ungrafted Carignano on Sant'Antioco is believed to be over 100 years old.

appellations.name: Vernaccia di Oristano
appellations.summary: Sardinia's first DOC (1971) and one of Italy's most extraordinary wines. In the lower Tirso valley around Oristano and Cabras, Vernaccia grapes ferment to high natural alcohol (at least 15%) and the wine is aged for years in partially filled chestnut or oak barrels, where a veil of yeast (*flor*, called *sa murra* locally) forms on the surface, as in Jerez. The result is dry, amber and nutty, with almond, sea salt, dried apricot and a long, oxidative finish, like a fino turning amontillado. Superiore needs three years in barrel, Riserva four; a fortified version exists. Production has fallen to about 22 ha.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial sands and silts (*bennaxi*) of the lower Tirso valley near the lagoons of Cabras, with hot, dry summers.
appellations.nerd_note: Contini, founded in 1898 in Cabras, keeps casks of Vernaccia decades old, and its Antico Gregori is a solera-style blend of old vintages.

appellations.name: Malvasia di Bosa
appellations.summary: A rare wine from the Planargia hills around Bosa on the west coast, from Malvasia di Sardegna (the same grape as Malvasia di Lipari and Greco di Bianco). It is made dry or sweet, often aged under flor like Vernaccia, giving a golden, nutty, salty wine; sweet versions come from late-harvested grapes. The late Giovanni Battista Columbu kept it alive and made it famous through Slow Food.

appellations.name: Monica di Sardegna
appellations.summary: An island-wide DOC for Monica, a red grape probably brought by Spanish monks, giving soft, fruity, light reds for early drinking; superiore and frizzante versions exist. The old Monica di Cagliari sweet style is now part of the Cagliari DOC.

appellations.name: Moscato di Sardegna
appellations.summary: An island-wide DOC for sweet and sparkling Moscato, with subzones Gallura and Tempio Pausania for the spumante. About 47 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 135,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Moscato di Sorso-Sennori
match: Moscato di Sorso / Moscato di Sennori / Moscato di Sorso - Sennori
appellations.summary: A small DOC for sweet Moscato, naturally sweet or fortified, from the hills of Sorso and Sennori north of Sassari overlooking the Gulf of Asinara. The wines are golden, with orange blossom and apricot; production is tiny.

appellations.name: Nasco di Cagliari
appellations.summary: Nasco is an ancient white grape of the Campidano plain around Cagliari, with a musky, aromatic perfume (the name may come from the Latin *muscus*, musk). It is made dry, sweet or fortified; Argiolas's Iselis and Cantina di Dolianova keep it alive.

appellations.name: Nuragus di Cagliari
appellations.summary: Nuragus, named after the nuraghi, the Bronze Age stone towers that dot Sardinia, is a productive, neutral white grape possibly brought by the Phoenicians. The DOC around Cagliari makes light, fresh whites.

appellations.name: Girò di Cagliari
appellations.summary: Girò is a rare red grape of Spanish origin used for sweet and fortified red wines around Cagliari; only a few hectares remain. Cantina di Dolianova and Meloni make it.

appellations.name: Cagliari
appellations.summary: A DOC created in 2011 that absorbed the old Malvasia di Cagliari, Monica di Cagliari and Moscato di Cagliari DOCs, for the sweet and fortified traditions of the south. About 19 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 153,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Mandrolisai
appellations.grapes: Bovale Sardo minimum 35%, Cannonau 20 to 35%, Monica 20 to 35%
appellations.summary: A high inland DOC in the centre of the island around Sorgono, Atzara and Samugheo, on schist and granite at 500 to 700 m. Its reds blend Bovale, Cannonau and Monica, often from old mixed vineyards, and are fresher and more structured than coastal wines.

appellations.name: Campidano di Terralba
appellations.summary: A red DOC on the sandy western plain south of Oristano, built on Bovale. The sands kept many vines ungrafted. About 27 ha were declared in 2021, giving roughly 61,000 bottles a year.

appellations.name: Arborea
appellations.summary: A DOC on the reclaimed land around Arborea, south of Oristano, drained and settled in the 1920s and 1930s by farmers from the Veneto and Romagna, who planted Sangiovese and Trebbiano. It is almost dormant.

appellations.name: Alghero
appellations.grapes: Torbato, Vermentino, Chardonnay, Sauvignon; Cagnulari, Cannonau, Cabernet, Sangiovese
appellations.summary: A DOC around Alghero, the Catalan-speaking town on the northwest coast, dominated by Sella & Mosca. It is the home of Torbato, a white grape of Catalan origin (Tourbat in Roussillon) that survives almost only here, and of Cagnulari, a local red. The Anghelu Ruju passito (Cannonau) and Marchese di Villamarina (Cabernet) are Sella & Mosca classics.

appellations.name: Sardegna Semidano
appellations.summary: A DOC for Semidano, a rare aromatic white grape that once covered much of central Sardinia. Its Mogoro subzone, around the village of Mogoro in the Marmilla, holds most of the remaining vines; the cooperative Il Nuraghe keeps it going.

sites.name: Castellina (UGA)
sites.text: One of the three founding members of the medieval Lega del Chianti, Castellina sits on the ridge that splits the Pesa and Elsa valleys. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: Castelnuovo Berardenga (UGA)
sites.text: The southernmost and warmest UGA, where Chianti Classico runs down toward the clay hills of the Crete Senesi. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: Gaiole (UGA)
sites.text: Gaiole spreads across the eastern Monti del Chianti, a high, wooded commune that includes Brolio, Coltibuono, Ama and Rietine. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: Greve (UGA)
sites.text: The Greve UGA is the northern and eastern part of the commune once Panzano, Lamole and Montefioralle are carved out. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: Lamole (UGA)
sites.text: A tiny hamlet of terraces high above Greve (roughly 500 to 650 m), with dry-stone walls rebuilt by hand and sandstone soils (macigno) that give pale, high-toned, floral Sangiovese. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: Montefioralle (UGA)
sites.text: A walled medieval village on the hill just west of Greve, believed to be the family home of Amerigo Vespucci. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: Panzano (UGA)
sites.text: Panzano is the frazione in the southwest of Greve commune famous for the Conca d'Oro, a south-facing amphitheatre of galestro and alberese that collects heat and gives some of the most complete Sangiovese in Tuscany. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: Radda (UGA)
sites.text: Radda was the capital of the Lega del Chianti and is now the reference for high-altitude, galestro-driven Sangiovese: pale, perfumed and nervy, sometimes austere in youth. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: San Casciano (UGA)
sites.text: The northern gateway to the zone, on lower, gentler hills toward Florence, with sandstone and Pliocene sands. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: San Donato in Poggio (UGA)
sites.text: This UGA joins the western half of Barberino Tavarnelle with the northern tip of Poggibonsi, centred on the walled village of San Donato. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: Vagliagli (UGA)
sites.text: A hamlet in western Castelnuovo Berardenga, higher and cooler than the southern part of the commune, with alberese and sandstone. It is one of the 11 UGAs in force since the 2023 rules.

sites.name: Tenuta Tignanello (Antinori)
sites.text: The 47-hectare Tignanello vineyard, on a southwest slope of galestro and alberese near Mercatale in the San Casciano UGA, gave its name in 1971 to the wine that, with Sassicaia, launched the Super Tuscan era: a Sangiovese with Cabernet aged in French barriques, sold as vino da tavola because it broke the Chianti rules (no white grapes). Its upper parcel gives Solaia, mostly Cabernet.

sites.name: Antinori nel Chianti Classico (Bargino)
sites.text: Antinori's headquarters winery, opened in 2012 at Bargino, is buried in the hillside under a roof of vines, with two terracotta-lined slits as the only facade. The family has made wine since 1385, 26 generations.

sites.name: Castello di Ama
sites.text: A hamlet-estate at about 480 m in the Gaiole UGA, revived from the 1970s by the Sebasti and Carini families and winemaker Marco Pallanti. Its single-vineyard Chianti Classicos (Bellavista, La Casuccia) became Gran Selezione, and L'Apparita (1985) was one of Italy's first great Merlots. The estate also hosts a site-specific contemporary art collection.

sites.name: Fontodi (Conca d'Oro)
sites.text: Giovanni Manetti's organic estate sits in the Conca d'Oro, Panzano's south-facing amphitheatre of galestro. Flaccianello della Pieve, a pure Sangiovese from the Pieve vineyard first made in 1981, is one of Tuscany's benchmark reds; Vigna del Sorbo is its Gran Selezione.

sites.name: Montevertine
sites.class: IGT Toscana (outside the DOCG by choice)
sites.text: Sergio Manetti bought this Radda farm in 1967 and left the Chianti DOC in 1981 rather than add white grapes; his Le Pergole Torte (from 1977) was one of the first pure-Sangiovese Super Tuscans, aged in large casks and loved for its pale, perfumed, high-altitude style. His son Martino keeps the same style today.

sites.name: Isole e Olena
sites.text: Paolo De Marchi rebuilt this pair of hamlets in the San Donato in Poggio UGA from 1976, and his Cepparello (first vintage 1980), pure Sangiovese, became a Super Tuscan classic; he also made the zone's first Syrah. The estate was sold to the EPI group (owners of Biondi-Santi) in 2022.

sites.name: Castello di Brolio
sites.text: The red-brick castle of the Ricasoli family, owners since 1141, above the Arbia valley in Gaiole. Here Baron Bettino Ricasoli, Italy's second prime minister, experimented with Chianti blends and in a letter of 26 September 1872 described Sangioveto for aroma and vigour, Canaiolo to soften it and Malvasia only for wines meant for early drinking. That letter is the root of the 'Chianti formula'.

sites.name: Badia a Coltibuono
sites.text: An 11th-century Vallombrosan abbey in the Gaiole hills (about 630 m) whose monks planted vines here; the Stucchi Prinetti family has owned it since 1846 and keeps a cellar of old vintages back to the 1930s. The farm has been organic since 2000.

sites.name: Fèlsina
sites.text: On the southeastern edge of the zone in Castelnuovo Berardenga, where Chianti Classico meets the Crete Senesi. Fèlsina's Rancia (Gran Selezione) and Fontalloro (Sangiovese IGT straddling the Chianti Classico and Colli Senesi line) were shaped by the late oenologist Franco Bernabei.

sites.name: Castell'in Villa
sites.text: A fortified hamlet in Castelnuovo Berardenga run since the 1970s by Princess Coralia Pignatelli, known for traditional, long-aged Chianti Classico Riserva released only when ready, with library vintages back to 1971.

sites.name: Querciabella (Ruffoli)
sites.text: High in Ruffoli above Greve, Querciabella converted to organic farming in 1988 and to plant-based biodynamics without animal preparations in 2000. Camartina (Sangiovese-Cabernet) and Batàr (Chardonnay-Pinot Bianco) are its icons.

sites.name: Badia a Passignano
sites.text: A Vallombrosan abbey founded in 1049 near Tavarnelle, surrounded by Antinori vineyards since 1987; its Gran Selezione is one of the most visible in the zone. Monks here kept vineyard records for centuries.

sites.name: Castello dei Rampolla
sites.text: A Panzano estate owned by the Di Napoli family since 1739, biodynamic since 1994. Sammarco (from 1980, mostly Cabernet) and d'Alceo (Cabernet with Petit Verdot) are among the few great Bordeaux-variety wines from the Chianti hills.

sites.name: San Giusto a Rentennano
sites.text: A former Cistercian convent at the southern tip of Gaiole, run by the Martini di Cigala family. Percarlo, pure Sangiovese from 1983, and Vin San Giusto, one of the most concentrated Vin Santos in Tuscany, are its legends.

sites.name: Castello di Volpaia
sites.text: A fortified medieval village at about 600 m north of Radda, where the Stianti Mascheroni family hid a modern winery inside the old church and houses, connected by pipelines under the streets. Its Coltassala and Balifico were early Sangiovese-led Super Tuscans.

sites.name: Monteraponi
sites.text: A hilltop hamlet in Radda where Michele Braganti makes some of the most transparent, traditionally made Sangiovese in the zone (Baron'Ugo, Campitello) from organic vineyards at 420 to 570 m.

sites.name: Castello di Fonterutoli
sites.text: The Mazzei family has owned Fonterutoli, a hamlet south of Castellina, since 1435. Ser Lapo Mazzei, a Florentine notary, signed in 1398 one of the earliest documents to mention 'Chianti' wine. The family's three Gran Selezioni come from different altitudes and soils.

sites.name: Castello di Verrazzano
sites.text: Castle above Greve and family home of Giovanni da Verrazzano, the navigator who in 1524 was the first European to enter New York harbour. The estate makes Chianti Classico on 52 ha.

sites.name: Biondi-Santi Tenuta Greppo
sites.text: The birthplace of Brunello: the Greppo estate south of Montalcino where Clemente Santi and his grandson Ferruccio Biondi Santi isolated and bottled pure Sangiovese from the 1860s to 1888. Tancredi planted the oldest surviving plot here in 1936. The family sold a majority to Christopher Descours's EPI group in 2017. About 26 ha of vines in three sites.

sites.name: Case Basse (Soldera)
sites.text: Gianfranco Soldera bought this farm near Tavernelle, southwest of Montalcino, in 1972 and made uncompromising Sangiovese aged five years or more in large Slavonian oak, surrounded by his wife Graziella's garden of 1,500 old roses. On the night of 2 to 3 December 2012 a former employee opened the taps on ten casks, destroying six vintages; Soldera left the consorzio in 2013 and has since labelled the wine Toscana IGT. He died in 2019; the family continues.

sites.name: Poggio di Sotto
sites.text: Founded by Piero Palmucci near Castelnuovo dell'Abate and owned since 2011 by Claudio Tipa's ColleMassari group. About 20 ha of mostly south-facing vines at 200 to 440 m on clay, sand, gravel and galestro, looking toward Monte Amiata, give pale, fragrant, low-alcohol Brunello aged in large casks.

sites.name: Abbazia di Sant'Antimo
sites.text: A Romanesque abbey of pale travertine below Castelnuovo dell'Abate, said to have been founded by Charlemagne in 781. It gives its name to Montalcino's catch-all DOC, and Brunello vineyards run right up to its walls.

sites.name: Montosoli
sites.text: A hill just north of Montalcino town at about 300 to 350 m, regarded as the zone's finest north-facing cru, with galestro and sandstone. Altesino bottled the first single-vineyard Montosoli Brunello in 1975; Baricci, Caparzo (La Casa) and Canalicchio di Sopra also farm here.

sites.name: Castello Banfi
sites.text: The medieval Poggio alle Mura castle in southwest Montalcino, bought by the Italian-American Mariani brothers in 1978. Banfi planted on an industrial scale, researched Sangiovese clones and helped turn Brunello into an export brand; it also houses a glass museum.

sites.name: Il Poggione
sites.text: One of the oldest estates in Montalcino, founded by the Franceschi family in the 1890s, with about 125 ha around Sant'Angelo in Colle in the warm south of the zone. Its Brunello and Vigna Paganelli Riserva are textbook traditional wines.

sites.name: Lisini
sites.text: A family estate near Sant'Angelo in Colle, a founding member of the consorzio in 1967, famous for the Ugolaia single vineyard and for its tiny 'Prefillossero' plot of ungrafted, pre-phylloxera Sangiovese.

sites.name: Cerbaiona
sites.text: A small, high estate east of Montalcino at about 400 m, made famous by former airline pilot Diego Molinari from 1977 and sold to American investors in 2015. Its Brunello is dense and long-lived.

sites.name: Col d'Orcia
sites.text: A large organic estate on the southern slope toward the Orcia river, owned by the Cinzano family since 1973. Its Poggio al Vento Riserva comes from a single vineyard at about 350 m, and it still makes Moscadello di Montalcino.

sites.name: Tenuta San Guido (Sassicaia)
sites.text: Home of Sassicaia, between the Via Aurelia and the hills of Bolgheri. Mario Incisa della Rocchetta planted Cabernet here in the 1940s, and the 1968 vintage, released in 1971, began Italy's Bordeaux-blend revolution. The estate is also a horse-breeding farm (the champion Ribot was co-owned by the marchese) and includes a WWF wetland reserve, the Padule di Bolgheri.

sites.name: Viale dei Cipressi
sites.text: The five-kilometre avenue of cypresses from the oratory of San Guido on the Via Aurelia to the village of Bolgheri, immortalised by Giosuè Carducci's 1874 poem *Davanti San Guido*. It runs past Sassicaia's vineyards and is the classic approach to the appellation.

sites.name: Tenuta dell'Ornellaia
sites.text: Founded in 1981 by Lodovico Antinori (first vintage 1985), now owned by the Frescobaldi family. Ornellaia, a Bolgheri Superiore blend of Cabernet, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot, is one of Italy's most collected wines. Masseto, the pure Merlot from a hill of blue Pliocene clay on the estate, first made in 1986, became so famous that it got its own winery and brand in 2019.

sites.name: Grattamacco
sites.text: The second estate to bottle wine in Bolgheri after Sassicaia (from 1977), on a hilltop at about 100 to 200 m south of Castagneto Carducci. Its Bolgheri Superiore blends Cabernet with Sangiovese, a local signature.

sites.name: Le Macchiole
sites.text: Founded by Eugenio Campolmi in 1983 and run by his widow Cinzia Merli, Le Macchiole proved that Bolgheri could make great varietal wines: Paleo (pure Cabernet Franc since 2001), Messorio (Merlot) and Scrio (Syrah).

sites.name: Castello di Bolgheri
sites.text: The red-brick castle at the gate of Bolgheri village, at the end of the Viale dei Cipressi, seat of the della Gherardesca counts who once owned most of the land here. The family estate still makes Bolgheri Superiore.

sites.name: Tua Rita
sites.text: Rita Tua and Virgilio Bisti planted vines at Notri near Suvereto in 1984 as a hobby; their Redigaffi Merlot (first vintage 1994) became a cult wine and made Suvereto's name.

sites.name: Tenuta di Capezzana
sites.text: The Contini Bonacossi family estate that saved Carmignano: Count Ugo Contini Bonacossi lobbied for the DOC in the 1970s. Archives on the estate record wine here in 804. Its Villa di Capezzana and Trefiano are reference Carmignanos, and its Vin Santo is outstanding.

sites.name: Villa Medicea La Ferdinanda (Artimino)
sites.text: The 'villa of the hundred chimneys', built for Grand Duke Ferdinando I de' Medici in 1596 above the Barco Reale hunting park. It is part of the UNESCO Medici Villas listing and overlooks the Carmignano vineyards.

sites.name: San Gimignano
sites.text: The hill town of medieval towers (14 of about 72 survive), a UNESCO site, surrounded by the vineyards of Italy's first DOC, Vernaccia di San Gimignano (1966). The town's Vernaccia wine museum sits in the Rocca di Montestaffoli.

sites.name: Montenidoli
sites.text: Elisabetta Fagiuoli's estate west of San Gimignano, on fossil-rich marine sands and limestone, farmed without chemicals since 1965. Its long-aged Vernaccias (Fiore, Carato) showed what the grape can do.

sites.name: Fattoria Selvapiana
sites.text: A former summer residence of the bishops of Florence in Rùfina, owned by the Giuntini family since 1827. Its Bucerchiale Chianti Rùfina Riserva, a single-vineyard wine since 1979, is one of the longest-lived Chiantis.

sites.name: Castello di Nipozzano
sites.text: A Frescobaldi castle in the Rùfina subzone; the family has records of selling wine to Henry VIII and has farmed here since the 19th century. Montesodi, from a single plot, is its top Rùfina.

sites.name: Avignonesi (Le Capezzine)
sites.text: Avignonesi, based at Le Capezzine near Valiano, helped revive Vino Nobile in the 1980s and is famous for its Vin Santo and Occhio di Pernice. Owned by Virginie Saverys since 2009 and converted to biodynamics.

sites.name: Poderi Boscarelli
sites.text: The De Ferrari family estate at Cervognano, founded in 1962, one of the quiet benchmarks of Vino Nobile; its Nocio dei Boscarelli single vineyard and Pieve Cervognano wines show the area's elegance.

sites.name: Cantine Contucci
sites.text: An ancient family cellar beneath Palazzo Contucci on Montepulciano's main square, where wine has been aged for centuries in vaulted rooms cut into the rock. The Contucci family has been in Montepulciano for about a thousand years.

sites.name: Tempio di San Biagio
sites.text: Antonio da Sangallo the Elder's Renaissance church (1518 to 1545) below the walls of Montepulciano, set among vineyards. It gives its name to the San Biagio pieve, one of the 12 Vino Nobile UGAs.

sites.name: Fattoria Le Pupille
sites.text: Elisabetta Geppetti's estate at Istia d'Ombrone, a leading name in Morellino and the Maremma, known for the Saffredi blend first made in 1987.

sites.name: Scansano
sites.text: The hill village (about 500 m) that names Morellino di Scansano. It was the summer capital of the Grosseto administration in the 19th century, when officials fled the malarial coast.

sites.name: Castello Pomino (Frescobaldi)
sites.text: The Frescobaldi estate at Pomino, where the family planted Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco and Pinot Nero in 1855 at about 700 m. Its Benefizio was one of Italy's first barrique-fermented whites.

sites.name: Pieve Ascianello
sites.class: Pieve (UGA), Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG
sites.text: Ascianello is one of the 12 Pievi (UGAs) of Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, named after the old parish churches of the territory. From the 2021 vintage a Vino Nobile Pieve Ascianello must be at least 85% Sangiovese from the bottler's own vines (15 years or older) in this pieve, aged three years.

sites.class: Pieve (UGA), Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG
sites.text: Badia is one of the 12 Pievi (UGAs) of Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, named after the old parish churches of the territory. From the 2021 vintage a Vino Nobile Pieve Badia must be at least 85% Sangiovese from the bottler's own vines (15 years or older) in this pieve, aged three years.
