sites.class: Pieve (UGA), Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG
sites.text: Valiano is one of the 12 Pievi (UGAs) of Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, named after the old parish churches of the territory. From the 2021 vintage a Vino Nobile Pieve Valiano must be at least 85% Sangiovese from the bottler's own vines (15 years or older) in this pieve, aged three years.

sites.name: Montefalco
sites.text: The 'ringhiera dell'Umbria' (balcony of Umbria), a walled hill town at about 470 m with views over the Spoleto valley, Assisi and Spello. Sagrantino grows on the slopes all around; the town's Settimana Enologica has celebrated the wine since 1980.

sites.name: Arnaldo Caprai
sites.text: The estate that made dry Sagrantino famous. Founded in 1971 and run by Marco Caprai since 1988, it worked with the University of Milan on clonal selection and released the landmark 25 Anni (first vintage 1993) to mark the estate's 25th year.

sites.name: Paolo Bea
sites.text: A family farm at Cerrete below Montefalco where Giampiero Bea and his family make long-macerated, unfiltered Sagrantino (Pagliaro, Cerrete) in a cellar he designed himself, half buried in the hill. A reference for traditional and natural Umbrian wine.

sites.name: Lungarotti and MUVIT wine museum
sites.text: The Museo del Vino (MUVIT) in Palazzo Graziani-Baglioni in Torgiano, opened in 1974 by Giorgio and Maria Grazia Lungarotti, holds Etruscan and Roman vessels, majolica, engravings and pressing equipment covering 5,000 years of wine. The Lungarotti winery, maker of Rubesco, is on the edge of the village.

sites.name: Orvieto underground cellars
sites.text: The city of Orvieto stands on a tufa butte riddled with more than a thousand Etruscan and medieval caves, wells and cellars. The constant cool temperature made them ideal for slow fermentation of the old sweet Orvieto; several are open to visitors.

sites.name: Castello della Sala
sites.text: A 14th-century castle north of Orvieto owned by the Antinori family since 1940. Here Renzo Cotarella and Piero Antinori created Cervaro della Sala (first vintage 1985), a barrel-fermented Chardonnay with a little Grechetto that became one of Italy's most famous whites, and the botrytised Muffato della Sala.

sites.name: Palazzone
sites.text: A family estate at Rocca Ripesena just west of Orvieto, in a 13th-century building that once sheltered pilgrims to Rome. Giovanni Dubini's Campo del Guardiano is a single-vineyard Orvieto Classico Superiore released after a year or more in bottle and known to age 20 years.

sites.name: Cupramontana
sites.text: The self-styled capital of Verdicchio, a hill town at about 500 m in the heart of the Classico zone. Its grape festival, the Sagra dell'Uva, dates from 1928, among the oldest in Italy, and it hosts the Museo Internazionale dell'Etichetta, a museum of wine labels.

sites.name: Villa Bucci
sites.text: The Bucci family estate near Ostra Vetere, with about 25 ha of organic Verdicchio spread across five sites around Montecarotto and Serra de' Conti, some planted in the 1960s. Ampelio Bucci and oenologist Giorgio Grai made Villa Bucci Riserva, aged in old large casks, a benchmark for long-lived Verdicchio.

sites.name: Fazi Battaglia (Castelplanio)
sites.text: The winery that launched Verdicchio's green amphora bottle in 1953, a design that sold the wine worldwide. It is now part of the Bertani Domains group.

sites.name: Matelica
sites.text: A small town in the upper Esino valley, the centre of the Verdicchio di Matelica zone, closed off from the sea by hills so its whites are more acidic and saline.

sites.name: Monte Conero
sites.text: A 572 m limestone headland covered in Mediterranean scrub, the only promontory on the Adriatic coast between Trieste and the Gargano. Montepulciano vineyards cover its lower slopes toward Sirolo, Camerano and Ancona.

sites.name: Moroder
sites.text: A family farm in the Conero park at Montacuto, owned by the Moroder family since the 1800s. Its Dorico Cònero Riserva helped establish the DOCG.

sites.name: Morro d'Alba
sites.text: A walled village whose ramparts include a covered walkway (La Scarpa) around the old town; the home of the rose-scented Lacrima grape.

sites.name: Serrapetrona
sites.text: A mountain village at about 470 m in the province of Macerata, the only home of the triple-fermented red sparkling Vernaccia di Serrapetrona. Its growers dry part of the Vernaccia Nera crop on racks in lofts through the winter before adding it to the base wine.

sites.name: Offida
sites.text: A hill town known for bobbin lace and the Gothic church of Santa Maria della Rocca, centre of the Offida DOCG and of the Pecorino revival.

sites.name: Frascati
sites.text: A hill town 20 km from Rome, famous for its papal and princely villas (Villa Aldobrandini, Villa Torlonia) and as the source of Rome's everyday white. Its *fraschette*, taverns serving porchetta with jugs of local wine, keep the old Roman habit alive.

sites.name: Castel de Paolis
sites.text: An estate near Grottaferrata where Giulio Santarelli and the late professor Attilio Scienza replanted in the 1980s with dozens of varieties to study the volcanic soils; its Vigna Adriana white raised the ceiling for the area.

sites.name: Basilica di San Flaviano (Montefiascone)
sites.text: A two-storey Romanesque church below Montefiascone that holds the tombstone of the legendary German bishop Johannes Defuk (or Fugger), who in the Est! Est!! Est!!! story died in 1113 after drinking too much of the local wine.

sites.name: Piglio
sites.text: A hill town in the Ciociaria at about 620 m, centre of Lazio's only red DOCG, Cesanese del Piglio. Its vineyards lie on red clay and limestone slopes facing the Sacco valley, and its September grape festival dates back decades.

sites.name: Olevano Romano
sites.text: A hill town east of Rome painted by 19th-century German Romantic artists; today the home of the Cesanese revival led by Damiano Ciolli.

sites.name: Valentini (Loreto Aprutino)
sites.text: The Valentini family estate at Loreto Aprutino, in the hills west of Pescara. Edoardo Valentini (1934 to 2006) made Trebbiano, Cerasuolo and Montepulciano that are among Italy's most sought-after wines; his son Francesco Paolo continues, bottling only a fraction of the crop.

sites.name: Emidio Pepe
sites.text: Founded in 1964 at Torano Nuovo by Emidio Pepe, whose wines are destemmed by hand, foot-trodden, fermented with native yeasts and aged in bottle for years; the estate keeps a library of hundreds of thousands of old bottles, decanted by hand before release.

sites.name: Abbazia di San Clemente a Casauria
sites.text: A Benedictine abbey founded in 871 by Emperor Louis II, rebuilt in the 12th century, in the Pescara valley. It gives its name to the Casauria DOCG (2025), and Zaccagnini's San Clemente Montepulciano is named for it.

sites.name: Cataldi Madonna (Ofena)
sites.text: In the Tirino valley at Ofena, nicknamed 'the oven of Abruzzo' for its daytime heat, with cold nights from the Gran Sasso. Luigi Cataldi Madonna makes Pecorino, Cerasuolo (Piè delle Vigne) and Montepulciano (Tonì) in the Alto Tirino subzone.

sites.name: Torre dei Beati
sites.text: An organic estate at Loreto Aprutino founded by Adriana Galasso and Fausto Albanesi in 1999, known for Mazzamurello Montepulciano and Giocheremo con i Fiori Trebbiano.

sites.name: Tollo
sites.text: The town (Latin *Tullum*) whose commune alone forms the Terre Tollesi DOCG; its large cooperative, Cantina Tollo, is one of Abruzzo's biggest producers.

sites.name: Di Majo Norante
sites.text: The Di Majo Norante family estate at Campomarino near the Adriatic, Molise's pioneer quality winery and an early champion of Tintilia, Aglianico (Contado) and the Ramitello blend.

sites.name: Mastroberardino (Atripalda)
sites.text: The family winery in Atripalda, run for ten generations, that kept Irpinia's grapes alive. Antonio Mastroberardino bottled Taurasi, Fiano and Greco when they were nearly forgotten; the 1968 Taurasi Riserva became a legend. The historic cellar has frescoes celebrating wine.

sites.name: Pompeii vineyards (Foro Boario)
sites.text: Inside the excavated city of Pompeii, Mastroberardino and the archaeological park have replanted about 1.5 ha in 15 plots where Roman vineyards stood, including the Foro Boario, identified by root cavities in the ash. The project was conceived in the mid-1990s; the Villa dei Misteri wine (Piedirosso and Sciascinoso, with Aglianico added from 2007) has been made since the early 2000s, with proceeds supporting research and the site.

sites.name: Villa dei Misteri
sites.text: A suburban villa outside Pompeii's walls, famous for its fresco cycle and for the wine press found in its farm wing, evidence of the villa's working winery. It names the wine made from Pompeii's replanted Roman vineyards.

sites.name: Taurasi
sites.text: The hill village above the Calore valley whose name was given to the DOCG. Its castle hosts an enoteca regionale.

sites.name: Montemarano
sites.text: A high (about 820 m) Taurasi commune with some of the coldest vineyards in the DOCG, home to Salvatore Molettieri's Vigna Cinque Querce and known for slow-ripening, acidic Aglianico harvested into November.

sites.name: Lapio
sites.text: A hill commune above the Calore valley regarded as one of the best sites for Fiano, with high, steep slopes of clay and limestone; Colli di Lapio and Rocca del Principe are based here.

sites.name: Tufo
sites.text: The village of Greco di Tufo, built over the old sulphur mines once run by the Di Marzo family; the sulphur seams are often blamed, or credited, for the flinty edge of local Greco.

sites.name: Feudi di San Gregorio
sites.text: Founded in 1986 at Sorbo Serpico by the Capaldo and Ercolino families, Feudi drove the Irpinian revival of the 1990s with modern Fiano, Greco and Taurasi and a striking winery designed by Hikaru Mori.

sites.name: Monte Massico
sites.text: The 813 m ridge between Mondragone and Sessa Aurunca that the Romans called Mons Massicus. Its slopes were the Ager Falernus, source of Falernian, the most famous wine of antiquity.

sites.name: Villa Matilde
sites.text: Founded in the 1960s at Cellole by the lawyer Francesco Paolo Avallone, who set out to rediscover the grapes of ancient Falernian, Villa Matilde was the first to bottle Falerno del Massico seriously.

sites.name: Marisa Cuomo (Furore)
sites.text: A cellar dug into the cliff at Furore on the Amalfi Coast, with vines on terraces from sea level to 550 m. Fiorduva, from Fenile, Ginestra and Ripoli, made Furore famous.

sites.name: Fiordo di Furore
sites.text: A narrow gorge where a torrent meets the sea under a road bridge, the most dramatic spot of the Furore subzone; terraced vines rise above it.

sites.name: Pithekoussai (Lacco Ameno)
sites.text: The site of the first Greek colony in the western Mediterranean, founded on Ischia around 770 BC. A tomb here held Nestor's cup, a drinking cup with a verse promising that whoever drinks from it will be seized by desire, one of the oldest Greek inscriptions; it is in the Villa Arbusto museum.

sites.name: Casa d'Ambra
sites.text: The oldest winery on Ischia (1888), based at Forio, which kept Biancolella and Forastera alive. Its Frassitelli vineyard on Monte Epomeo is reached by monorail.

sites.name: Montevetrano
sites.text: Silvia Imparato's estate near San Cipriano Picentino, whose Montevetrano blend (Cabernet, Merlot and Aglianico), first made in 1991 with Riccardo Cotarella, was one of the first southern Italian wines to win cult status abroad; it is sold as IGT Colli di Salerno.

sites.name: Mustilli
sites.text: The family estate in Sant'Agata de' Goti where Leonardo Mustilli bottled the first varietal Falanghina in 1979, starting the grape's modern career. Its cellars run under the old town.

sites.name: Museo della Civiltà del Vino Primitivo
sites.text: A wine museum in the old cellars of the Produttori di Manduria cooperative (founded 1932), with cement vats, tools and the history of Primitivo.

sites.name: Gianfranco Fino
sites.text: Gianfranco Fino and Simona Natale began in 2004 with old bush vines near Manduria; their Es Primitivo, from alberello vines 50 to 90 years old, became Puglia's most celebrated red.

sites.name: Gioia del Colle
sites.text: A town on the Murge plateau with a Norman-Swabian castle, where the priest Francesco Filippo Indellicati selected and named the Primitivo grape around 1799.

sites.name: Polvanera
sites.text: Filippo Cassano's estate near Gioia del Colle, with cellars dug into the limestone, making unoaked Primitivo at different alcohol levels from old vines.

sites.name: Leone de Castris
sites.text: Founded in 1665, the Leone de Castris winery in Salice Salentino bottled Five Roses in 1943, widely cited as Italy's first bottled rosé, made at the request of an American general for his troops.

sites.name: Cosimo Taurino
sites.text: The Taurino family estate at Guagnano, whose late-harvest Negroamaro Patriglione and Notarpanaro helped bring the Salento to world attention in the 1980s.

sites.name: Castel del Monte
sites.text: Frederick II's octagonal castle (c. 1240) on a hill of the Murge, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with eight octagonal towers. It gives its name to the DOC and its three DOCGs.

sites.name: Rivera
sites.text: The De Corato family estate near Andria, whose Il Falcone (since 1971) and Puer Apuliae made Nero di Troia known beyond Puglia.

sites.name: Locorotondo
sites.text: A circular white town on a hill above the Valle d'Itria and its trulli, one of the 'most beautiful villages of Italy', home of a light Verdeca-based white.

sites.name: Monte Vulture
sites.text: An extinct stratovolcano (1,326 m) whose crater holds the two Monticchio lakes. Its ash and tuff soils carry the vineyards of Aglianico del Vulture down the eastern flank.

sites.name: Barile cave cellars (Sheshë)
sites.text: On the edge of Barile, a district of wine caves (the Sheshë, from the Albanian for 'plain') dug into volcanic tuff by Arbëreshë settlers from the 15th century. Pier Paolo Pasolini filmed scenes of The Gospel According to Matthew here in 1964.

sites.name: Paternoster
sites.text: Founded in 1925 in Barile, one of the historic houses of the Vulture; its Don Anselmo Aglianico is a long-standing benchmark. Owned by Tommasi since 2016.

sites.name: Elena Fucci (Contrada Solagna del Titolo)
sites.text: Elena Fucci's family vineyard at about 600 m in Contrada Solagna del Titolo above Barile, the source of Titolo, one of the most acclaimed Aglianicos of the 21st century.

sites.name: Cantine del Notaio
sites.text: Gerardo Giuratrabocchetti's winery in Rionero in Vulture, which ages its Aglianico in 17th-century Franciscan caves cut into the volcanic tuff in the town centre, where the temperature stays cool and steady all year.

sites.name: Venosa
sites.text: The Roman Venusia, birthplace of the poet Horace (65 BC), who wrote often about wine. It lies on the eastern edge of the Aglianico del Vulture zone.

sites.name: Librandi (Rocca di Neto and Cirò Marina)
sites.text: Founded in 1953 by Antonio and Nicodemo Librandi in Cirò Marina, Librandi became Calabria's flagship producer. Its Duca Sanfelice Cirò Rosso Riserva and Gravello (Gaglioppo-Cabernet) set the standard, and its experimental vineyard at Rocca di Neto holds a collection of some 200 Calabrian varieties.

sites.name: Cirò
sites.text: The hill town above the Ionian coast that names Calabria's best-known wine and, since 2025, its first DOCG. It was the home of the 16th-century astronomer Luigi Lilio, author of the Gregorian calendar.

sites.name: Punta Alice (Krimisa)
sites.text: The cape north of Cirò Marina where the Greek temple of Apollo Aleo stood; according to local tradition, its wine (Krimisa) was given to Olympic victors.

sites.name: Bianco
sites.text: A small town on the Ionian coast near Capo Bruzzano, close to the ancient Greek city of Locri, home of the sweet Greco di Bianco passito, made from grapes dried on cane mats in the sun.

sites.name: Contrada Rampante
sites.text: One of the highest contrade on the north slope, roughly 740 to 1,000 m above Solicchiata, partly above the old DOC limit. Its sandy, stony lava and old bush vines give some of Etna's most delicate, high-toned Nerello. Passopisciaro's 'Contrada R' and Pietradolce's Archineri and Vigna Barbagalli (pre-phylloxera vines at about 900 m) come from here. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Calderara Sottana
sites.text: A lower-north-slope contrada between Randazzo and Passopisciaro, at about 600 to 700 m, on stony lava. Tenuta delle Terre Nere's Calderara Sottana is a benchmark, and its pre-phylloxera 'La Vigna di Don Peppino', from ungrafted vines over 140 years old, comes from here. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Feudo di Mezzo
sites.text: A central-north contrada near Passopisciaro at roughly 650 to 700 m, with deep, fine volcanic soils and some very old vines. Terre Nere (Il Quadro delle Rose), Planeta, Graci and Pietradolce all bottle it. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Santo Spirito
sites.text: Upslope from Passopisciaro at about 700 to 800 m, on terraces of older, weathered lava. Terre Nere's Santo Spirito is one of its principal crus, and Passopisciaro and Pietradolce also farm here. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Sciara Nuova
sites.text: Sciara means lava flow: this contrada sits on a 17th-century flow in Randazzo at roughly 800 to 850 m, with coarse, young, stony soil. Passopisciaro's 'Contrada S' and Tasca's Tascante Sciaranuova come from it. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Barbabecchi
sites.text: High above Solicchiata at about 870 to 910 m, Barbabecchi is home to ungrafted Nerello planted around 1910 that give Frank Cornelissen's Magma, one of Etna's most famous and most expensive wines. The soil is lean volcanic sand and basalt gravel. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Guardiola
sites.text: Rising above Passopisciaro to about 1,000 m, Guardiola is one of the highest red-wine contrade on Etna, on the edge of a 1947 lava flow. Passopisciaro's 'Contrada G' and Terre Nere's Guardiola are both from here. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Monte Serra
sites.text: A small extinct cone on the southeastern slope at Viagrande, at about 500 m, where Benanti, based in the village, has its Monte Serra vineyard. Warmer and closer to the sea than the north slope, it gives rounder Nerello. (Commune: Viagrande.)

sites.name: Contrada Arcurìa
sites.text: A north-slope contrada near Passopisciaro at about 600 to 700 m; Graci's winery and its Arcurìa Rosso and Bianco take their name from it, and Passopisciaro uses its fruit in Passorosso. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Feudo
sites.text: A Randazzo contrada at about 700 m where Giuseppe Russo (Girolamo Russo) makes 'Feudo' from old vines on terraces near Montelaguardia. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Porcaria
sites.class: Unofficial contrada (not in the Etna DOC list)
sites.text: A lower north-slope contrada near Passopisciaro at about 650 m, on deep, rich old lava, giving one of the fuller, darker contrada wines. Porcaria is not among the 133 contrade in the 2022 Etna rules, so its name cannot appear on an Etna DOC label; Passopisciaro sells its 'Contrada P' as Terre Siciliane IGT. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Chiappemacine
sites.class: Unofficial contrada (not in the Etna DOC list)
sites.text: The lowest of Passopisciaro's contrade, at about 550 m toward the Alcantara valley, with clay-richer, deeper soil and a warmer site; its 'Contrada C' is the most opulent of the set. Like Porcaria it is missing from the 2022 list of official contrade, and the wine is sold as Terre Siciliane IGT. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Pietra Marina
sites.text: A contrada near Verzella, below Solicchiata. It should not be confused with Benanti's famous Pietra Marina Etna Bianco Superiore, a brand name for Carricante from Milo on the east slope. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada San Lorenzo
sites.text: On the northwest edge of the DOC beyond Randazzo, San Lorenzo is considered the coldest contrada, on lava 15,000 to 60,000 years old. Terre Nere and Girolamo Russo bottle it. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Calderara
sites.text: The contrada around the old Calderara station on the Circumetnea railway between Randazzo and Passopisciaro, next to Calderara Sottana, and home to Terre Nere's cellar. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Zottorinotto
sites.text: A contrada near Solicchiata at about 650 to 750 m, on dark volcanic sand, worked by Pietradolce and Frank Cornelissen among others. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Muganazzi
sites.text: A Castiglione contrada at about 650 m between Passopisciaro and Solicchiata; Graci and Fessina have vines here. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Verzella
sites.text: A hamlet and contrada below Solicchiata near the Alcantara valley, at about 550 to 650 m; its older vineyards are among the warmer north-slope sites. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Moscamento
sites.text: A Castiglione contrada near Rovittello in the northeast, on old lava terraces at about 650 to 700 m; the estate Moscamento 1896 takes its name from it. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Marchesa
sites.text: A north-slope contrada near Passopisciaro at about 600 to 700 m, worked by small growers and bottled by Graci and others. (Commune: Castiglione di Sicilia.)

sites.name: Contrada Montelaguardia
sites.text: A hamlet and contrada east of Randazzo along the old Bourbon road, with terraces at about 700 to 800 m. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Allegracore
sites.text: A Randazzo contrada just outside the medieval town, on the northern edge of the DOC, at about 700 m. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Croce Monaci
sites.text: A high Randazzo contrada with some vines said to be 130 years old or more, cited among Etna's oldest plantings. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Campo Re
sites.text: A contrada on the western side of Randazzo, at roughly 700 to 750 m, near the northern limit of the vineyard zone. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Taccione
sites.text: A contrada near Montelaguardia in Randazzo, at about 700 m on the north slope, home to old bush-vine vineyards on stony lava worked by small local growers. (Commune: Randazzo.)

sites.name: Contrada Caselle
sites.text: An east-slope contrada in Milo, at about 850 m, facing the sea and catching plenty of rain: classic Carricante country. Pietradolce's Archineri Bianco and Vigna Sant'Andrea come from 130 to 150-year-old Carricante here, and Benanti's Pietra Marina draws on Milo fruit. (Commune: Milo.)

sites.name: Contrada Rinazzo
sites.text: A Milo contrada at 700 to 800 m on the east slope, source of Etna Bianco Superiore Carricante. (Commune: Milo.)

sites.name: Contrada Fornazzo
sites.text: A hamlet and contrada high in Milo that was nearly overrun by the 1979 lava flow; its Carricante vineyards are among the coolest on the east slope. (Commune: Milo.)

sites.name: Contrada Monte Ilice
sites.text: A small extinct cone on the southeastern slope near Trecastagni, at about 750 to 800 m, with very old vines on its sides. (Commune: Trecastagni.)

sites.name: Contrada Cavaliere
sites.text: The only contrada of Santa Maria di Licodia, on the southwestern slope at about 900 to 1,000 m. Benanti's Contrada Cavaliere Bianco and Rosso come from here, warm by day but very cold by night. (Commune: Santa Maria di Licodia.)

sites.name: Benanti (Viagrande)
sites.text: Giuseppe Benanti restarted his family's 19th-century winery at Viagrande in 1988, working with the oenologist Salvo Foti, and proved that Etna could make world-class wine at a time when almost nobody bottled it. Its Pietra Marina (Carricante from Milo) is the reference Etna Bianco Superiore.

sites.name: Barone di Villagrande (Milo)
sites.text: The Nicolosi family has made wine at Milo on the east slope since 1727. Its Etna Bianco Superiore, from Carricante on terraces above the sea, is one of the longest-running examples of the style.

sites.name: Tenuta delle Terre Nere
sites.text: Founded in 2002 by Marco de Grazia, the American-born importer who championed Etna as 'the Burgundy of the Mediterranean'. About 45 to 50 ha across nine north-slope contrade at 600 to 1,000 m, bottled separately as Calderara Sottana, Feudo di Mezzo, Santo Spirito, Guardiola and San Lorenzo, plus a pre-phylloxera cuvée.

sites.name: Passopisciaro (Vini Franchetti)
sites.text: Founded in 2000 by Andrea Franchetti (of Tenuta di Trinoro in Tuscany), who restored abandoned terraces at about 1,000 m. Since 2008 it bottles separate contrade (C, G, P, R, S: Chiappemacine, Guardiola, Porcaria, Rampante, Sciaranuova), one of the first projects to show Etna's site differences.

sites.name: Frank Cornelissen
sites.text: The Belgian former wine broker settled in Solicchiata in 2001 and makes radical low-intervention wines without sulphur or wood, fermented in tubs and aged in buried terracotta and fibreglass. Magma, from ungrafted vines in Barbabecchi, and Munjebel are cult wines.

sites.name: Pietradolce (Solicchiata)
sites.text: Founded in 2005 by Michele Faro of a family of plant nurserymen, Pietradolce farms 30 ha on the north slope, 11 of them pre-phylloxera bush vines 80 to 120 years old, and 2 ha of very old Carricante at Caselle in Milo.

sites.name: Cantine Florio (Marsala)
sites.text: The baglio founded by Vincenzo Florio in 1833 on the seafront of Marsala, between the English houses of Woodhouse and Ingham. Its vaulted cellars, built of local tufa, hold casks of Marsala Vergine and are among the great wine buildings of Italy. Florio later absorbed its English rivals.

sites.name: Marco De Bartoli (Samperi)
sites.text: The baglio at Contrada Samperi where Marco De Bartoli (1944 to 2011) revived the unfortified, solera-aged *perpetuum* that predates English Marsala, bottled as Vecchio Samperi, and made Marsala Superiore and Vergine of uncompromising quality. His children continue, also on Pantelleria (Bukkuram).

sites.name: Mozia and the Whitaker Museum
sites.text: The island of San Pantaleo in the Stagnone lagoon, site of the Phoenician city of Motya, was bought by Joseph 'Pip' Whitaker of the Ingham-Whitaker Marsala dynasty, who excavated it from the early 1900s. The museum holds the marble Youth of Motya; the island also has a Grillo vineyard managed by Tasca d'Almerita.

sites.name: Donnafugata (Khamma, Pantelleria)
sites.text: Donnafugata's Pantelleria estate at Khamma, where it makes Ben Ryé Passito from Zibibbo in walled hollows and dry-stone terraces. The family also built a walled garden (*giardino pantesco*) restoration project with FAI nearby.

sites.name: Bukkuram (Pantelleria)
sites.text: The contrada and estate in southern Pantelleria where Marco De Bartoli began making Bukkuram Passito in 1984, one of the reference wines of the island.

sites.name: Pantelleria alberello landscape
sites.text: Pantelleria's low, head-trained Zibibbo bushes, planted in hollows and protected by dry-stone walls, were inscribed by UNESCO in 2014 as Intangible Cultural Heritage, the first agricultural practice ever listed. The Khamma and Ghirlanda areas are good places to see them.

sites.name: Hauner (Salina)
sites.text: Carlo Hauner, a Milanese designer and painter, moved to Salina in the 1960s and revived Malvasia delle Lipari, which had nearly vanished after phylloxera. The family winery at Lingua continues.

sites.name: Capofaro (Salina)
sites.text: Tasca d'Almerita's resort-vineyard around the lighthouse of Capo Faro on Salina, with Malvasia vines running to the cliff edge and Stromboli on the horizon.

sites.name: COS (Vittoria)
sites.text: Founded in 1980 by three friends (Cilia, Occhipinti, Strano), COS became a pioneer of biodynamic farming and of amphora ageing in Sicily (Pithos, from 2000), and a reference for Cerasuolo di Vittoria.

sites.name: Arianna Occhipinti
sites.text: Arianna Occhipinti, niece of COS co-founder Giusto Occhipinti, started with one hectare in 2004; her Frappato and Il Siccagno Nero d'Avola made her one of Italy's best-known natural winemakers.

sites.name: Palari (Santo Stefano Briga)
sites.text: Salvatore Geraci's family estate in the hills south of Messina, whose Palari Faro saved the DOC from extinction in the 1990s.

sites.name: Planeta (Ulmo, Sambuca di Sicilia)
sites.text: The Planeta family's first estate, on Lake Arancio near Sambuca di Sicilia, where the 1995 vintage and the Ulmo barrel-fermented Chardonnay launched one of the leading names of the new Sicily. The family now has wineries in Menfi, Vittoria, Noto, Etna and Capo Milazzo.

sites.name: Monte Kronio (Sciacca)
sites.text: Analysis published in 2017 of residues in Copper Age storage jars from a cave on Monte Kronio found tartaric acid and other compounds consistent with wine, dated to about 4000 BC, among the oldest evidence of winemaking in Italy.

sites.name: Duca di Salaparuta (Casteldaccia)
sites.text: The Duke of Salaparuta founded the Corvo winery at Casteldaccia near Palermo in 1824; Corvo became Sicily's most famous wine brand, and the Duca Enrico (1984, Nero d'Avola) was one of the first great Nero d'Avolas.

sites.name: Tenuta Regaleali (Tasca d'Almerita)
sites.text: The Tasca d'Almerita family estate since 1830, several hundred hectares of vineyards on the high inland plateau between Sclafani Bagni and Vallelunga, at 400 to 900 m. Rosso del Conte (from 1970, mostly Nero d'Avola and Perricone) helped define modern Sicilian red.

sites.name: Mamoiada
sites.text: A Barbagia village at about 650 m famous for its masked carnival (the Mamuthones) and for dozens of tiny family Cannonau producers on granite sands, such as Sedilesu and Montisci.

sites.name: Giuseppe Sedilesu (Mamoiada)
sites.text: A family winery in the centre of Mamoiada, one of the first to bottle the village's Cannonau in the 2000s, from old bush vines on granite.

sites.name: Oliena
sites.text: A village below the limestone wall of Monte Corrasi, home of 'Nepente di Oliena', the Cannonau that Gabriele D'Annunzio praised in 1909, and of the Cantina di Oliena cooperative.

sites.name: Jerzu
sites.text: The 'city of wine' of the Ogliastra, built on a slope below limestone tacchi; its Antichi Poderi di Jerzu cooperative makes most of the Jerzu subzone Cannonau.

sites.name: Capo Ferrato
sites.text: The southeastern cape near Muravera that names the Capo Ferrato subzone of Cannonau di Sardegna, the warmest of the three.

sites.name: Argiolas (Serdiana)
sites.text: The Argiolas family winery at Serdiana in the Trexenta hills north of Cagliari. With Giacomo Tachis it created Turriga (first vintage 1988), a Cannonau-led blend that became Sardinia's most famous red.

sites.name: Cantina di Santadi
sites.text: The cooperative of Santadi in the Sulcis, transformed under president Antonello Pilloni and consultant Giacomo Tachis into a quality leader, with Terre Brune (Carignano, from 1984) and Rocca Rubia.

sites.name: Sella & Mosca
sites.text: Founded in 1899 by the Piedmontese engineer Erminio Sella and lawyer Edgardo Mosca, who cleared scrubland near Alghero and planted one of the largest single vineyards in Europe. Its land holds the Anghelu Ruju necropolis, a pre-Nuragic cemetery of rock-cut tombs (about 3000 BC) found in 1903 while planting vines.

sites.name: Cantina Gallura (Tempio Pausania)
sites.text: The cooperative of Tempio Pausania, founded in 1956, one of the reference producers of Vermentino di Gallura from granite vineyards in the highlands.

sites.name: Capichera (Arzachena)
sites.text: The Ragnedda family estate near Arzachena, inland from the Costa Smeralda, which from the 1980s made late-harvested, barrel-aged Vermentino that challenged ideas of what the grape could be (bottled for years outside the DOCG).

sites.name: Contini (Cabras)
sites.text: Founded in 1898 by Salvatore Contini in Cabras, by the lagoon west of Oristano, the leading house for flor-aged Vernaccia di Oristano, with old casks dating back decades.

sites.name: Sa Osa (Cabras)
sites.text: A Nuragic settlement near Cabras where a well yielded thousands of waterlogged grape seeds dated to about 1300 to 1100 BC, some identified as cultivated, early evidence of viticulture in Sardinia.

sites.name: Bosa
sites.text: A colourful town on the Temo river below the Malaspina castle, centre of the Malvasia di Bosa DOC, whose vineyards climb the Planargia terraces nearby.
